parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term 'delegation'.
parts.answer: Passing authority (the power to make decisions or carry out a task) from a manager to a subordinate, while the manager keeps overall responsibility.
parts.working: 1 mark: passing authority/power to complete a task down the hierarchy to a subordinate; 1 mark: manager still accountable/retains ultimate responsibility.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one benefit to the manager of a 120-room hotel in Murree of delegating tasks to department supervisors.
parts.answer: The manager is freed from routine work (e.g. drawing up housekeeping rotas), so can spend time on strategic issues such as winning conference bookings in the off-season. Also accept: supervisors know their areas better so decisions are quicker; supervisors are motivated and developed for promotion.
parts.working: 1 mark for knowledge of the term/concept; up to 2 marks for explaining it in the context of the business (application). e.g. benefit identified (time freed / faster decisions / motivation) 1; linked to hotel departments such as housekeeping, front desk or restaurant 1; consequence for the hotel 1.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Ahmed manages a garment factory in Faisalabad that makes T-shirts for a European retailer to very tight deadlines. He uses an autocratic leadership style. Analyse one advantage and one disadvantage of autocratic leadership for this factory.
parts.answer: Advantage: decisions are made quickly by Ahmed alone, so when the retailer changes an order at short notice the production lines can be re-planned at once and the tight delivery deadline is met, protecting the contract. Disadvantage: machinists have no say, so they may feel undervalued; labour turnover and absenteeism may rise, raising recruitment and training costs and threatening output quality.
parts.working: Advantage: quick decisions / clear instructions / control of quality under deadlines. Disadvantage: low motivation, no use of workers' ideas, dependence on one person, higher labour turnover. Marks: knowledge 1, application 1, analysis 3. Level 2 (3–5): a developed chain of analysis (cause → effect → impact) applied to this business. Level 1 (1–2): knowledge with limited application; no developed analysis.

stem: CodeNest is a software house in Karachi with 35 programmers. The founder, Farah, lets each team decide how and when to complete client projects and rarely checks progress. Staff enjoy the freedom, but last year two client apps were delivered late.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify one leadership style that Farah appears to use.
parts.answer: Laissez-faire.
parts.working: 1 mark: laissez-faire (teams decide how and when to work and Farah rarely checks progress). Do not accept democratic: in a democratic style the leader consults but still makes or confirms the decision.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the term 'emotional intelligence'.
parts.answer: The ability of a leader to recognise, understand and manage their own emotions and those of others (Goleman: self-awareness, self-regulation, motivation, empathy, social skills). At CodeNest, Farah might notice a stressed programmer before a deadline and give support, keeping the team productive.
parts.working: 1 mark: understanding and managing own emotions; 1 mark: understanding/responding to others' emotions (empathy, social skills); 1 mark: application to CodeNest.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one role of a manager that Farah may be neglecting.
parts.answer: Controlling/monitoring: setting targets and checking progress against them. Because nobody checks progress, two client apps were delivered late, damaging CodeNest's reputation. Also accept planning or coordinating.
parts.working: 1 mark: a valid managerial role (Fayol: plan, organise, command, coordinate, control; or Mintzberg role); 2 marks: explained with reference to late projects at CodeNest.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether emotional intelligence is the most important quality for the manager of a hospital emergency department.
parts.answer: For: staff work under extreme stress; an emotionally intelligent manager notices burnout, calms conflict between doctors and nurses, and shows empathy to patients' families, which keeps the team effective and reduces staff turnover. Against: in emergencies, decisive (sometimes autocratic) decision-making, clinical knowledge, and organisational skills such as planning shifts and controlling resources may matter more; a caring manager who cannot prioritise could put lives at risk. Judgement: emotional intelligence is necessary but not sufficient; it is most important for long-term retention and teamwork, while technical competence and decisiveness matter most during a crisis. The best manager combines both.
parts.working: Analysis points: EI (self-awareness, empathy, social skills) and its effect on stress, teamwork, retention; alternative qualities: decisiveness, clinical expertise, planning/organising, communication. Evaluation: depends on situation (crisis vs routine), experience of team, hospital culture. Mark scheme: AO1 knowledge 2, AO2 application 2, AO3 analysis 2, AO4 evaluation 6. Level 3 (9–12): developed analysis in context plus a supported judgement that answers the question for this business (e.g. 'it depends on…' weighed, with a clear conclusion). Level 2 (5–8): developed analysis with some, limited or unsupported evaluation. Level 1 (1–4): knowledge and some application; little or no analysis.

stem:
SunGrid installs solar panels across Punjab. Timeline:
2021: Founder Imran Qureshi makes all decisions himself; demand rises as electricity prices increase. Revenue Rs 900 million.
2022: Revenue Rs 1,450 million. Labour turnover reaches 28 %. Two senior engineers resign, saying they were 'never consulted'.
2023: Large commercial projects run three months late. Customer complaints double.
2024: Imran attends a leadership course, introduces weekly staff forums and delegates installation scheduling to four regional managers.
2025: Labour turnover falls to 12 %; complaints fall by 40 %; revenue Rs 1,900 million but operating profit margin 9 % (14 % in 2021).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the effectiveness of Imran Qureshi's leadership of SunGrid between 2021 and 2025.
parts.answer: Effective: in 2021–22 his autocratic, fast decisions let SunGrid exploit rising demand; revenue grew strongly. The switch to a more democratic style in 2024 (weekly forums, delegating installation scheduling to regional managers) coincided with labour turnover falling and customer complaints dropping. Less effective: the 2022–23 style caused high labour turnover (28 %) and the loss of two senior engineers, which delayed the commercial projects; the change of style came late and only after damage was done. Judgement: overall moderately effective — he adapted his style to the situation (Tannenbaum–Schmidt continuum), and later results improved, but revenue growth came partly from the market (energy prices) rather than leadership, and profit margin is still below 2021 levels. A full judgement needs data on profit and employee satisfaction after 2025.
parts.working: Use the timeline: autocratic phase and its results; turnover and resignations; change to democratic style; later turnover and complaint data. Consider external factors (energy prices, demand) versus leadership. Judgement on overall effectiveness with criteria (growth, staff, customers). Levels: Level 4 (16–20): accurate knowledge, strong use of the case data, three or four developed chains of analysis and a well-supported judgement/recommendation throughout, specific to this business and its situation. Level 3 (11–15): developed analysis in context with some supported evaluation. Level 2 (6–10): some analysis, mostly descriptive use of the case; evaluation weak or unsupported. Level 1 (1–5): knowledge with little application.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term 'induction training'.
parts.answer: Training given to new employees when they join, to introduce them to the business, its people, procedures, facilities and culture.
parts.working: 1 mark: for new employees / on joining; 1 mark: introduces the organisation, its rules, colleagues, health and safety, culture.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one difference between a job description and a person specification for a pharmacist at a hospital in Peshawar.
parts.answer: A job description sets out the job itself — title, duties (e.g. dispensing medicines, checking prescriptions), responsibilities and hours — whereas a person specification sets out the qualities of the ideal candidate, e.g. a pharmacy degree, registration with the pharmacy council and attention to detail.
parts.working: 1 mark: job description = duties/tasks of the job; 1 mark: person specification = skills, qualifications, experience needed by the person; 1 mark: applied to a hospital pharmacist.

stem: FreshMart runs 14 supermarkets in Lahore. It is installing self-service tills in all stores, so 40 checkout jobs will no longer be needed. It needs a new store manager and plans to promote one of its assistant managers. New shelf-stackers are chosen by a short interview and a one-day work trial.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify one method of selection used by FreshMart.
parts.answer: Interview (or work trial / aptitude test).
parts.working: 1 mark: interview, test or work trial (shown in the data).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the term 'internal recruitment'.
parts.answer: Filling a vacancy with a person who already works for the business, e.g. by promotion or transfer. FreshMart filling the store manager post with an existing assistant manager would be internal recruitment.
parts.working: 1 mark: vacancy filled from existing employees; 1 mark: development (promotion/transfer/advertised internally); 1 mark: application to FreshMart.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one difference between dismissal and redundancy, using FreshMart as an example.
parts.answer: Dismissal is ending employment because of the employee's fault (e.g. a cashier caught stealing or repeated lateness), whereas redundancy is ending employment because the job is no longer needed (e.g. checkout staff no longer needed after self-service tills are installed); redundant staff usually receive compensation.
parts.working: 1 mark each: dismissal = fault of employee/misconduct/incompetence; redundancy = job no longer exists, not the worker's fault; 1 mark applied to FreshMart (self-service tills, store closure).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Kohsar Pharma plans to send 15 laboratory technicians on an off-the-job course. The course fee is Rs 48,000 per technician and lasts 3 working days. Each technician produces output worth Rs 5,200 per day that will be lost while they are away.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total cost to Kohsar Pharma of sending the technicians on the course.
parts.working: Course fees = 15 × Rs 48,000 = Rs 720,000 (M1). Lost output = 15 × 3 × Rs 5,200 = Rs 234,000 (M1). Total = Rs 954,000 (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one benefit to Kohsar Pharma of training staff on-the-job instead.
parts.answer: On-the-job training takes place while the technicians keep working on Kohsar Pharma's own machines, so there is no lost output (saving the Rs 234,000 of lost output) and the training is specific to its production lines.
parts.working: 1 mark for knowledge of the term/concept; up to 2 marks for explaining it in the context of the business (application).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: SkyLink is a new regional airline based in Islamabad. It plans to select 60 cabin crew using a one-day assessment centre that includes group tasks, role plays of difficult passengers and interviews. Analyse two benefits to SkyLink of using an assessment centre to select cabin crew.
parts.answer: 1. Better match between candidate and job: role plays show how a candidate actually deals with an angry passenger, which an interview alone cannot show; SkyLink is less likely to appoint unsuitable crew, reducing labour turnover and retraining costs and protecting its new brand's reputation for service. 2. Teamwork skills can be observed: crew must work closely in a small cabin during emergencies; group tasks reveal who communicates and cooperates well, improving safety and customer satisfaction, which matters for a new airline trying to build loyalty.
parts.working: Benefits: more reliable/valid selection; tests real job skills; teamwork, communication observed; fair comparison of many candidates; reduces costly mistakes in recruiting 60 staff. Mark scheme: AO1 knowledge 2, AO2 application 2, AO3 analysis 4. Level 2 (5–8): two developed chains of analysis, each clearly applied to this business. Level 1 (1–4): knowledge and/or application with undeveloped or generic analysis. Evaluation earns no extra marks.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A restaurant chain in Dubai with 22 branches needs a new head chef to design its menus. Evaluate whether external recruitment is better than internal recruitment for this vacancy.
parts.answer: External: brings new ideas and cuisines, a wider pool of talent and possibly experience from top hotels — useful if the chain wants to refresh menus to compete; but it is expensive (agency fees, advertising), slower, riskier (the person is unknown) and may demotivate existing senior chefs who hoped for promotion. Internal: cheaper and faster, the candidate already knows the chain's suppliers, kitchens and brand, and promotion motivates staff; but the pool is small and the menu may not change much, and a vacancy is created lower down. Judgement: depends on the chain's objective — if it wants a radical menu change or the internal chefs lack menu-design experience, external is better despite the cost; if consistency and culture are priorities and a strong sous-chef exists, internal is better.
parts.working: Analysis of cost, time, risk, new ideas, motivation, knowledge of the business. Evaluation must weigh these for a head chef role in a multi-branch Dubai chain. Mark scheme: AO1 knowledge 2, AO2 application 2, AO3 analysis 2, AO4 evaluation 6. Level 3 (9–12): developed analysis in context plus a supported judgement that answers the question for this business (e.g. 'it depends on…' weighed, with a clear conclusion). Level 2 (5–8): developed analysis with some, limited or unsupported evaluation. Level 1 (1–4): knowledge and some application; little or no analysis.

stem: BrightBox makes cardboard packaging in Sialkot. In 2025 it produced 86,400 boxes per month with an average of 240 employees. During 2025, 30 employees left the business.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate labour productivity at BrightBox in 2025 (boxes per employee).
parts.answer: 360 boxes per employee
parts.working: Labour productivity = output ÷ number of employees (M1) = 86,400 ÷ 240 = 360 (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate labour turnover at BrightBox in 2025.
parts.working: Labour turnover = employees leaving ÷ average number employed × 100 (M1) = 30 ÷ 240 × 100 = 12.5 % (A1).

author: HomiLabs

stem: A call centre in Karachi had 130 employees in 2024 and 150 in 2025. Each employee was expected to work 230 days per year. Days lost to absence were 1,180 in 2024 and 1,950 in 2025. In 2025 management raised the target from 70 to 90 calls per shift.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the absenteeism rate at the call centre for 2024 and 2025. Give your answers to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two possible reasons for the change in the absenteeism rate.
parts.answer: 1. Low motivation/stress: the new target of 90 calls per shift increases pressure on agents, leading to stress-related sickness. 2. New staff: 20 extra agents joined, and new, less committed or poorly inducted staff may be absent more often. Also accept poor working conditions, lack of flexible hours.
parts.working: For each reason: 1 mark identified, 1 mark explained in context of the call centre (target, new recruits).

author: HomiLabs

stem: City Care Hospital in Rawalpindi will open a new 80-bed wing in 18 months. It currently employs 210 nurses, and labour turnover among nurses is 15 % a year, as many leave to work abroad.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the term 'workforce plan'.
parts.answer: A forecast of the number and type of employees (skills, roles) a business will need in future, compared with its current workforce, with a plan to close the gap through recruitment, training, redeployment or redundancy. For City Care Hospital, it would set out how many nurses, doctors and technicians are needed when the new wing opens.
parts.working: 1 mark: forecast of future staffing needs (number + skills); 1 mark: comparison with current workforce / actions to fill gap; 1 mark: application to the hospital.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two factors City Care Hospital should consider when preparing its workforce plan.
parts.answer: 1. Forecast demand for its services — the 80-bed wing and expected patient numbers determine how many nurses are needed per shift. 2. Labour market conditions — a shortage of qualified nurses (many emigrate) means it may need to start recruiting or training early or raise pay. Also accept: labour turnover/retirements, budget, technology, legal staffing ratios.
parts.working: For each factor: 1 mark identified, 1 mark explained in context.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Pure Springs bottles mineral water. Before installing a new bottling machine it filled 54,000 litres per day with 45 production workers. After installation it filled 63,000 litres per day with 42 workers. The rejection rate for faulty bottles rose from 1.2 % to 2.0 %.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage change in labour productivity (litres per worker per day) after the new bottling machine was installed.
parts.answer: Productivity rose from 1,200 to 1,500 litres per worker per day: an increase of 25 %.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate whether labour productivity is the best measure of employee performance at Pure Springs.
parts.answer: For: productivity is easy to measure and directly links labour to output and unit labour cost, so the 25 % rise suggests better performance and lower costs. Against: the rise is largely due to the new machine (capital), not employees; productivity ignores quality (rejected bottles rose), safety, absenteeism, labour turnover and customer satisfaction; pushing productivity may harm morale. Other measures: absenteeism, labour turnover, wastage rates, appraisal results. Judgement: productivity is a useful measure but not the best on its own here; Pure Springs should use a balanced set of measures because the change in productivity mostly reflects investment in machinery.
parts.working: Must use the calculated result and note the effect of the machine. Compare with other HR measures (absenteeism, turnover, quality/wastage, appraisal). Mark scheme: AO1 knowledge 2, AO2 application 2, AO3 analysis 2, AO4 evaluation 6. Level 3 (9–12): developed analysis in context plus a supported judgement that answers the question for this business (e.g. 'it depends on…' weighed, with a clear conclusion). Level 2 (5–8): developed analysis with some, limited or unsupported evaluation. Level 1 (1–4): knowledge and some application; little or no analysis.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term 'soft HRM'.
parts.answer: An approach to managing people that treats employees as a valuable resource to be developed, with long-term planning, two-way communication, training, empowerment and attention to employees' needs.
parts.working: 1 mark: employees seen as valuable asset/resource; 1 mark: long-term development, consultation, empowerment, motivation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one benefit to a call centre in Lahore of employing staff on part-time contracts.
parts.answer: Call volumes peak in the evenings and at weekends; part-time agents can be scheduled for just these hours, so the call centre matches staffing to demand and avoids paying full-time staff during quiet periods, lowering labour cost per call.
parts.working: 1 mark for knowledge of the term/concept; up to 2 marks for explaining it in the context of the business (application).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Galaxy Motors is a car dealership in Islamabad with 18 sales staff. Sales have been flat for two years. The new manager plans to introduce management by objectives (MBO). Analyse two ways MBO could improve the performance of the sales staff.
parts.answer: 1. Agreed, specific targets: each salesperson agrees, say, 6 cars a month and a customer-satisfaction score with the manager; because they took part in setting them, they are committed and know exactly what is expected, so effort rises and flat sales may grow. 2. Regular review: progress is reviewed monthly, so weaknesses (e.g. poor follow-up of test drives) are identified and training given, improving conversion rates and long-term performance; achievement of targets can be linked to recognition, raising motivation.
parts.working: Points: SMART agreed objectives, link to corporate objectives, ownership and motivation, appraisal/feedback, identifies training needs. Mark scheme: AO1 knowledge 2, AO2 application 2, AO3 analysis 4. Level 2 (5–8): two developed chains of analysis, each clearly applied to this business. Level 1 (1–4): knowledge and/or application with undeveloped or generic analysis. Evaluation earns no extra marks.

stem: FunLand is a theme park near Lahore. It employs 60 permanent staff and hires 150 ride operators on temporary contracts for the busy summer season.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the term 'performance appraisal'.
parts.answer: A regular (e.g. annual) formal assessment of an employee's performance against agreed targets or job requirements, usually through a meeting with a manager, which identifies strengths, weaknesses and training needs. At FunLand, ride supervisors could be appraised on safety record and guest feedback.
parts.working: 1 mark: evaluating employee's work/performance; 1 mark: against targets/criteria, regularly, with feedback and training needs; 1 mark: application to FunLand.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one disadvantage to FunLand of employing most of its ride operators on temporary contracts.
parts.answer: Temporary staff may have little loyalty and leave after the summer season, so FunLand must recruit and train new ride operators every year; inexperience raises the risk of safety mistakes on rides, which could damage the park's reputation.
parts.working: 1 mark for knowledge of the term/concept; up to 2 marks for explaining it in the context of the business (application).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Saadat-Noor Bank (an invented bank) was formed by a merger of two banks in 2024. Appendix 1: 4,200 employees, 260 branches; the board plans to close 40 branches by 2027 and move customers to a new mobile app. Appendix 2: staff survey 2025 — 41 % of employees satisfied (68 % in 2023); labour turnover 21 %. Appendix 3: staff from the two former banks follow different procedures and complain about unclear roles. Appendix 4: operating profit fell 12 % in 2025; the board wants to cut costs.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Advise the board of Saadat-Noor Bank on the HRM strategy it should use to improve employee performance over the next three years.
parts.answer: Options: (1) Hard HRM — cut costs, strict targets, performance-related pay, close monitoring; fits the board's cost-saving objective and the need to reduce duplication after the merger, and quickly improves measurable productivity; but risks worsening the already low morale (staff survey 41 % satisfied), raising labour turnover above 20 % and damaging customer service. (2) Soft HRM — consultation, training in digital banking, career paths, flexible working; addresses the culture clash and skills gap for the new app, builds commitment; but is costly and slow while profit is falling. Recommendation: a mainly soft approach for branch and digital staff (retraining for the app, consultation on branch changes, clear communication), with hard elements (clear KPIs, performance-related bonuses) for productivity; justify with the data on turnover, satisfaction and the strategic need for skilled digital staff. Depends on finance available and the CEO's willingness to change culture.
parts.working: Use Appendices: merger, satisfaction survey, labour turnover, branch closures, digital strategy. Weigh hard vs soft HRM, flexible working, training, MBO, PRP. Clear recommendation with conditions. Levels: Level 4 (16–20): accurate knowledge, strong use of the case data, three or four developed chains of analysis and a well-supported judgement/recommendation throughout, specific to this business and its situation. Level 3 (11–15): developed analysis in context with some supported evaluation. Level 2 (6–10): some analysis, mostly descriptive use of the case; evaluation weak or unsupported. Level 1 (1–5): knowledge with little application.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term 'workforce diversity'.
parts.answer: The range of differences between employees in an organisation, such as gender, age, ethnicity, religion, disability, education and background.
parts.working: 1 mark: differences/variety among employees; 1 mark: examples (gender, age, ethnicity, disability, background).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one benefit to an advertising agency in Karachi of having a diverse workforce.
parts.answer: Staff from different backgrounds, age groups and regions bring different ideas and understand different customer groups, so the agency can create campaigns that appeal to a wider range of consumers (e.g. Urdu, Sindhi and English-speaking audiences), winning more clients.
parts.working: 1 mark for knowledge of the term/concept; up to 2 marks for explaining it in the context of the business (application).

stem: Apex Engineering employs 900 staff, of whom 32 % are women. It has 120 managers, of whom 18 are women.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of managers at Apex Engineering who are women.
parts.working: Women managers = 18 (M1); total managers = 120; 18 ÷ 120 × 100 (M1) = 15 % (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one way Apex Engineering could promote equality of opportunity in promotion.
parts.answer: Use clear, published promotion criteria and mixed interview panels, so decisions are based on skills and results rather than gender; together with mentoring for women engineers, this could increase the share of women in management from 15 %.
parts.working: 1 mark for knowledge of the term/concept; up to 2 marks for explaining it in the context of the business (application). Accept: training/mentoring programmes, flexible working for carers, blind CV screening, equality policy and monitoring.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Bolan Steelworks employs 1,500 people near Karachi, of whom 3 % are women. It has a shortage of qualified engineers. Two of its European customers now ask suppliers to report on workforce equality.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether introducing a diversity and equality policy will improve the performance of Bolan Steelworks.
parts.answer: Improve: a wider recruitment pool helps fill the skills shortage of engineers; diverse teams generate more ideas and better problem-solving; a fair reputation attracts graduates and meets the expectations of export customers who audit suppliers; equality may lower labour turnover. Not improve (or not quickly): costs of training, changes to facilities (separate rest areas, childcare); resistance from existing staff and a traditional culture may cause conflict; a policy on paper without management commitment changes nothing; performance depends more on investment in machinery and steel prices. Judgement: likely to improve performance in the long term if top management actively implements it and links it to the skills shortage, but short-term benefits are limited.
parts.working: Points: talent pool, creativity, reputation/CSR, customer expectations, legal compliance; costs, resistance, culture, implementation. Judgement linked to the steel company context. Mark scheme: AO1 knowledge 2, AO2 application 2, AO3 analysis 2, AO4 evaluation 6. Level 3 (9–12): developed analysis in context plus a supported judgement that answers the question for this business (e.g. 'it depends on…' weighed, with a clear conclusion). Level 2 (5–8): developed analysis with some, limited or unsupported evaluation. Level 1 (1–4): knowledge and some application; little or no analysis.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse one benefit to a garment exporter in Faisalabad of providing a free health clinic and subsidised meals for its 2,000 workers.
parts.answer: Better health and nutrition reduce illness, so absenteeism falls; with fewer absent machinists, production lines run at full speed and export orders are delivered on time, protecting contracts with foreign buyers and lowering the cost of temporary cover. (Alternatively: welfare improves loyalty, lowers labour turnover and recruitment/training costs; helps pass buyers' ethical audits.)
parts.working: Chain: welfare → healthier/more loyal staff → lower absence/turnover → output, costs, reputation with buyers. Marks: knowledge 1, application 1, analysis 3. Level 2 (3–5): a developed chain of analysis (cause → effect → impact) applied to this business. Level 1 (1–2): knowledge with limited application; no developed analysis.

stem: Marvi Logistics has a managing director. Four directors report to the managing director. Each director is responsible for 6 depot managers, and each depot manager supervises 9 drivers and warehouse staff.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the number of levels of hierarchy at Marvi Logistics.
parts.answer: 4 levels
parts.working: Managing director, directors, depot managers, drivers/warehouse staff = 4 (B1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the span of control of each depot manager.
parts.working: Each depot manager directly supervises 9 employees (B1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the total number of employees at Marvi Logistics.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: TeleWave, a mobile network operator, plans to remove one layer of regional managers (delayering). Analyse two effects of delayering on TeleWave.
parts.answer: 1. Lower costs and faster communication: removing a layer of well-paid regional managers cuts salary costs; messages pass through fewer levels, so decisions on network faults and promotions are made faster, improving responsiveness to customers in a fast-changing market. 2. Wider spans of control: remaining managers supervise more staff, which can empower and motivate employees through more responsibility, but may overload managers, reduce supervision and lower morale among staff who lose promotion opportunities; service quality could fall.
parts.working: Effects: cost saving, faster communication, empowerment, wider span, workload/stress, fewer promotion opportunities, redundancy costs, morale. Mark scheme: AO1 knowledge 2, AO2 application 2, AO3 analysis 4. Level 2 (5–8): two developed chains of analysis, each clearly applied to this business. Level 1 (1–4): knowledge and/or application with undeveloped or generic analysis. Evaluation earns no extra marks.

stem: Delta Engineering Consultants in Lahore employs 300 engineers in four functional departments: civil, electrical, mechanical and environmental. Most of its contracts (e.g. a new dam, a hospital building) need engineers from several departments working together. Clients have complained of slow communication between departments.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether a matrix structure is the most suitable organisational structure for Delta Engineering Consultants.
parts.answer: For: projects need civil, electrical and environmental engineers together; a matrix lets specialists from functional departments join project teams, sharing expertise, improving coordination and flexibility, and speeding up delivery for clients such as the dam project. Against: staff have two bosses (functional head and project manager), causing conflicting priorities, confusion and stress; more managers increase costs; disagreements over resources. Alternatives: functional structure (clear lines, but poor cross-department coordination), project-based teams. Judgement: suitable given the project-based work and the need for multi-disciplinary teams, provided roles and priorities are clearly defined and project managers are trained; otherwise conflict may outweigh benefits.
parts.working: Analysis of matrix features (two lines of authority, project teams) against functional/hierarchical alternatives; evaluation in context of an engineering consultancy. Mark scheme: AO1 knowledge 2, AO2 application 2, AO3 analysis 2, AO4 evaluation 6. Level 3 (9–12): developed analysis in context plus a supported judgement that answers the question for this business (e.g. 'it depends on…' weighed, with a clear conclusion). Level 2 (5–8): developed analysis with some, limited or unsupported evaluation. Level 1 (1–4): knowledge and some application; little or no analysis.

author: HomiLabs

stem: MediPack packs tablets into boxes for pharmaceutical companies. Packing staff are paid Rs 35 per box packed. Any worker who packs more than 1,200 boxes in a week also receives a bonus of Rs 2,000. Last week Ayesha packed 1,240 boxes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Ayesha's pay for the week.
parts.working: 1,240 × Rs 35 = Rs 43,400 (M1); output above 1,200 so add bonus Rs 2,000 → Rs 45,400 (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one disadvantage to MediPack of paying packing staff by piece rate.
parts.answer: Workers are paid for quantity, so they may rush and make mistakes, e.g. putting the wrong number of tablets in packs; in medicine packing this could lead to product recalls and damage MediPack's reputation, so quality checks must increase.
parts.working: 1 mark for knowledge of the term/concept; up to 2 marks for explaining it in the context of the business (application). Accept: quality falls, unsuitable for work where output is hard to measure, workers resist new methods, stress.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term 'job enrichment'.
parts.answer: Redesigning a job to give the employee more responsibility, more challenging tasks and more control over how the work is done (vertical loading).
parts.working: 1 mark: increasing responsibility / challenge / decision-making; 1 mark: making work more meaningful / complete unit of work / vertical extension.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how Herzberg's two-factor theory could help a bank branch manager reduce dissatisfaction among cashiers.
parts.answer: Herzberg says hygiene factors (pay, working conditions, supervision, job security) do not motivate but cause dissatisfaction if poor. The branch manager should first fix hygiene factors — e.g. fair pay, a comfortable cash counter area and reasonable supervision — so cashiers are not dissatisfied, then use motivators such as recognition and responsibility.
parts.working: 1 mark: hygiene factors vs motivators; 1 mark: poor hygiene factors cause dissatisfaction; 1 mark: applied to cashiers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether financial rewards are the most effective way to motivate nurses in a private hospital in Lahore.
parts.answer: For: nurses' pay may be low relative to cost of living; Maslow's lower needs and Taylor's view suggest pay matters; competitive pay reduces emigration and turnover; bonuses for extra shifts help cover staff shortages. Against: Herzberg sees pay as a hygiene factor — it removes dissatisfaction but does not motivate long-term; nursing is a vocation, so recognition, responsibility, training and career progression (Herzberg's motivators, Maslow's esteem/self-actualisation), good working conditions, safe staffing levels and respectful management may be more effective; performance-related pay is hard to measure in nursing and can harm teamwork. Judgement: pay must first be competitive (otherwise nurses leave), but beyond that non-financial methods are more effective; it depends on current pay levels and the hospital's finances.
parts.working: Use motivation theories (Taylor, Maslow, Herzberg, Mayo/McClelland) and payment methods; weigh against non-financial methods; context of nursing/private hospital. Mark scheme: AO1 knowledge 2, AO2 application 2, AO3 analysis 2, AO4 evaluation 6. Level 3 (9–12): developed analysis in context plus a supported judgement that answers the question for this business (e.g. 'it depends on…' weighed, with a clear conclusion). Level 2 (5–8): developed analysis with some, limited or unsupported evaluation. Level 1 (1–4): knowledge and some application; little or no analysis.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term 'collective bargaining'.
parts.answer: Negotiation between employers and a trade union (representing a group of employees) over pay, working conditions and other terms of employment.
parts.working: 1 mark: negotiation between management/employer and trade union / employee representatives; 1 mark: about pay and conditions on behalf of all workers.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one barrier to effective communication at a parcel delivery company with drivers working across the country.
parts.answer: Physical distance: drivers are on the road most of the day and rarely visit the depot, so notices and meetings do not reach them; important messages, e.g. route changes, may be missed, causing late deliveries. Also accept: too many layers, jargon, information overload, poor choice of medium, language differences.
parts.working: 1 mark for knowledge of the term/concept; up to 2 marks for explaining it in the context of the business (application).

stem: Chenab Spinning employs 2,400 workers in a spinning mill. Last month managers announced, without consulting the union, that new automated spinning machines will replace 300 jobs over two years. Inflation is 14 % and the union is demanding a 20 % pay rise. The union has threatened a strike.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether improving communication with employees is the most effective way for Chenab Spinning to avoid industrial action.
parts.answer: For: the dispute arose partly because the automation plan was announced without consultation; regular two-way communication (works councils, consultation with the union, explaining reasons for change) builds trust and lets concerns about job losses be addressed early, so strikes are less likely. Against: communication cannot remove the real conflict of interest — workers fear losing 300 jobs and want pay rises above inflation; the most effective measures may be negotiation through collective bargaining, offering retraining/redeployment, no-compulsory-redundancy agreements, pay deals, or using ACAS-style conciliation/arbitration (or the national equivalent). Judgement: communication is a necessary first step and may be most effective at preventing future disputes, but for this dispute it must be combined with a negotiated agreement on jobs and pay.
parts.working: Consider: communication/consultation, collective bargaining, compromise on pay, redeployment and training, arbitration, employee participation (works councils). Evaluate in context of automation and inflation. Mark scheme: AO1 knowledge 2, AO2 application 2, AO3 analysis 2, AO4 evaluation 6. Level 3 (9–12): developed analysis in context plus a supported judgement that answers the question for this business (e.g. 'it depends on…' weighed, with a clear conclusion). Level 2 (5–8): developed analysis with some, limited or unsupported evaluation. Level 1 (1–4): knowledge and some application; little or no analysis.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Basmati Gold exports rice from Pakistan to the USA. It prices its rice at Rs 250,000 per tonne. The exchange rate changed from US$1 = Rs 280 to US$1 = Rs 300.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the US dollar price of one tonne of Basmati Gold rice before and after the change in the exchange rate. Give your answers to the nearest cent.
parts.answer: Before: $892.86; after: $833.33 per tonne.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how this change in the exchange rate affects the competitiveness of Basmati Gold in the USA.
parts.answer: The rupee has depreciated, so with the rupee price unchanged the dollar price falls by about $60 a tonne; Basmati Gold's rice becomes cheaper for US importers than rice from rival exporting countries, so demand and export volume should rise (or the firm can raise its rupee price and earn a higher margin).
parts.working: 1 mark: rupee depreciation makes exports cheaper in dollars; 1 mark: more price competitive vs rival suppliers; 1 mark: consequence (more sales / option to raise margin).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: The central bank has raised its interest rate from 12 % to 17 %. Analyse two effects of this rise on AutoPak, a car manufacturer that sells most of its cars to customers who buy on credit (car loans).
parts.answer: 1. Lower demand: car loans become more expensive, so monthly repayments rise; many middle-income customers postpone buying, so AutoPak's sales and revenue fall, leaving spare capacity and higher unit fixed costs. 2. Higher costs of finance: AutoPak's own overdraft/loan interest rises, raising costs and reducing profit; it may delay investment in a new model, harming long-term competitiveness. (Also: rupee may appreciate, making imported parts cheaper.)
parts.working: Effects: consumer demand for credit-financed goods, cost of borrowing for the firm, investment decisions, exchange rate, inventory costs. Mark scheme: AO1 knowledge 2, AO2 application 2, AO3 analysis 4. Level 2 (5–8): two developed chains of analysis, each clearly applied to this business. Level 1 (1–4): knowledge and/or application with undeveloped or generic analysis. Evaluation earns no extra marks.

stem: Kayu Craft makes mid-priced wooden furniture in Malaysia. 70 % of its sales are in Malaysia and 30 % are exported. Malaysia is joining a regional trade agreement that will remove tariffs on furniture traded between member countries over three years. Manufacturers in two other member countries have labour costs about 25 % lower than Kayu Craft.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether Kayu Craft will benefit from Malaysia joining the new regional trade agreement.
parts.answer: Benefits: removal of tariffs on furniture exports makes Kayu Craft's products cheaper in member countries, opening a larger market and economies of scale; cheaper imported fittings and varnish lower costs. Threats: tariffs also fall on imports, so lower-cost rivals from Vietnam and Indonesia gain access to Malaysia, where 70 % of sales are made; Kayu Craft must compete on price or differentiate; meeting common product standards may add costs. Judgement: depends on whether its cost and quality allow it to compete — as a mid-priced, design-led firm with only 30 % exports, the threat to its home market may outweigh export gains in the short term, unless it uses the agreement to expand exports aggressively and develop its design USP.
parts.working: Use data: share of home vs export sales, competitors' costs, tariff changes. Weigh opportunities (exports, cheaper inputs) against threats (imports, standards). Clear judgement. Mark scheme: AO1 knowledge 2, AO2 application 2, AO3 analysis 2, AO4 evaluation 6. Level 3 (9–12): developed analysis in context plus a supported judgement that answers the question for this business (e.g. 'it depends on…' weighed, with a clear conclusion). Level 2 (5–8): developed analysis with some, limited or unsupported evaluation. Level 1 (1–4): knowledge and some application; little or no analysis.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Bake House is a bakery in Quetta. Its monthly sales revenue is Rs 2,000,000, ingredient costs are Rs 1,200,000 and other costs are Rs 500,000. Inflation causes ingredient costs to rise by 12 %. Bake House raises its prices by 5 %, and the number of items sold stays the same. Other costs do not change.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Bake House's monthly profit after the changes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one other way inflation could affect Bake House.
parts.answer: Employees will ask for higher wages to keep up with rising prices, increasing Bake House's costs further; if it cannot pass these on to price-sensitive customers, profit falls again. Also accept: customers' real incomes fall so they buy fewer cakes; uncertainty delays investment.
parts.working: 1 mark for knowledge of the term/concept; up to 2 marks for explaining it in the context of the business (application).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: The government has raised the national minimum wage by 25 %. Analyse two effects of this change on BurgerHub, a fast-food chain with 1,200 employees, most of whom are paid the minimum wage.
parts.answer: 1. Higher costs: wage costs rise by up to 25 %, a large share of a labour-intensive fast-food firm's costs; unless prices rise, profit margins fall, and higher menu prices may reduce demand from price-sensitive young customers. 2. Motivation and staff turnover: better pay may reduce labour turnover and absenteeism, lowering recruitment and training costs and improving service speed; BurgerHub may also respond by investing in self-order kiosks to reduce staff numbers. Also: higher incomes of low-paid workers may increase demand for fast food.
parts.working: Effects: wage costs/prices/profit; motivation/turnover; substitution of capital for labour; demand effect of higher incomes. Mark scheme: AO1 knowledge 2, AO2 application 2, AO3 analysis 4. Level 2 (5–8): two developed chains of analysis, each clearly applied to this business. Level 1 (1–4): knowledge and/or application with undeveloped or generic analysis. Evaluation earns no extra marks.

stem: SkyBlue Airways (an invented Pakistani airline). Appendix 1: GDP is forecast to fall by 1.5 % next year. Appendix 2: jet fuel prices rose 30 % in 12 months; fuel is 38 % of SkyBlue's costs and is priced in US dollars. Appendix 3: the rupee fell 15 % against the US dollar. Appendix 4: domestic load factor (percentage of seats filled) fell from 81 % to 68 %; international load factor stayed at 79 %. Appendix 5: a foreign low-cost airline has started flights on SkyBlue's two most profitable routes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Advise SkyBlue Airways on the strategy it should follow over the next two years in response to these changes in its external environment.
parts.answer: Options: (1) Cut costs — reduce routes with low load factors, delay delivery of new aircraft, renegotiate leases, hedge fuel; protects cash during recession. (2) Change marketing — cut fares on domestic routes to fill seats (demand is price-elastic in recession), focus on business travellers and the Hajj/Umrah and diaspora markets where demand is less affected. (3) Exploit the weak rupee: overseas customers find SkyBlue cheaper, so expand international routes priced in foreign currency, while noting that fuel and leases are priced in dollars and become more expensive. Recommendation: a combination — protect cash flow (fuel hedging, temporary route cuts), keep fleet investment only for fuel-efficient aircraft, and focus on routes with foreign-currency revenue; justify with appendix data (load factor fall, fuel share of costs, dollar-denominated costs). Conditions: depends on how long the recession lasts and competitors' actions.
parts.working: Must use appendices: recession/GDP, fuel price, exchange rate, load factors, competitor entry. Consider economic, political, competitive factors. Clear prioritised recommendation. Levels: Level 4 (16–20): accurate knowledge, strong use of the case data, three or four developed chains of analysis and a well-supported judgement/recommendation throughout, specific to this business and its situation. Level 3 (11–15): developed analysis in context with some supported evaluation. Level 2 (6–10): some analysis, mostly descriptive use of the case; evaluation weak or unsupported. Level 1 (1–5): knowledge with little application.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term 'corporate social responsibility (CSR)'.
parts.answer: The idea that a business should consider the interests of society and all stakeholders (e.g. the environment, employees, local communities), not just shareholders' profits, going beyond legal requirements.
parts.working: 1 mark: responsibility to society/stakeholders/environment; 1 mark: beyond legal duty / not only profit for owners.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one way a cement manufacturer could reduce its impact on the environment.
parts.answer: Fit filters to kiln chimneys to reduce dust emissions, protecting the health of nearby villagers; or use waste heat recovery/solar power, cutting fossil fuel use and CO₂ emissions per tonne of cement.
parts.working: 1 mark for knowledge of the term/concept; up to 2 marks for explaining it in the context of the business (application).

stem: ChocoDelight makes premium chocolate bars sold in supermarkets in the UAE. It buys only Fairtrade cocoa, which costs 15 % more than other cocoa but guarantees farmers a minimum price.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify one stakeholder group that benefits from ChocoDelight's use of Fairtrade cocoa.
parts.answer: Cocoa farmers (suppliers).
parts.working: 1 mark: farmers/suppliers (accept customers who value ethics).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the term 'ethical decision'.
parts.answer: A decision based on what is morally right (honest, fair, responsible) rather than only on what is legal or most profitable. For ChocoDelight, paying farmers a fair price even though cheaper cocoa is available is an ethical decision.
parts.working: 1 mark: morally right/fair; 1 mark: beyond legal requirements/may reduce profit; 1 mark: application.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one reason why ChocoDelight might continue to use Fairtrade cocoa even though it costs 15 % more.
parts.answer: Its target customers are willing to pay more for ethical products; the Fairtrade label differentiates its chocolate from cheaper brands, supporting a premium price and brand loyalty, so the higher cost is covered by higher revenue.
parts.working: 1 mark for knowledge of the term/concept; up to 2 marks for explaining it in the context of the business (application). Also accept: protect reputation, secure reliable long-term supply, motivate staff, owners' values.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: StyleMart is a clothing retailer that buys clothes from 40 factories in Bangladesh and Pakistan. It is considering paying independent auditors to inspect working conditions in all its suppliers' factories every year. Analyse two benefits to StyleMart of auditing its suppliers.
parts.answer: 1. Protects reputation: if a supplier is found using child labour or unsafe buildings, media coverage could lead to boycotts; audits identify problems before a scandal, protecting StyleMart's brand and sales among ethically aware young customers. 2. Supply reliability and quality: factories with safe conditions and fair treatment have lower labour turnover, fewer accidents and strikes, so deliveries are more reliable and quality more consistent, reducing lost sales from stock-outs. Also: meets demands of investors/retail partners; marketing advantage.
parts.working: Benefits: reputation/brand, customer loyalty, investor expectations, reliable supply, legal compliance, competitive advantage. Mark scheme: AO1 knowledge 2, AO2 application 2, AO3 analysis 4. Level 2 (5–8): two developed chains of analysis, each clearly applied to this business. Level 1 (1–4): knowledge and/or application with undeveloped or generic analysis. Evaluation earns no extra marks.

stem: ClearGlass makes glass bottles. In 2023 it produced 2,000 tonnes of glass a month and emitted 4,600 tonnes of CO₂ a month. After installing a more efficient furnace, in 2025 it produced 2,600 tonnes a month and emitted 5,200 tonnes of CO₂ a month.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage reduction in CO₂ emissions per tonne of glass produced between 2023 and 2025. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why total emissions rose even though the business became more sustainable.
parts.answer: Output rose by 30 % (from 2,000 to 2,600 tonnes), so although each tonne of glass now causes 13 % less CO₂, the larger volume means total emissions rose from 4,600 to 5,200 tonnes. Growth offset the efficiency gain.
parts.working: 1 mark: output increased; 1 mark: emissions per unit fell; 1 mark: growth in output outweighs the per-unit reduction (with data).

author: HomiLabs

stem: FizzCo makes soft drinks in Pakistan and sells 90 % of them in plastic bottles. The government is considering a tax on single-use plastic. Changing all filling lines to glass and cans would cost Rs 1.8 billion. FizzCo's market research shows that 35 % of urban customers would pay 5 % more for drinks in returnable glass bottles.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether FizzCo should replace all its plastic bottles with glass bottles and cans within three years.
parts.answer: For: growing consumer and government pressure (proposed tax on single-use plastic) means continued plastic use could raise costs and damage the brand; being first to switch may attract environmentally aware customers and protect long-term sales; glass can be returned and refilled. Against: glass bottles cost more, are heavier (higher fuel cost and emissions in transport), break more easily; investment in new filling lines (Rs 1.8 billion) strains finance; rivals still using plastic may undercut on price in a price-sensitive market. Alternatives: recycled plastic (rPET), bottle-return scheme, gradual change. Judgement: a phased change, starting with premium/urban products and recycled plastic, is better than a full switch in three years unless the plastic tax is confirmed; depends on customer willingness to pay and finance.
parts.working: Weigh costs, finance, customers' price sensitivity, legislation, reputation, competitors, whether glass is truly more sustainable. Judgement in context. Mark scheme: AO1 knowledge 2, AO2 application 2, AO3 analysis 2, AO4 evaluation 6. Level 3 (9–12): developed analysis in context plus a supported judgement that answers the question for this business (e.g. 'it depends on…' weighed, with a clear conclusion). Level 2 (5–8): developed analysis with some, limited or unsupported evaluation. Level 1 (1–4): knowledge and some application; little or no analysis.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: 'Corporate social responsibility is just a marketing tool for banks.' Evaluate this view for a large commercial bank in Pakistan.
parts.answer: Supporting: banks publicise CSR (tree planting, scholarships) in advertising to improve their image and attract depositors; spending is small compared with profits; some banks fund polluting industries while promoting green image ('greenwashing'). Against: CSR can be genuine and strategic — financial inclusion schemes (microfinance, accounts for women), ethical lending policies that refuse funding for harmful projects, and fair treatment of staff create long-term value for society; regulators and international investors increasingly require ESG reporting; employees are motivated by real CSR. Judgement: for many banks CSR has a marketing element, but whether it is 'just' marketing depends on whether CSR is built into core decisions (lending, products, employment) or is only publicity; the evidence lies in actions rather than advertising.
parts.working: Arguments for/against, use of examples in banking, judgement with criteria for genuine CSR. Mark scheme: AO1 knowledge 2, AO2 application 2, AO3 analysis 2, AO4 evaluation 6. Level 3 (9–12): developed analysis in context plus a supported judgement that answers the question for this business (e.g. 'it depends on…' weighed, with a clear conclusion). Level 2 (5–8): developed analysis with some, limited or unsupported evaluation. Level 1 (1–4): knowledge and some application; little or no analysis.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term 'horizontal integration'.
parts.answer: When a business merges with or takes over another business in the same industry at the same stage of production (e.g. two hotel chains joining).
parts.working: 1 mark: merger/takeover/integration; 1 mark: same industry and same stage of production.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why many small businesses survive in the hairdressing industry.
parts.answer: Hairdressing offers a personal service where customers value a relationship with a stylist near their home; small salons can provide flexible, personalised service with low start-up costs, so large chains have little cost advantage. Also accept: local niche markets, low barriers to entry, limited economies of scale.
parts.working: 1 mark for knowledge of the term/concept; up to 2 marks for explaining it in the context of the business (application).

stem: SwiftRide is a ride-hailing app in Pakistan. Total market revenue: 2024 Rs 24 billion; 2025 Rs 30 billion. SwiftRide's revenue: 2024 Rs 3.6 billion; 2025 Rs 5.1 billion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate SwiftRide's market share in 2024 and in 2025.
parts.working: Market share = firm's sales ÷ total market sales × 100 (M1). 2024: 3.6 ÷ 24 × 100 = 15 % (A1). 2025: 5.1 ÷ 30 × 100 = 17 % (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why SwiftRide's growth may cause problems for the business.
parts.answer: Rapid growth (revenue up 42 %) may lead to diseconomies of scale or overtrading: SwiftRide may not have enough drivers or working capital to meet demand, causing long waiting times and a cash-flow crisis despite rising sales.
parts.working: 1 mark for knowledge of the term/concept; up to 2 marks for explaining it in the context of the business (application).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Green Valley Dairy is a co-operative of 600 milk farmers. It plans to buy a chain of 25 dairy shops in Lahore. Analyse two benefits to Green Valley Dairy of this forward vertical integration.
parts.answer: 1. Higher added value: the co-operative can sell milk, yoghurt and butter directly to consumers at retail prices instead of selling to wholesalers at low farm-gate prices; it captures the retailer's profit margin, increasing farmers' incomes. 2. Guaranteed outlet and market information: the shops provide an assured outlet for the members' milk, reducing the risk of retailers switching to rival suppliers; direct contact with customers gives information on demand, helping the co-operative develop new products.
parts.working: Benefits: control of distribution, retail margin, guaranteed outlet, brand building, market information, barrier to competitors. Mark scheme: AO1 knowledge 2, AO2 application 2, AO3 analysis 4. Level 2 (5–8): two developed chains of analysis, each clearly applied to this business. Level 1 (1–4): knowledge and/or application with undeveloped or generic analysis. Evaluation earns no extra marks.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A bakery chain with 12 shops in Islamabad wants to double its size in five years. Evaluate whether internal (organic) growth is better than taking over a rival chain.
parts.answer: Internal: opening new shops gradually keeps control and culture, lower risk, can be funded from retained profit; but slow and may let rivals take the best locations. Takeover: rapid growth, instant market share and locations, removes a competitor and may give economies of scale in buying flour and distribution; but expensive (premium over value), needs large external finance, risk of culture clash, different recipes/quality standards, and the rival may have hidden problems; potential diseconomies of scale. Judgement: depends on finance available, whether a suitable rival is for sale at a fair price, and how urgent growth is. For a quality-focused bakery where product consistency is key, organic growth is usually safer; a takeover is better only if a well-run rival with good locations is available.
parts.working: Compare speed, cost, risk, control, culture, finance, market share, economies of scale. Judgement in context. Mark scheme: AO1 knowledge 2, AO2 application 2, AO3 analysis 2, AO4 evaluation 6. Level 3 (9–12): developed analysis in context plus a supported judgement that answers the question for this business (e.g. 'it depends on…' weighed, with a clear conclusion). Level 2 (5–8): developed analysis with some, limited or unsupported evaluation. Level 1 (1–4): knowledge and some application; little or no analysis.

stem: TechTrade is a Pakistani electronics retailer. It is considering a joint venture with a Chinese manufacturer to assemble mobile phones in Pakistan.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify one way of measuring the size of a business.
parts.answer: Number of employees (or revenue, capital employed, market share, output).
parts.working: 1 mark for any valid measure.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the term 'joint venture'.
parts.answer: Two or more businesses agree to share capital, risks, resources and profits by setting up a new, separate business for a particular project, while remaining independent. For example, TechTrade could form a joint venture with a Chinese electronics maker to assemble phones in Pakistan.
parts.working: 1 mark: two or more firms; 1 mark: share costs, risk and profits / create a separate enterprise; 1 mark: application.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one problem that TechTrade might face if it grows by forming a joint venture.
parts.answer: The partners may disagree about objectives — for example the Chinese partner may want to import more components while TechTrade wants local suppliers — leading to slow decisions and conflict, and profits must be shared.
parts.working: 1 mark for knowledge of the term/concept; up to 2 marks for explaining it in the context of the business (application).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term 'entrepreneur'.
parts.answer: A person who identifies a business opportunity, organises resources (land, labour, capital) to start a business and takes the financial risk.
parts.working: 1 mark: identifies opportunity/starts business; 1 mark: organises factors of production and/or takes risk.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one quality an entrepreneur needs when starting a food-delivery business.
parts.answer: Resilience: many new delivery businesses make losses at first; an entrepreneur must keep going despite setbacks such as late riders or bad reviews, learning and improving until the business becomes profitable. Accept: innovation, risk-taking, self-confidence, hard work, leadership.
parts.working: 1 mark for knowledge of the term/concept; up to 2 marks for explaining it in the context of the business (application).

stem: HerCraft is a new social enterprise in Hunza that trains women to make handicrafts and sells their work online. Its founder has written a business plan and applied to a development bank for a loan of Rs 3 million.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the term 'social enterprise'.
parts.answer: A business with social or environmental objectives that uses most of its profits to further those objectives rather than paying them to owners. HerCraft trains women artisans and reinvests profits in training, so it is a social enterprise.
parts.working: 1 mark: business with social/environmental aims; 1 mark: profits reinvested to meet these aims (triple bottom line); 1 mark: application to HerCraft.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one purpose of a business plan for HerCraft.
parts.answer: To obtain finance: the business plan sets out HerCraft's market research, sales forecasts and cash-flow forecast, which the development bank needs before giving a Rs 3 million loan. Also accept: to set objectives and reduce risk, guide decisions.
parts.working: 1 mark for knowledge of the term/concept; up to 2 marks for explaining it in the context of the business (application).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse one way in which entrepreneurs help the economy of Pakistan.
parts.answer: Entrepreneurs create new businesses that employ people; for example a new software start-up hires graduates, so unemployment falls, incomes rise and these workers spend more, creating demand for other businesses (multiplier effect) and more tax revenue for the government. Accept: innovation, exports/foreign currency, competition and lower prices.
parts.working: Chain: entrepreneurship → jobs/innovation/exports → incomes, tax, economic growth. Marks: knowledge 1, application 1, analysis 3. Level 2 (3–5): a developed chain of analysis (cause → effect → impact) applied to this business. Level 1 (1–2): knowledge with limited application; no developed analysis.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether a business plan is essential for the success of a new mobile app start-up.
parts.answer: Essential: forces founders to research the market and competitors, set objectives, forecast cash flows and costs (apps may take years to earn revenue), and is required by investors and banks, so it helps survival. Not essential: app markets change rapidly — a detailed plan may become out of date quickly; start-ups often succeed by experimenting and changing direction (pivoting) based on user feedback; success depends more on the product, the founders' skills, finance and timing; a plan is only useful if it is realistic and used. Judgement: some form of plan is important, especially to raise venture capital and manage cash, but it should be short and flexible; on its own it does not guarantee success.
parts.working: Purposes and limitations of business plans, specific to app start-ups (fast change, investor finance, uncertain revenue). Mark scheme: AO1 knowledge 2, AO2 application 2, AO3 analysis 2, AO4 evaluation 6. Level 3 (9–12): developed analysis in context plus a supported judgement that answers the question for this business (e.g. 'it depends on…' weighed, with a clear conclusion). Level 2 (5–8): developed analysis with some, limited or unsupported evaluation. Level 1 (1–4): knowledge and some application; little or no analysis.

stem: Zara runs a travel agency in Multan as a sole trader. She wants to expand by opening a second office and is considering forming a private limited company.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the sector of the economy in which Zara's business operates.
parts.answer: Tertiary sector.
parts.working: 1 mark: tertiary (services).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the term 'limited liability'.
parts.answer: The owners (shareholders) of a company are only responsible for its debts up to the amount they invested; their personal assets are safe if the business fails. If Zara forms a private limited company, her house would not be at risk.
parts.working: 1 mark: owners' liability limited to amount invested; 1 mark: personal possessions protected; 1 mark: application.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one disadvantage to Zara of operating as a sole trader.
parts.answer: Unlimited liability: if her travel agency cannot pay its debts, for example after airlines cancel flights and customers demand refunds, Zara's personal assets such as her car could be taken. Also accept: limited capital, long hours, no continuity.
parts.working: 1 mark for knowledge of the term/concept; up to 2 marks for explaining it in the context of the business (application).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term 'public limited company'.
parts.answer: A company owned by shareholders, with limited liability, whose shares can be bought and sold by the public on a stock exchange.
parts.working: 1 mark: limited liability company owned by shareholders; 1 mark: shares sold to the general public / traded on a stock exchange.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one difference between the public sector and the private sector, using an example of each from the healthcare industry.
parts.answer: The public sector is owned and controlled by the government, e.g. a government district hospital, and aims to provide a service for everyone; the private sector is owned by individuals or shareholders, e.g. a private clinic, usually aiming for profit.
parts.working: 1 mark: ownership/control (government vs private individuals); 1 mark: objectives (service vs profit) or finance; 1 mark: suitable examples.

stem: Malik & Sons is a partnership of four brothers that distributes building materials in Lahore. They plan to borrow Rs 40 million to build a new warehouse.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse two advantages for Malik & Sons of converting from a partnership into a private limited company.
parts.answer: 1. Limited liability: the partners currently have unlimited liability for the firm's debts, including the Rs 40 million loan for the new warehouse; as shareholders their personal assets would be protected, so they are more willing to take the expansion risk. 2. Easier to raise capital: the company can sell shares to family members or a new investor without changing the partnership agreement, and banks may lend more to a company with separate legal identity and continuity, helping finance the expansion.
parts.working: Advantages: limited liability, separate legal identity/continuity, raising capital by selling shares (privately), status with suppliers/banks. Mark scheme: AO1 knowledge 2, AO2 application 2, AO3 analysis 4. Level 2 (5–8): two developed chains of analysis, each clearly applied to this business. Level 1 (1–4): knowledge and/or application with undeveloped or generic analysis. Evaluation earns no extra marks.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Zarrar Foods Ltd (an invented company) is a family-owned private limited company making spices and sauces. It needs Rs 2 billion to build a new factory. Bank interest rates are 17 %. The family owns all the shares and wants to keep control.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether Zarrar Foods Ltd should become a public limited company to finance its expansion.
parts.answer: For: an IPO could raise the large sum (Rs 2 billion) needed for the new factory without debt, keeping gearing low as interest rates are high; listing raises status and makes it easier to borrow later. Against: the family may lose control (more than 50 % of shares sold could allow a takeover); costly to float (fees, prospectus) and must publish detailed accounts; shareholders may pressure for short-term dividends, conflicting with the family's long-term objectives; share prices depend on market conditions. Alternatives: bank loans, private equity, selling shares privately. Judgement: depends on how much the family values control and how much finance is needed; selling a minority stake (e.g. 30 %) through flotation could balance finance and control.
parts.working: Weigh finance, control, cost of flotation, disclosure, short-termism, alternatives; context of family ownership. Mark scheme: AO1 knowledge 2, AO2 application 2, AO3 analysis 2, AO4 evaluation 6. Level 3 (9–12): developed analysis in context plus a supported judgement that answers the question for this business (e.g. 'it depends on…' weighed, with a clear conclusion). Level 2 (5–8): developed analysis with some, limited or unsupported evaluation. Level 1 (1–4): knowledge and some application; little or no analysis.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term 'stakeholder'.
parts.answer: Any individual or group that has an interest in, or is affected by, the activities and decisions of a business (e.g. employees, customers, suppliers, the local community, government).
parts.working: 1 mark: individual or group with an interest in / affected by a business; 1 mark: examples or 'affects or is affected by its decisions'.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one difference between a shareholder and a stakeholder.
parts.answer: A shareholder owns part of a company by holding shares and receives dividends; a stakeholder is a wider group — anyone affected by the business, e.g. local residents near a factory — who need not own any part of it. All shareholders are stakeholders, but not all stakeholders are shareholders.
parts.working: 1 mark each for correct description of each; 1 mark for the difference made clear (ownership).

stem: Thar Minerals plans to open a second coal mine in the Thar desert. It would create 800 jobs and increase profits by an estimated 30 %. The mine would use large amounts of underground water, and 3 villages would need to move.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse two possible conflicts between stakeholder groups caused by Thar Minerals' expansion.
parts.answer: 1. Shareholders vs local community: shareholders want the expansion for higher profit and dividends, but villagers face dust, water shortages and loss of grazing land; protests could delay the project and raise costs. 2. Employees vs shareholders: employees want the promised local jobs and higher wages, while managers aim to keep costs low with machinery and contract workers to maximise returns; this may cause disputes. Also: government (revenue) vs environmental groups.
parts.working: Conflicts identified with reasons for each group's objectives and consequences for the business. Mark scheme: AO1 knowledge 2, AO2 application 2, AO3 analysis 4. Level 2 (5–8): two developed chains of analysis, each clearly applied to this business. Level 1 (1–4): knowledge and/or application with undeveloped or generic analysis. Evaluation earns no extra marks.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether shareholders should be the most important stakeholder group for a private hospital.
parts.answer: Shareholders: they provide the capital and own the hospital; without returns they may sell shares or withhold investment needed for new equipment. Other stakeholders: patients' health and safety must come first — ethically, legally (regulation) and commercially (reputation); doctors and nurses are vital and scarce; the government regulates and may refer patients. Conflicts: profit pressure may lead to understaffing or unnecessary tests. Judgement: in a hospital, patient welfare is a precondition of long-term profit, so shareholders' interests are best served by putting patients (and staff) first; shareholders matter most for strategic financing decisions. Stakeholder priority may shift with circumstances (e.g. during a financial crisis).
parts.working: Shareholder vs stakeholder concepts; specific to healthcare; supported judgement. Mark scheme: AO1 knowledge 2, AO2 application 2, AO3 analysis 2, AO4 evaluation 6. Level 3 (9–12): developed analysis in context plus a supported judgement that answers the question for this business (e.g. 'it depends on…' weighed, with a clear conclusion). Level 2 (5–8): developed analysis with some, limited or unsupported evaluation. Level 1 (1–4): knowledge and some application; little or no analysis.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a SMART objective, using an example for a coffee shop.
parts.answer: An objective that is Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Realistic (or Relevant) and Time-bound, e.g. 'increase sales of breakfast items by 15 % within 6 months'.
parts.working: 1 mark: meaning of SMART (at least most letters correct); 1 mark: a valid example meeting all criteria.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why a business might change its objectives.
parts.answer: Changes in the external environment, e.g. a recession: a growing business may switch from growth to survival or cost reduction because demand falls and cash is short. Also accept: new owners/management, change in competition, stage of business life cycle, achievement of previous objectives.
parts.working: 1 mark for knowledge of the term/concept; up to 2 marks for explaining it in the context of the business (application).

stem: ClipShare is a new short-video app launched in Pakistan 18 months ago by two founders with funding from a venture capital firm. It has 2 million users, makes a loss and earns revenue only from a small number of advertisements.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether profit maximisation should be the main objective of ClipShare.
parts.answer: For: investors expect a return; making a profit proves the model works and funds future development. Against: for a new social media platform, network effects mean users and growth (market share) are more important at first — charging or showing many ads too early could drive users to rivals; venture capitalists often accept losses in return for growth; survival (cash flow) may matter more in year one; other objectives (user trust, data security, CSR) protect long-term value. Judgement: in the short term ClipShare should prioritise growth in users and survival; profit maximisation becomes appropriate once a large user base is established — objectives depend on stage of the business life cycle and owners' expectations.
parts.working: Profit maximisation vs survival, growth, market share, CSR; life cycle; stakeholders (investors). Supported judgement. Mark scheme: AO1 knowledge 2, AO2 application 2, AO3 analysis 2, AO4 evaluation 6. Level 3 (9–12): developed analysis in context plus a supported judgement that answers the question for this business (e.g. 'it depends on…' weighed, with a clear conclusion). Level 2 (5–8): developed analysis with some, limited or unsupported evaluation. Level 1 (1–4): knowledge and some application; little or no analysis.

author: HomiLabs

stem: CoolBreeze makes ceiling fans in Gujrat. Its fixed costs are Rs 1,800,000 per month. Each fan sells for Rs 900 (to retailers) and has variable costs of Rs 600.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the break-even level of output per month for CoolBreeze.
parts.answer: 6,000 fans
parts.working: Contribution per unit = 900 − 600 = Rs 300 (M1). Break-even = fixed costs ÷ contribution per unit = 1,800,000 ÷ 300 (M1) = 6,000 fans (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate CoolBreeze's margin of safety in units if it sells 7,500 fans a month.
parts.answer: 1,500 fans
parts.working: Margin of safety = actual output − break-even output (M1) = 7,500 − 6,000 = 1,500 (A1).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term 'contribution per unit'.
parts.answer: The selling price of one unit minus the variable cost of producing that unit; the amount each unit contributes towards fixed costs and then profit.
parts.working: 1 mark: selling price − variable cost per unit; 1 mark: amount available to pay fixed costs / contribute to profit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one limitation of break-even analysis for a business that sells umbrellas.
parts.answer: Break-even analysis assumes all output is sold at a constant price; umbrella sales are highly seasonal and the business may cut prices at the end of the rainy season, so actual sales and revenue may differ greatly from the chart, making the break-even point misleading. Also accept: costs not linear (bulk discounts), fixed costs change, single product assumption, only as accurate as data.
parts.working: 1 mark for knowledge of the term/concept; up to 2 marks for explaining it in the context of the business (application).

stem: Bag Bazaar makes school bags. Its fixed costs are Rs 960,000 per month. Each bag sells for Rs 2,400 and has variable costs of Rs 1,600.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many school bags Bag Bazaar must sell each month to make a profit of Rs 400,000.
parts.answer: 1,700 bags
