parts.working: Contribution per bag = 2,400 − 1,600 = Rs 800 (M1). Required contribution = 960,000 + 400,000 = Rs 1,360,000 (M1). Output = 1,360,000 ÷ 800 = 1,700 bags (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why Bag Bazaar may not achieve its target profit even if it sells this number of bags.
parts.answer: Variable costs may rise — e.g. the price of imported zips and fabric rises after a fall in the rupee — reducing contribution per bag below Rs 800, so the same sales give less profit. Also accept: price cuts to sell that many bags, fixed costs rise.
parts.working: 1 mark for knowledge of the term/concept; up to 2 marks for explaining it in the context of the business (application).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Sitara Shoes normally sells school shoes at Rs 1,600 a pair. Variable costs are Rs 950 a pair and fixed costs are fully covered by current sales. A supermarket chain offers to buy 2,000 extra pairs at Rs 1,150 a pair. Sitara Shoes has spare capacity.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total contribution Sitara Shoes would earn from the special order.
parts.working: Contribution per pair = 1,150 − 950 = Rs 200 (M1). Total = 2,000 × 200 (M1) = Rs 400,000 (A1). (Fixed costs are already covered, so this adds Rs 400,000 to profit.)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one non-financial factor Sitara Shoes should consider before accepting the order.
parts.answer: Existing customers who pay Rs 1,600 may find out that the chain store paid only Rs 1,150 and demand lower prices too, damaging relationships and future revenue. Also accept: capacity/whether the order affects delivery to regular customers, chance of repeat orders, effect on brand image, workforce overtime.
parts.working: 1 mark for knowledge of the term/concept; up to 2 marks for explaining it in the context of the business (application).

author: HomiLabs

stem: GreenCup is a café chain. Its fixed costs are Rs 600,000 a month. It sells coffee at Rs 500 a cup. The variable cost per cup has risen from Rs 260 to Rs 300 because of higher milk and coffee bean prices.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the change in GreenCup's monthly break-even output caused by the rise in variable costs.
parts.answer: Break-even rises from 2,500 to 3,000 cups, an increase of 500 cups.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one way GreenCup could reduce its break-even output.
parts.answer: Raise its price: if customers are loyal to its organic coffee and demand is price inelastic, a higher price increases contribution per cup, so fewer cups are needed to cover the Rs 600,000 of fixed costs. Also accept: cut variable costs (cheaper supplier), cut fixed costs (cheaper rent).
parts.working: 1 mark for knowledge of the term/concept; up to 2 marks for explaining it in the context of the business (application).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Juicy Fresh sells cartons of mango juice to shops at Rs 400 each. It sells 30,000 cartons a month. Variable cost is Rs 220 a carton and fixed costs are Rs 4,500,000 a month. The marketing manager forecasts that if the price rises to Rs 440, sales will fall to 26,000 cartons a month.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the change in Juicy Fresh's monthly profit if it raises its price to Rs 440 and the marketing manager's forecast is correct.
parts.answer: Profit rises from Rs 900,000 to Rs 1,220,000: an increase of Rs 320,000.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate whether Juicy Fresh should raise its price to Rs 440.
parts.answer: For: the calculation shows profit rises by Rs 320,000 a month (about 36 %) because contribution per carton rises from Rs 180 to Rs 220, outweighing the 13 % fall in volume; break-even falls from 25,000 to about 20,455 cartons, so the margin of safety rises from 5,000 to about 5,545 cartons. Against: the forecast of 26,000 cartons may be wrong — if demand is more price elastic (rivals keep prices at Rs 400), sales could fall further; below about 24,545 cartons at Rs 440 the profit would be lower than now (break-even at Rs 440 is 4,500,000 ÷ 220 ≈ 20,455 cartons); lost market share may be hard to regain and retailers may give less shelf space; unit costs may rise as output falls if some costs are semi-variable. Judgement: raise the price only if the forecast is reliable (e.g. based on test pricing) and the brand is strong enough; otherwise a smaller rise or improving the product first.
parts.working: Use the calculation and contribution concept; consider reliability of forecast, PED, competitors, market share, brand, long-term effects. Mark scheme: AO1 knowledge 2, AO2 application 2, AO3 analysis 2, AO4 evaluation 6. Level 3 (9–12): developed analysis in context plus a supported judgement that answers the question for this business (e.g. 'it depends on…' weighed, with a clear conclusion). Level 2 (5–8): developed analysis with some, limited or unsupported evaluation. Level 1 (1–4): knowledge and some application; little or no analysis.

author: HomiLabs

stem: TrekGear makes camping tents. Its fixed costs are Rs 3,150,000 a year and the variable cost of each tent is Rs 1,250.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the price TrekGear must charge for each tent to break even at 4,500 tents a year.
parts.working: At break-even, total revenue = total cost: 4,500 × P = 3,150,000 + 4,500 × 1,250 (M1). Fixed cost per tent = 3,150,000 ÷ 4,500 = Rs 700 (M1). P = 700 + 1,250 = Rs 1,950 (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: TrekGear sets this price and sells 6,000 tents. Calculate its margin of safety in sales revenue.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate what TrekGear's profit would be at 6,000 tents.
parts.working: Each tent beyond break-even adds its contribution: 1,500 × (1,950 − 1,250) = Rs 1,050,000 (M1 A1).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Extract from the statement of financial position of Medico Pharmacies (Rs million): inventory 7.6; trade receivables 6.2; cash 4.6; total current assets 18.4; current liabilities 11.5.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Medico Pharmacies' current ratio and acid test ratio. Give your answers to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: Current ratio 1.60 : 1; acid test ratio 0.94 : 1
parts.working: Current ratio = current assets ÷ current liabilities = 18.4 ÷ 11.5 (M1) = 1.60 (A1). Acid test = (current assets − inventory) ÷ current liabilities = (18.4 − 7.6) ÷ 11.5 (M1) = 0.94 (A1).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Mehran Electronics, income statement extract for the year (Rs million): revenue 84.0; cost of sales 50.4; operating expenses (overheads) 21.0.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Mehran Electronics' gross profit margin and operating profit margin.
parts.answer: Gross profit margin 40 %; operating profit margin 15 %

parts.label: b
parts.text: Mehran Electronics' operating profit margin was 18 % last year. Explain one possible reason for the change.
parts.answer: Operating (overhead) expenses have risen relative to sales, e.g. higher rent or advertising for new stores, so less of each rupee of revenue is left as operating profit.
parts.working: 1 mark: valid reason (overheads up / gross margin down); 1 mark: explained.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Karakoram Cement, latest accounts (Rs million): operating profit 27; total equity 120; non-current liabilities 60.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Karakoram Cement's return on capital employed (ROCE) and gearing ratio.
parts.answer: ROCE 15 %; gearing 33.3 %
parts.working: Capital employed = equity + non-current liabilities = 120 + 60 = 180 (M1). ROCE = 27 ÷ 180 × 100 = 15 % (A1). Gearing = non-current liabilities ÷ capital employed × 100 = 60 ÷ 180 × 100 (M1) = 33.3 % (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain whether Karakoram Cement should finance a new kiln with a further Rs 40 million long-term loan.
parts.answer: New gearing = 100 ÷ 220 × 100 = 45.5 %, which is above 40 %, so the company would become highly geared; interest payments would rise when interest rates are high, increasing risk. However, ROCE (15 %) may be above the interest rate, so borrowing could increase returns to shareholders if the kiln earns a similar return. Judgement: possible, but risky — consider equity or a smaller loan.
parts.working: 1 mark: new gearing calculated or recognised as rising above 40–45 %; 1 mark: risk of interest burden; 1 mark: compare ROCE with interest rate; 1 mark: judgement.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Royal Furnishings sells furniture to hotels on credit. Data for the year (Rs million): revenue 60; cost of sales 36; opening inventory 5; closing inventory 7; trade receivables at year end 9.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Royal Furnishings' inventory turnover ratio (times per year).
parts.answer: 6 times
parts.working: Average inventory = (5 + 7) ÷ 2 = 6 (M1). Inventory turnover = cost of sales ÷ average inventory = 36 ÷ 6 = 6 times (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate Royal Furnishings' days' sales in receivables. Give your answer to the nearest day.
parts.answer: 55 days
parts.working: Trade receivables ÷ revenue × 365 (M1) = 9 ÷ 60 × 365 = 54.75 ≈ 55 days (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Royal Furnishings gives customers 30 days' credit. Explain one way it could improve its days' sales in receivables.
parts.answer: Chase overdue customers or offer a small discount for payment within 30 days, so cash is collected sooner and receivables fall from about 55 days towards 30. Also accept debt factoring, stricter credit checks.
parts.working: 1 mark: valid method; 1 mark: explained effect.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Saffron Weaves plc (an invented company), latest year: profit for the year after tax Rs 450 million; number of shares issued 150 million; total dividends paid Rs 180 million; current share price Rs 40.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Saffron Weaves plc's dividend per share and dividend yield.
parts.answer: Dividend per share Rs 1.20; dividend yield 3 %
parts.working: DPS = total dividends ÷ number of shares = 180 ÷ 150 = Rs 1.20 (M1 A1). Dividend yield = DPS ÷ share price × 100 = 1.20 ÷ 40 × 100 = 3 % (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate Saffron Weaves plc's dividend cover.
parts.answer: 2.5 times
parts.working: Dividend cover = profit for the year (after tax) ÷ total dividends = 450 ÷ 180 (M1) = 2.5 times (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain what the dividend cover tells a potential shareholder.
parts.answer: Profit is 2.5 times the dividend paid, so the dividend is well covered — it could be maintained even if profit fell, and 60 % of profit is retained for reinvestment.
parts.working: 1 mark: interpretation of 2.5 (dividend affordable/safe); 1 mark: retained profit / sustainability of dividend.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Horizon Hotels (Rs million): operating profit 2024: 36, 2025: 33. Capital employed 2024: 240, 2025: 300. In October 2025 the company opened a new resort in Swat, financed by a Rs 60 million loan.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Horizon Hotels' ROCE for 2024 and 2025.
parts.working: ROCE = operating profit ÷ capital employed × 100 (M1). 2024: 36 ÷ 240 × 100 = 15 % (A1). 2025: 33 ÷ 300 × 100 = 11 % (M1 A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate whether ratio analysis gives an investor enough information to decide whether to buy shares in Horizon Hotels.
parts.answer: Useful: ROCE fell from 15 % to 11 % after the Rs 60 million investment in the new resort, suggesting capital is being used less efficiently; ratios allow comparison over time and with rivals, and liquidity/gearing ratios show risk. Limitations: the new resort opened late in 2025, so its full profit is not yet included — ROCE may recover; ratios use historical data, while investors care about the future (tourism forecasts, security situation, exchange rates); no industry benchmark is given; accounts can be window-dressed; non-financial factors (brand, management quality, reviews, location) matter. Judgement: ratios are a useful starting point but not enough; the investor needs trend data over several years, competitor ratios, investor ratios (dividend yield, P/E) and qualitative information about the resort's prospects.
parts.working: Use the ROCE result and the timing of the investment; limitations of ratio analysis; other information needed; judgement. Mark scheme: AO1 knowledge 2, AO2 application 2, AO3 analysis 2, AO4 evaluation 6. Level 3 (9–12): developed analysis in context plus a supported judgement that answers the question for this business (e.g. 'it depends on…' weighed, with a clear conclusion). Level 2 (5–8): developed analysis with some, limited or unsupported evaluation. Level 1 (1–4): knowledge and some application; little or no analysis.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Noor Traders, a wholesaler, has current liabilities of Rs 400,000. Its current ratio is 1.5 : 1 and its acid test ratio is 0.9 : 1.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the value of Noor Traders' inventory.
parts.working: Current assets = 1.5 × 400,000 = Rs 600,000 (M1). Current assets − inventory = 0.9 × 400,000 = Rs 360,000 (M1). Inventory = 600,000 − 360,000 = Rs 240,000 (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Noor Traders uses Rs 100,000 of its cash to pay suppliers (trade payables). Calculate the new current ratio. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why this payment improves the current ratio even though the business has less cash.
parts.answer: Equal amounts are removed from current assets and current liabilities; because the ratio is above 1, the liabilities fall by a larger proportion (25 %) than the assets (about 17 %), so the ratio rises.
parts.working: 1 mark: both CA and CL fall by the same amount; 1 mark: proportional effect when the ratio is above 1.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Need for finance and sources of finance

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term 'capital expenditure'.
parts.answer: Spending on non-current assets that will be used in the business for more than one year, such as buildings, machinery and vehicles.
parts.working: 1 mark: purchase of non-current/fixed assets; 1 mark: used for more than one year (with example).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one difference between capital expenditure and revenue expenditure for a printing business.
parts.answer: Capital expenditure buys long-lasting assets, e.g. a new printing press used for ten years; revenue expenditure is spending on day-to-day running costs used up within the year, e.g. ink, paper and wages. Revenue expenditure is recorded as a cost in the income statement, capital expenditure on the statement of financial position.
parts.working: 1 mark each: correct meaning of each with printing examples; 1 mark: the difference (time period / accounting treatment).

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Need for finance and sources of finance
stem: Fashion Avenue is a clothing retailer that owns its head office building in Lahore. It needs Rs 25 million to open 5 new stores and is considering several sources of finance, including crowdfunding.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify one internal source of finance available to Fashion Avenue.
parts.answer: Retained earnings (also accept sale of assets / sale and leaseback / reducing inventory).
parts.working: 1 mark: retained earnings or sale of assets.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the term 'sale and leaseback'.
parts.answer: Selling a non-current asset, such as a building, to another organisation and immediately renting (leasing) it back, so the business raises a lump sum of cash but keeps using the asset. Fashion Avenue could sell its Lahore head office to a property company and lease it back.
parts.working: 1 mark: sell an asset; 1 mark: lease/rent it back and continue to use it; 1 mark: application.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one disadvantage to Fashion Avenue of using crowdfunding to raise finance.
parts.answer: If the target (Rs 25 million) is not reached, Fashion Avenue may receive nothing; the campaign also makes its expansion plans public, so rival retailers can copy its new store concept. Also accept: cost of the platform fee and rewards, time-consuming.
parts.working: 1 mark for knowledge of the term/concept; up to 2 marks for explaining it in the context of the business (application).

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Need for finance and sources of finance

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse two factors City Metro Buses should consider when choosing a source of finance to buy 10 electric buses costing Rs 300 million.
parts.answer: 1. Cost of finance: a bank loan at 17 % interest would add large interest payments each year, reducing profit; a government green grant would be cheaper (no repayment), so City Metro should check eligibility. 2. Gearing and risk: the company already has large loans; more debt raises gearing and the risk of being unable to repay if passenger numbers fall, so leasing the buses or issuing shares may be safer. Also: amount needed, use (long-term asset → long-term finance), legal form, control.
parts.working: Factors: cost, amount, time period/use, existing gearing, legal structure, control, flexibility, availability of grants. Mark scheme: AO1 knowledge 2, AO2 application 2, AO3 analysis 4. Level 2 (5–8): two developed chains of analysis, each clearly applied to this business. Level 1 (1–4): knowledge and/or application with undeveloped or generic analysis. Evaluation earns no extra marks.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Need for finance and sources of finance

parts.label: a
parts.text: A pharmacy chain with 15 branches wants to open 10 more branches. Evaluate whether retained earnings are the best source of finance for this expansion.
parts.answer: For: no interest or repayment, so no extra cash outflow; no loss of control (no new shareholders); no gearing increase; quick to access. Against: may not be enough — opening 10 branches needs large sums for leases, fit-out and inventory; using all retained profit leaves little for emergencies and working capital (medicine inventory); shareholders may want dividends; opportunity cost. Alternatives: bank loan (if ROCE > interest rate, increases returns), leasing equipment, issuing shares, supplier credit for inventory. Judgement: retained earnings are the best starting point but probably insufficient; a mix — retained earnings plus a medium-term loan or phased opening — is likely best, depending on the amount of profit retained and the current gearing.
parts.working: Compare retained earnings with alternatives on cost, control, risk, amount, time; judgement for pharmacy chain. Mark scheme: AO1 knowledge 2, AO2 application 2, AO3 analysis 2, AO4 evaluation 6. Level 3 (9–12): developed analysis in context plus a supported judgement that answers the question for this business (e.g. 'it depends on…' weighed, with a clear conclusion). Level 2 (5–8): developed analysis with some, limited or unsupported evaluation. Level 1 (1–4): knowledge and some application; little or no analysis.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Silk Route Café, budget and actual figures for March (Rs): Sales revenue — budget 1,500,000, actual 1,380,000. Total costs — budget 1,100,000, actual 1,050,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the variance for sales revenue, total costs and profit for Silk Route Café in March, stating whether each is favourable or adverse.
parts.answer: Sales revenue: Rs 120,000 adverse; total costs: Rs 50,000 favourable; profit: Rs 70,000 adverse.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one benefit to Silk Route Café of setting budgets.
parts.answer: Budgets set targets for each month, so the owner can compare actual results with the plan; the adverse revenue variance in March alerts her quickly to falling sales so she can act, e.g. by promoting evening meals. Also accept: control of spending, motivation, coordination, planning.
parts.working: 1 mark for knowledge of the term/concept; up to 2 marks for explaining it in the context of the business (application).

author: HomiLabs

stem: TileWorks budgeted to make 10,000 boxes of floor tiles in April with a material cost of Rs 4,500,000. It actually made 11,000 boxes, and the actual material cost was Rs 5,200,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the flexed budget for material costs and the material cost variance, stating whether it is favourable or adverse.
parts.answer: Flexed budget Rs 4,950,000; variance Rs 250,000 adverse.
parts.working: Budgeted material cost per unit = 4,500,000 ÷ 10,000 = Rs 450 (M1). Flexed budget = 11,000 × 450 = Rs 4,950,000 (M1). Variance = 5,200,000 − 4,950,000 = Rs 250,000 adverse (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why comparing actual material costs with the original budget would be misleading.
parts.answer: The original budget was for 10,000 units but 11,000 were made; comparing Rs 5.2 million with Rs 4.5 million shows a Rs 700,000 adverse variance, but most of that is due to the higher output, not inefficiency. The flexed budget shows the true overspend is only Rs 250,000, which may be due to higher material prices or wastage.
parts.working: 1 mark: different output levels; 1 mark: the original variance overstates the problem (with figures); 1 mark: flexed variance reflects efficiency/price.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether zero-based budgeting is suitable for a private university.
parts.answer: Benefits: each department (e.g. engineering, business, administration) must justify every rupee from zero each year, which removes wasteful spending carried forward from previous budgets, and allocates funds to priorities such as new courses and IT; encourages managers to think about value for money. Drawbacks: very time-consuming for many departments and academics; managers may exaggerate needs; may favour short-term savings over long-term research; requires skilled managers; may create conflict between faculties. Alternatives: incremental budgeting (simple but may continue waste), flexible budgets. Judgement: suitable for discretionary areas (marketing, administration, events) or every few years, but full annual ZBB for all departments is likely too costly; depends on whether the university faces financial pressure.
parts.working: Explain ZBB vs incremental; benefits and costs in the university context; judgement. Mark scheme: AO1 knowledge 2, AO2 application 2, AO3 analysis 2, AO4 evaluation 6. Level 3 (9–12): developed analysis in context plus a supported judgement that answers the question for this business (e.g. 'it depends on…' weighed, with a clear conclusion). Level 2 (5–8): developed analysis with some, limited or unsupported evaluation. Level 1 (1–4): knowledge and some application; little or no analysis.

stem: Paragon Stationers, data for the year (Rs million): revenue 42.0; purchases 27.0; opening inventory 4.0; closing inventory 6.0; operating expenses 9.5.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Paragon Stationers' cost of sales for the year.
parts.answer: Rs 25.0 million
parts.working: Cost of sales = opening inventory + purchases − closing inventory (M1) = 4.0 + 27.0 − 6.0 = Rs 25.0 million (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate Paragon Stationers' gross profit and operating profit.
parts.answer: Gross profit Rs 17.0 million; operating profit Rs 7.5 million
parts.working: Gross profit = 42.0 − 25.0 = Rs 17.0m (B1). Operating profit = 17.0 − 9.5 = Rs 7.5m (B1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one reason why a business with a high operating profit could still run short of cash.
parts.answer: Profit is recorded when sales are made, not when cash is received; if Paragon sells to schools on 90 days' credit, it may have high profit but little cash to pay suppliers and wages. Also accept: cash spent on non-current assets or inventory, loan repayments.
parts.working: 1 mark for knowledge of the term/concept; up to 2 marks for explaining it in the context of the business (application).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Hilltop Foods, statement of financial position extract (Rs million): non-current assets 85; current assets 30; current liabilities 18; non-current liabilities 25.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Hilltop Foods' working capital (net current assets).
parts.answer: Rs 12 million
parts.working: 30 − 18 = Rs 12 million (B1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate Hilltop Foods' net assets and state the value of total equity.
parts.answer: Net assets = total equity = Rs 72 million
parts.working: Net assets = non-current assets + current assets − current liabilities − non-current liabilities (M1) = 85 + 30 − 18 − 25 (M1) = Rs 72 million; total equity equals net assets = Rs 72 million (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Hilltop Foods holds inventory of frozen food that cost Rs 2 million but, because it is close to its sell-by date, can now only be sold for Rs 1.2 million. Explain how this inventory should be valued and the effect on profit.
parts.answer: Inventory is valued at the lower of cost and net realisable value, so it should be recorded at Rs 1.2 million, not Rs 2 million. Writing it down by Rs 0.8 million reduces the value of current assets and reduces profit for the year by Rs 0.8 million.
parts.working: 1 mark: lower of cost and net realisable value; 1 mark: value Rs 1.2m; 1 mark: profit and current assets fall by Rs 0.8m.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Tandoor Express is a restaurant chain. It opened 6 new branches in 2025 (now 20 branches). Data (Rs million): 2024 — revenue 120, gross profit 54, operating profit 14.4. 2025 — revenue 150, gross profit 58.5, operating profit 12.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Tandoor Express's gross profit margin and operating profit margin for 2024 and 2025.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate whether raising menu prices is the best way for Tandoor Express to improve its profitability.
parts.answer: Evidence: revenue grew 25 % after opening 6 new branches, but both margins fell — GPM from 45 % to 39 % (food costs rising faster than prices, or discounting) and OPM from 12 % to 8 % (higher overheads such as rent of new branches). Raising prices: would restore gross margin if demand is price inelastic (loyal customers, strong brand), but in a competitive casual-dining market customers may switch to rivals, reducing volume and revenue. Alternatives: cut food costs (bulk buying across 20 branches, reduce waste, menu engineering), control overheads (close loss-making branches, renegotiate rents), increase sales per branch (delivery apps, promotions at quiet times). Judgement: a small, targeted price rise on popular dishes may help, but the main problem is costs after rapid expansion, so cost control is likely more effective; depends on PED and rivals' prices.
parts.working: Use calculated margins to diagnose the cause; weigh price rise vs cost control vs volume; PED; judgement. Mark scheme: AO1 knowledge 2, AO2 application 2, AO3 analysis 2, AO4 evaluation 6. Level 3 (9–12): developed analysis in context plus a supported judgement that answers the question for this business (e.g. 'it depends on…' weighed, with a clear conclusion). Level 2 (5–8): developed analysis with some, limited or unsupported evaluation. Level 1 (1–4): knowledge and some application; little or no analysis.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Kids Corner sells children's clothes. Cash-flow forecast (Rs): opening balance on 1 July 150,000. Cash inflows — July 620,000; August 540,000; September 710,000. Cash outflows — July 580,000; August 690,000; September 640,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the net cash flow and closing balance for each month.
parts.answer: July: net +40,000, closing 190,000. August: net −150,000, closing 40,000. September: net +70,000, closing 110,000.
parts.working: Net cash flow = inflows − outflows (M1). July 620,000 − 580,000 = +40,000; closing 150,000 + 40,000 = 190,000 (A1). August −150,000; closing 40,000 (A1). September +70,000; closing 110,000 (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one way Kids Corner could deal with the negative net cash flow in August.
parts.answer: Arrange a short-term bank overdraft for August, when it buys school uniforms in bulk, to cover the outflow until September sales come in. Also accept: delay payment to suppliers, ask for supplier credit, reduce purchases, sell surplus inventory.
parts.working: 1 mark for knowledge of the term/concept; up to 2 marks for explaining it in the context of the business (application).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Pak Agro Supplies sells seeds and fertiliser to farmers on credit until harvest. Current assets: inventory Rs 3,600,000; trade receivables Rs 2,900,000; cash Rs 500,000. Current liabilities: Rs 4,300,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Pak Agro Supplies' working capital.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how debt factoring could improve Pak Agro Supplies' cash flow.
parts.answer: A factoring company would pay Pak Agro around 80–90 % of the Rs 2.9 million owed by farmers immediately, instead of waiting until harvest when farmers pay, so it has cash now to buy fertiliser; the cost is the factor's fee, which reduces profit.
parts.working: 1 mark for knowledge of the term/concept; up to 2 marks for explaining it in the context of the business (application).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one danger of holding too much working capital.
parts.answer: Money tied up in excess inventory or cash earns no return (opportunity cost); for example, unsold seed stock may go out of date.
parts.working: 1 mark: idle resources/opportunity cost; 1 mark: example or consequence.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether cash flow is more important than profit for a new event-management company.
parts.answer: Cash flow more important: new firms often fail from lack of cash, not lack of profit; the company must pay venues, caterers and staff in advance of events, while clients may pay after the event; without cash it cannot pay suppliers and may be forced to close even with profitable bookings; banks are cautious with new firms. Profit important: over time the business must be profitable to survive, reward owners and attract investment; a positive cash flow from loans or owners' capital cannot last if events are priced below cost. Judgement: in the first year cash flow is more important for survival (manage deposits, payment terms, overdraft), but profit becomes the key measure of long-term success; both are linked — managing deposits from clients can help both.
parts.working: Difference between cash and profit; timing of payments for events; survival vs long-term; judgement. Mark scheme: AO1 knowledge 2, AO2 application 2, AO3 analysis 2, AO4 evaluation 6. Level 3 (9–12): developed analysis in context plus a supported judgement that answers the question for this business (e.g. 'it depends on…' weighed, with a clear conclusion). Level 2 (5–8): developed analysis with some, limited or unsupported evaluation. Level 1 (1–4): knowledge and some application; little or no analysis.

stem: Golden Biscuits is considering a new oven costing Rs 12 million. Expected net cash flows (Rs million): Year 1: 3.0; Year 2: 4.0; Year 3: 4.5; Year 4: 4.5; Year 5: 3.0. The oven has no value at the end of Year 5.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the payback period for the new oven. Give your answer in years and months.
parts.answer: 3 years 1 month
parts.working: Cumulative cash flow: end Y1 3.0m, Y2 7.0m, Y3 11.5m (M1). Remaining 0.5m ÷ 4.5m × 12 = 1.33 ≈ 1 month → payback 3 years 1 month (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the average rate of return (ARR) for the new oven.
parts.working: Total net cash flow = 19.0m; total profit = 19.0 − 12.0 = 7.0m (M1). Annual average profit = 7.0 ÷ 5 = 1.4m (M1). ARR = 1.4 ÷ 12.0 × 100 = 11.7 % (A1).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Fresh Fields, a fruit exporter, is considering building a cold store costing Rs 16 million. Expected net cash flows (Rs million): Year 1: 5.0; Year 2: 6.0; Year 3: 6.0; Year 4: 4.0. Discount factors at 10 %: Year 1 0.909; Year 2 0.826; Year 3 0.751; Year 4 0.683.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the net present value (NPV) of the cold store project.
parts.answer: Rs 0.739 million (about Rs 739,000)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why the NPV result may be unreliable.
parts.answer: The cash flows are forecasts four years ahead; fruit harvests, electricity prices or the rental demand for cold storage may differ, and the 10 % discount rate may change if interest rates rise.
parts.working: 1 mark: forecasts uncertain / discount rate choice; 1 mark: explained with context.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Al-Noor Retail has Rs 22 million to invest and must choose one project. Expected net cash flows (Rs million): Project A (automated warehouse line): Year 1: 9; Year 2: 9; Year 3: 9. Project B (two new stores): Year 1: 4; Year 2: 9; Year 3: 15. Discount factors at 8 %: Year 1 0.926; Year 2 0.857; Year 3 0.794.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the NPV of each project at a discount rate of 8 %.
parts.answer: Project A (automated line): Rs 1.193 million. Project B (new store openings): Rs 1.327 million.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate which project Al-Noor Retail should choose.
parts.answer: Financial: both have positive NPV; B is slightly higher (Rs 1.327m vs Rs 1.193m) but the difference is small. A has a slightly quicker payback (about 2 years 5 months vs about 2 years 7 months) but returns much more cash early (Rs 18m in two years versus Rs 13m) and steadier cash flows, so it is less risky; B depends on large, uncertain cash flows in Year 3 from new stores. Non-financial: A (automation in the warehouse) may cause redundancies and resistance but improves efficiency and accuracy; B builds market presence and brand, supporting growth objectives; B's forecasts depend on market research reliability and competition. Judgement: given the small NPV difference, choose A if the company is short of cash or risk-averse; choose B if its objective is growth and the store forecasts are reliable. A sensitivity check of B's Year 3 cash flow is needed.
parts.working: Use NPV results (payback A: 2 + 4/9 years ≈ 2 years 5 months; B: 2 + 9/15 years ≈ 2 years 7 months) plus payback/risk and qualitative factors (objectives, staff, market). Supported decision. Mark scheme: AO1 knowledge 2, AO2 application 2, AO3 analysis 2, AO4 evaluation 6. Level 3 (9–12): developed analysis in context plus a supported judgement that answers the question for this business (e.g. 'it depends on…' weighed, with a clear conclusion). Level 2 (5–8): developed analysis with some, limited or unsupported evaluation. Level 1 (1–4): knowledge and some application; little or no analysis.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Product, branding and new product development

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term 'product life cycle'.
parts.answer: The stages a product passes through from its launch to its withdrawal from the market: introduction, growth, maturity and decline (with development before launch), shown by its sales over time.
parts.working: 1 mark: stages a product goes through over time / sales over its life; 1 mark: names stages (introduction, growth, maturity, decline).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one extension strategy a company could use for a brand of washing powder in the maturity stage.
parts.answer: Relaunch it with a new formula (e.g. 'works in cold water') and new packaging, advertised to show the benefit; this gives customers a reason to buy again, so sales rise and the maturity stage is extended. Also accept: new markets, new uses, new sizes, price cut, promotions.
parts.working: 1 mark for knowledge of the term/concept; up to 2 marks for explaining it in the context of the business (application).

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Product, branding and new product development
stem: SnackPak's main brand, Crunchy Chips, has sold about 2 million packs a month for four years. SnackPak is developing baked lentil crisps for health-conscious consumers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the stage of the product life cycle that Crunchy Chips appears to be in.
parts.answer: Maturity (or saturation).
parts.working: 1 mark: maturity — sales high but no longer growing.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the term 'new product development'.
parts.answer: The process of creating a new product, from generating and screening ideas, concept testing, business analysis and product development to test marketing and launch. For SnackPak, developing baked lentil crisps would involve this process.
parts.working: 1 mark: creating/designing new products; 1 mark: stages of the process (ideas → screening → development → test → launch); 1 mark: application.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one benefit to SnackPak of test marketing its baked lentil crisps before a national launch.
parts.answer: Selling the crisps in one city first (e.g. Islamabad) shows real customer reactions to taste, price and packaging; SnackPak can change the product before spending heavily on a national launch, reducing the risk of an expensive failure.
parts.working: 1 mark for knowledge of the term/concept; up to 2 marks for explaining it in the context of the business (application).

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Product, branding and new product development
stem: BrightHome sells home electrical goods. Its SolarLite solar lamps had sales of Rs 45 million last year in a market worth Rs 300 million, growing at 18 % a year. The market leader had sales of Rs 60 million. BrightHome's AC Fans are the market leader in a market that is no longer growing.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the market share of SolarLite lamps.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate SolarLite's relative market share compared with the market leader.
parts.working: Relative market share = own share ÷ largest rival's share = 45 ÷ 60 (M1) = 0.75 (A1) — below 1, so SolarLite is not the market leader.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Using the Boston Matrix, explain one reason why BrightHome should continue to invest in SolarLite lamps.
parts.answer: SolarLite is in a fast-growing market (18 % a year) but has a relative share below 1, so it is a question mark (problem child); with investment in promotion and distribution it could increase share and become a star, and later a cash cow, providing future cash flow when the AC Fans cash cow declines.
parts.working: 1 mark: identifies question mark (high growth, low relative share); 1 mark: investment could make it a star; 1 mark: portfolio balance/future cash.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Product, branding and new product development

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse one benefit to a bottled water company of having a strong brand.
parts.answer: Bottled water is similar whatever the brand, so a strong, trusted brand (associated with purity and safety) creates customer loyalty; customers choose it over cheaper rivals, so demand becomes more price inelastic and the company can charge a premium price, increasing its profit margin. Also accept: easier to launch new products, retailers give shelf space.
parts.working: Chain: brand → recognition/trust/loyalty → less price sensitive/repeat purchases → higher price/sales/profit. Marks: knowledge 1, application 1, analysis 3. Level 2 (3–5): a developed chain of analysis (cause → effect → impact) applied to this business. Level 1 (1–2): knowledge with limited application; no developed analysis.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Product, branding and new product development
stem: MediGen is a Pakistani pharmaceutical company that mostly makes generic medicines (copies of medicines whose patents have expired). Its profit fell by 20 % last year as several new competitors cut prices. It currently spends 1 % of revenue on R&D; multinational rivals spend about 15 %.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether increasing spending on research and development (R&D) is the best way for MediGen to remain competitive.
parts.answer: For: in pharmaceuticals, new and improved medicines (and patents) provide a USP and higher margins; MediGen's main products are generics facing price competition, so R&D into new formulations could differentiate it; R&D can also improve processes, lowering costs. Against: R&D is very expensive and risky — most projects fail and returns come after many years; MediGen's profit has fallen, so finance is limited; larger multinationals have far bigger R&D budgets. Alternatives: cost leadership through efficient production of generics, licensing products from overseas firms, joint ventures, strong distribution to pharmacies and doctors, export markets. Judgement: some targeted R&D (e.g. improving delivery forms of existing medicines) is worthwhile, but given limited funds and the generic market, efficiency and marketing may be more important in the short term; depends on finance and the firm's long-term strategy.
parts.working: R&D benefits/risks in context of a generic medicine maker; alternative routes to competitiveness; judgement. Mark scheme: AO1 knowledge 2, AO2 application 2, AO3 analysis 2, AO4 evaluation 6. Level 3 (9–12): developed analysis in context plus a supported judgement that answers the question for this business (e.g. 'it depends on…' weighed, with a clear conclusion). Level 2 (5–8): developed analysis with some, limited or unsupported evaluation. Level 1 (1–4): knowledge and some application; little or no analysis.

author: HomiLabs

stem: ComfortStep sells trainers online. When it raised the price from Rs 500 (per pair, wholesale) to Rs 550, weekly sales fell from 2,000 pairs to 1,700 pairs.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the price elasticity of demand for ComfortStep's trainers.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the change in ComfortStep's weekly revenue from the trainers.
parts.answer: Revenue falls by Rs 65,000

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the revenue changed in this way.
parts.answer: Demand is price elastic (PED −1.5, greater than 1 in absolute value): the percentage fall in quantity is larger than the percentage rise in price, so total revenue falls.
parts.working: 1 mark: demand elastic; 1 mark: %ΔQ > %ΔP so revenue falls.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Royal Tours sells holiday packages in Pakistan. Average real incomes rose by 6 % and the number of holidays sold rose from 40,000 to 43,600, with no other changes. In a separate period, a 20 % increase in advertising spending led to a 5 % increase in holidays sold.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the income elasticity of demand for Royal Tours' holidays.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the promotional (advertising) elasticity of demand.
parts.working: Promotional elasticity = %Δ quantity demanded ÷ %Δ advertising spending = 5 ÷ 20 (M1) = 0.25 (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how Royal Tours could use these results in its marketing planning.
parts.answer: Holidays are a luxury (YED +1.5), so demand will rise strongly when incomes grow; Royal Tours can plan more capacity and premium packages in a boom, but should prepare for a sharp fall in a recession. The low promotional elasticity (0.25) shows extra advertising has little effect on sales, so it may be better to spend on other parts of the mix.
parts.working: 1 mark: interprets YED (luxury, sensitive to income); 1 mark: interprets promotional elasticity (inelastic, advertising ineffective); 1 mark: planning use.

author: HomiLabs

stem: PureCool sells air coolers. Quarterly sales (thousand units): Year 1 — Q1 42, Q2 58, Q3 66, Q4 50. Year 2 — Q1 46, Q2 62, Q3 74, Q4 54.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the four-quarter centred moving average for Year 1 Quarter 3 and Year 1 Quarter 4.
parts.answer: Year 1 Q3: 54.5; Year 1 Q4: 55.5 (thousand units)
parts.working: Four-quarter moving totals: Y1Q1–Q4 = 216; Y1Q2–Y2Q1 = 220; Y1Q3–Y2Q2 = 224 (M1). Centred total for Y1Q3 = 216 + 220 = 436; ÷ 8 = 54.5 (M1 A1). Y1Q4 = (220 + 224) ÷ 8 = 55.5 (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the seasonal variation for Year 1 Quarter 3.
parts.working: Actual − centred moving average = 66 − 54.5 = +11.5 (B1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one limitation of using moving averages to forecast PureCool's sales.
parts.answer: Moving averages assume past trends and seasonal patterns will continue; an unusually hot summer, a new competitor or a price change would make the forecast inaccurate.
parts.working: 1 mark: based on past data/assumes continuation; 1 mark: example of external change for an air cooler business.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Frosty sells ice cream tubs. Quarterly sales (thousand tubs): Year 1 — Q1 120, Q2 210, Q3 260, Q4 150. Year 2 — Q1 132, Q2 226, Q3 284, Q4 162.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the centred moving averages for Year 1 Quarter 3 and Year 2 Quarter 2.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the average change in the trend per quarter between Year 1 Quarter 3 and Year 2 Quarter 2.
parts.answer: 4.33 thousand per quarter

parts.label: c
parts.text: Using the trend and the Year 1 Quarter 3 seasonal variation, forecast Frosty's sales for Year 3 Quarter 3. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: 294.7 thousand tubs
parts.working: Seasonal variation Y1Q3 = 260 − 186.5 = +73.5 (M1). Y3Q3 is 5 quarters after Y2Q2 (M1). Trend = 199.5 + 5 × 4.3333 = 221.17 (M1). Forecast = 221.17 + 73.5 = 294.7 (A1).

author: HomiLabs

stem: AirIndus (an invented airline) carries 50,000 leisure passengers a month at an average fare of Rs 30,000. Its estimates: PED for leisure passengers −1.8; PED for business passengers −0.4. It has some empty seats on most flights.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the forecast change in monthly revenue from leisure passengers if AirIndus cuts leisure fares by 10 %.
parts.answer: Revenue rises from Rs 1.500 billion to Rs 1.593 billion: an increase of Rs 93 million.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate how useful price elasticity of demand estimates are to AirIndus when setting its fares.
parts.answer: Useful: they show leisure demand is elastic (−1.8), so a fare cut raises revenue (by Rs 93 million a month), while business demand is inelastic (−0.4), so business fares could be raised to increase revenue; supports price discrimination between segments. Limitations: PED estimates are based on past data and may change (new low-cost rival, recession, fuel costs); they assume other things are equal; revenue rising does not mean profit rises — 9,000 extra passengers need seats (capacity, load factor) and add variable costs (fuel, catering); rivals may match the cut, so the forecast increase may not happen; PED varies along the demand curve, so a larger cut may give a different result. Judgement: PED estimates are a useful guide for segment pricing, but AirIndus should combine them with cost/capacity data and competitor analysis and update them regularly.
parts.working: Use the calculation; PED by segment; assumptions and limitations; revenue vs profit; competitor reaction; judgement. Mark scheme: AO1 knowledge 2, AO2 application 2, AO3 analysis 2, AO4 evaluation 6. Level 3 (9–12): developed analysis in context plus a supported judgement that answers the question for this business (e.g. 'it depends on…' weighed, with a clear conclusion). Level 2 (5–8): developed analysis with some, limited or unsupported evaluation. Level 1 (1–4): knowledge and some application; little or no analysis.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term 'marketing objective'.
parts.answer: A goal for the marketing department, which helps achieve the business's corporate objectives, e.g. to increase market share to 20 % within two years.
parts.working: 1 mark: target/goal for marketing (sales, market share, brand awareness); 1 mark: linked to corporate objectives or with example.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why marketing objectives should be linked to a business's corporate objectives.
parts.answer: If a phone retailer's corporate objective is growth, a marketing objective such as increasing market share in new cities ensures marketing spending supports the overall aim rather than conflicting with it, e.g. by focusing on profit margin instead. This coordinates departments and uses resources efficiently.
parts.working: 1 mark for knowledge of the term/concept; up to 2 marks for explaining it in the context of the business (application).

stem: Nisa Organics sells premium organic flour, rice and honey in Karachi to high-income health-conscious families. It plans a new marketing strategy.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the term 'coordinated (integrated) marketing mix'.
parts.answer: The elements of the marketing mix (product, price, promotion, place) are consistent with each other and with the target market. For Nisa Organics, a premium organic product should have a premium price, be promoted through health and lifestyle media and sold in up-market stores and online.
parts.working: 1 mark: the 4Ps (or 4Cs); 1 mark: consistent/support each other and the target market; 1 mark: application.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one way the 4Cs (customer solution, cost to customer, communication, convenience) could help Nisa Organics plan its marketing.
parts.answer: Thinking of 'convenience' rather than just 'place' makes Nisa focus on how busy customers want to buy — e.g. home delivery through its app — so its products are easier to buy than rivals' and sales rise. Also accept: customer solution focuses on benefits (health), cost includes travel/time, communication is two-way (social media).
parts.working: 1 mark for knowledge of the term/concept; up to 2 marks for explaining it in the context of the business (application).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: VoltRide plans to launch an electric motorcycle in Lahore priced 30 % above petrol motorcycles; running costs are 70 % lower. Analyse two elements of the marketing mix that will be most important for the success of the launch.
parts.answer: 1. Promotion: customers are unfamiliar with electric motorcycles and worry about range and charging; promotion (test rides, social media showing running-cost savings) must explain the benefits to overcome the higher price, building awareness and trust that lead to sales. 2. Place (distribution and charging network): buyers need convenient dealers, servicing and charging points; agreements with petrol stations or offices for charging reduce 'range anxiety', making the product practical and increasing demand. Price (instalment/finance schemes) is also acceptable.
parts.working: Any two mix elements developed with clear links to an electric motorcycle launch. Mark scheme: AO1 knowledge 2, AO2 application 2, AO3 analysis 4. Level 2 (5–8): two developed chains of analysis, each clearly applied to this business. Level 1 (1–4): knowledge and/or application with undeveloped or generic analysis. Evaluation earns no extra marks.

stem: GlowSkin (an invented company) makes skin-care products in Pakistan. Appendix 1: market share 2025 — two multinationals 28 % and 22 %; GlowSkin 6 %; others 44 %. Appendix 2: online beauty sales grew 35 % in 2025; sales through traditional shops grew 3 %. 85 % of GlowSkin's sales are through traditional shops. Appendix 3: survey of women aged 18–30 in cities: 22 % had heard of GlowSkin; 64 % prefer 'natural' ingredients. Appendix 4: marketing budget Rs 120 million (multinationals spend over Rs 1 billion each).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Advise GlowSkin on the marketing strategy it should adopt to achieve its objective of increasing market share from 6 % to 10 % by 2028.
parts.answer: Analysis: the market is crowded with multinational brands; GlowSkin can build on the strong preference for 'natural' ingredients (64 % of young urban women); its weaknesses are low awareness among young urban consumers and dependence on traditional retailers. Options: (1) Target young urban women via digital and influencer marketing, e-commerce and a refreshed brand — builds awareness where the market is growing fastest (online beauty sales +35 %); (2) Product development: a premium 'natural' range to differentiate from multinationals; (3) Price: keep competitive pricing but avoid price wars with deeper-pocketed rivals; (4) Place: expand into pharmacies and online marketplaces. Recommendation: a coordinated mix focused on the young urban segment — USP of natural ingredients, digital promotion, online distribution, mid-range pricing — with a marketing budget increase funded from the cash-cow traditional range. Justify using appendix data; consider budget limits, competitor response, and need to measure progress (market share by channel). Judgement on feasibility of reaching 10 %.
parts.working: Use appendices on market share, growth by channel, survey results, budget. Coordinated marketing strategy with clear recommendation and conditions. Levels: Level 4 (16–20): accurate knowledge, strong use of the case data, three or four developed chains of analysis and a well-supported judgement/recommendation throughout, specific to this business and its situation. Level 3 (11–15): developed analysis in context with some supported evaluation. Level 2 (6–10): some analysis, mostly descriptive use of the case; evaluation weak or unsupported. Level 1 (1–5): knowledge with little application.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Nature of marketing (demand, mass/niche, USP, CRM)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term 'demand'.
parts.answer: The quantity of a product that consumers are willing and able to buy at each price over a given period of time.
parts.working: 1 mark: willing and able to buy (both needed); 1 mark: at a given price / over a period of time.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one factor that could cause demand for bicycles in Lahore to increase.
parts.answer: A rise in the price of petrol makes motorcycles and cars more expensive to run (substitutes become dearer), so more people switch to cycling for short journeys, increasing demand for bicycles at every price. Also accept: rising incomes, health trends, new cycle lanes, advertising.
parts.working: 1 mark for knowledge of the term/concept; up to 2 marks for explaining it in the context of the business (application).

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Nature of marketing (demand, mass/niche, USP, CRM)
stem: The market for packaged dairy products in Pakistan was worth Rs 40 billion in 2024 and Rs 46 billion in 2025. Dairy Delight's sales were Rs 6.9 billion in 2025. Its yoghurt is made only from milk from its own grass-fed herds and reaches shops within 24 hours.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage growth of the market for packaged dairy products between 2024 and 2025.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate Dairy Delight's market share in 2025.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain the term 'unique selling point (USP)', using Dairy Delight as an example.
parts.answer: A feature or benefit of a product that makes it different from competitors' products and gives customers a reason to buy it. Dairy Delight's yoghurt, made only from milk from its own grass-fed herds and delivered within 24 hours, is a USP.
parts.working: 1 mark: feature that differentiates; 1 mark: reason for customers to choose it; 1 mark: application.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Nature of marketing (demand, mass/niche, USP, CRM)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse one benefit to a mobile network operator of using customer relationship marketing (CRM).
parts.answer: By using data on each customer's calls and data use, the operator can offer personalised bundles and loyalty rewards; customers feel valued and are less likely to switch to a rival network, so customer churn falls; keeping existing customers costs less than attracting new ones, improving profit. Accept: higher lifetime value, word-of-mouth.
parts.working: Chain: CRM (data, personalised offers) → loyalty/retention → lower marketing cost per customer/steady revenue. Marks: knowledge 1, application 1, analysis 3. Level 2 (3–5): a developed chain of analysis (cause → effect → impact) applied to this business. Level 1 (1–2): knowledge with limited application; no developed analysis.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Nature of marketing (demand, mass/niche, USP, CRM)
stem: Peshawar Leather Works employs 25 craftsmen who make traditional handmade leather sandals (chappals). Each pair takes 6 hours to make and sells for Rs 9,000; factory-made sandals sell for Rs 2,500. It has recently started selling online to customers abroad.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether niche marketing is the right strategy for Peshawar Leather Works.
parts.answer: For: handmade leather sandals cannot compete on price with mass-produced footwear; a niche of high-income customers, tourists and the diaspora values craftsmanship and heritage, allowing premium prices and higher margins; less competition from large firms; online sales reach the niche worldwide. Against: a small market limits sales growth; the niche may shrink with changing fashion; if successful, larger firms may enter; dependence on few customers is risky; high unit costs. Mass marketing alternative: higher volume, economies of scale, but requires machinery and big promotion budgets, losing the handmade USP. Judgement: niche marketing suits its resources and USP; the key is to strengthen the brand (story, quality) and widen within the niche (export online) rather than move to mass marketing.
parts.working: Niche vs mass marketing; USP; scale, risks; context of handmade products; judgement. Mark scheme: AO1 knowledge 2, AO2 application 2, AO3 analysis 2, AO4 evaluation 6. Level 3 (9–12): developed analysis in context plus a supported judgement that answers the question for this business (e.g. 'it depends on…' weighed, with a clear conclusion). Level 2 (5–8): developed analysis with some, limited or unsupported evaluation. Level 1 (1–4): knowledge and some application; little or no analysis.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term 'primary market research'.
parts.answer: The collection of new (first-hand) information directly from potential or existing customers for a specific purpose, e.g. through surveys, interviews, observation or focus groups.
parts.working: 1 mark: first-hand/new data collected by (or for) the business; 1 mark: for a specific purpose / method example.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one disadvantage to a new gym of relying on secondary market research.
parts.answer: Secondary data (e.g. national reports on fitness trends) was collected for another purpose, so it may not tell the gym what people in its own area want — such as preferred opening hours or prices — and may be out of date, leading to poor decisions.
parts.working: 1 mark for knowledge of the term/concept; up to 2 marks for explaining it in the context of the business (application).

stem: FruitFlow surveyed 200 shoppers (120 women and 80 men) in one shopping mall in Islamabad about a new guava juice. 74 said they would buy it.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of respondents who said they would buy the new juice.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the term 'quota sampling'.
parts.answer: A sampling method in which the population is divided into groups (e.g. by age or gender) and the researcher chooses a set number of people from each group, in proportion to the target market, but not randomly. FruitFlow chose 120 women and 80 men to match its customer profile.
parts.working: 1 mark: population split into segments/groups; 1 mark: a set number interviewed from each group (non-random); 1 mark: application.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one reason why the survey results might not be reliable.
parts.answer: All 200 people were interviewed in one shopping mall in Islamabad, so they may have higher incomes than FruitFlow's national target market; also people may say they would buy but not actually do so. The sample is small relative to the market.
parts.working: 1 mark for knowledge of the term/concept; up to 2 marks for explaining it in the context of the business (application).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: JuiceCo plans to use a survey to decide whether to launch a sugar-free drink nationally. Analyse two factors that could affect the reliability of the results.
parts.answer: 1. Sample size and method: a small or convenience sample (e.g. only people at one office) may not represent the national market, so findings about demand could be wrong, leading to over-production and losses. 2. Questionnaire design and bias: leading questions ('Would you like a healthier drink?') encourage positive answers, and respondents may give socially acceptable answers; JuiceCo may overestimate demand. Also: interviewer bias, time lag, sampling frame.
parts.working: Factors: sample size, sampling method, questionnaire bias, respondent honesty, interviewer bias, timing, secondary data reliability. Mark scheme: AO1 knowledge 2, AO2 application 2, AO3 analysis 4. Level 2 (5–8): two developed chains of analysis, each clearly applied to this business. Level 1 (1–4): knowledge and/or application with undeveloped or generic analysis. Evaluation earns no extra marks.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether market research is worth the cost for a small café opening in Islamabad.
parts.answer: Worth it: reduces risk — learning about local customers (students, office workers), preferred prices, menus and opening times avoids costly mistakes; cheap methods exist (observation of footfall, short surveys, social media polls, competitor visits); helps obtain bank finance. Not worth it (or limited): professional research is expensive relative to a small budget; the owner may already know the area; results may be unreliable with small samples; tastes change quickly; can test and adapt quickly after opening. Judgement: low-cost primary and secondary research is worth it, especially for location and price decisions, but expensive formal research is not justified; the value depends on the size of the investment and owner's knowledge.
parts.working: Benefits vs costs; low-cost methods; reliability; small business context; judgement. Mark scheme: AO1 knowledge 2, AO2 application 2, AO3 analysis 2, AO4 evaluation 6. Level 3 (9–12): developed analysis in context plus a supported judgement that answers the question for this business (e.g. 'it depends on…' weighed, with a clear conclusion). Level 2 (5–8): developed analysis with some, limited or unsupported evaluation. Level 1 (1–4): knowledge and some application; little or no analysis.

stem: Sialkot Sports makes footballs. Revenue (Rs million): 2024 — exports 180, total 600. 2025 — exports 270, total 750.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate exports as a percentage of total revenue for Sialkot Sports in 2024 and 2025.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in export revenue between 2024 and 2025.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one reason why Sialkot Sports might want to increase its international sales.
parts.answer: Selling in more countries spreads risk: if demand for footballs falls in Pakistan, sales in Europe and the Gulf can keep revenue stable; foreign currency earnings also help when the rupee falls. Also accept: saturated home market, economies of scale, higher prices abroad.
parts.working: 1 mark for knowledge of the term/concept; up to 2 marks for explaining it in the context of the business (application).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Sabir Foods plans to sell its ready-to-cook spice mixes in Saudi Arabia. It is considering using a local agent rather than opening its own sales office. Analyse two benefits to Sabir Foods of using a local agent.
parts.answer: 1. Local knowledge: the agent understands Saudi consumers' tastes, retail chains and regulations (labelling, halal certification), so Sabir Foods avoids costly mistakes and gets products onto supermarket shelves faster, increasing sales. 2. Lower cost and risk: no need to invest in offices and staff abroad; the agent is paid commission on sales, so costs rise only if sales are made, reducing financial risk if the market entry fails. Also: faster entry, existing contacts.
parts.working: Benefits: local knowledge, contacts, lower investment and risk, speed, flexibility. Mark scheme: AO1 knowledge 2, AO2 application 2, AO3 analysis 4. Level 2 (5–8): two developed chains of analysis, each clearly applied to this business. Level 1 (1–4): knowledge and/or application with undeveloped or generic analysis. Evaluation earns no extra marks.

stem: TrendWear (an invented company) is a fast-fashion brand from Pakistan with 60 stores at home. Appendix 1: target countries Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda; average income per head is 40–60 % of Pakistan's in two of them. Appendix 2: 70 % of Kenya's 18–30 year olds use social media daily; much lower in rural Tanzania. Appendix 3: climate and dress customs differ between coastal and inland regions. Appendix 4: TrendWear's current advertising and designs are produced centrally in Lahore.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Advise TrendWear whether it should use a global (standardised) marketing strategy or adapt its marketing mix for each country when it expands into East Africa.
parts.answer: Global/standardised: same brand, designs, promotion — economies of scale in production and advertising, consistent brand image, lower cost; works for young, fashion-aware urban consumers who follow global trends online. Adapted (local/glocal): different climates, cultures (modest fashion in some areas), incomes (lower average income means smaller, cheaper ranges), distribution (markets and small shops vs malls), languages; adaptation increases relevance and sales but raises costs and complexity. Pan-regional approach: standardise the brand and core designs, adapt price points, sizing, product range and promotion channels by country. Recommendation: 'think global, act local' — keep the TrendWear brand and online presence, adapt price and product range using the appendix data (income per head, social media use, climate and dress customs), enter first the market with highest fit; justify; mention exchange-rate risk and need for local partners.
parts.working: Use appendices on incomes, culture, internet use and costs. Weigh standardisation vs adaptation; clear recommendation with conditions. Levels: Level 4 (16–20): accurate knowledge, strong use of the case data, three or four developed chains of analysis and a well-supported judgement/recommendation throughout, specific to this business and its situation. Level 3 (11–15): developed analysis in context with some supported evaluation. Level 2 (6–10): some analysis, mostly descriptive use of the case; evaluation weak or unsupported. Level 1 (1–5): knowledge with little application.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Rang Fashions makes kurtas. The cost of making each kurta is Rs 1,200. It uses cost-plus pricing with a mark-up of 35 %.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the selling price of each kurta using cost-plus pricing.
parts.working: Price = unit cost × (1 + mark-up) = 1,200 × 1.35 (M1) = Rs 1,620 (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the term 'penetration pricing'.
parts.answer: Setting a low price when launching a product to gain market share quickly, then raising it once customers are loyal. Rang Fashions could launch its kurtas at Rs 1,300 in the new online store to attract customers from established brands.
parts.working: 1 mark: low initial price; 1 mark: to gain market share/enter market, price rises later; 1 mark: application.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one disadvantage to Rang Fashions of using cost-plus pricing.
parts.answer: It ignores demand and competitors' prices: if rivals sell similar kurtas for Rs 1,400, Rang's Rs 1,620 price may be too high and sales could fall; or it may underprice a popular design customers would pay more for.
parts.working: 1 mark for knowledge of the term/concept; up to 2 marks for explaining it in the context of the business (application).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether price skimming is the best pricing strategy for the launch of a new smartwatch brand.
parts.answer: For: if the watch has new features (e.g. health monitoring), early adopters will pay a high price; skimming recovers R&D costs quickly, gives high margins and supports a premium image; price can be cut later to reach the mass market. Against: a new, unknown brand lacks the reputation that skimming relies on; the smartwatch market is competitive, with established brands and cheap alternatives, so customers may compare and refuse to pay a premium; high margins attract imitators; later price cuts may annoy early buyers. Alternatives: penetration pricing to gain share, competitive pricing. Judgement: skimming is appropriate only if the watch has a genuine, protected USP and a strong launch promotion; otherwise competitive or penetration pricing is likely better for a new brand.
parts.working: Skimming conditions (USP, inelastic demand, early adopters, brand), alternatives, competition; judgement. Mark scheme: AO1 knowledge 2, AO2 application 2, AO3 analysis 2, AO4 evaluation 6. Level 3 (9–12): developed analysis in context plus a supported judgement that answers the question for this business (e.g. 'it depends on…' weighed, with a clear conclusion). Level 2 (5–8): developed analysis with some, limited or unsupported evaluation. Level 1 (1–4): knowledge and some application; little or no analysis.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term 'channel of distribution'.
parts.answer: The route a product takes from the producer to the final consumer, including any intermediaries such as wholesalers, retailers or agents.
parts.working: 1 mark: route/path from producer to consumer; 1 mark: intermediaries (wholesaler, retailer, agent) or direct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one benefit to a new cosmetics brand of promoting its products on social media.
parts.answer: Social media allows the brand to target young women interested in beauty precisely and cheaply, e.g. with influencer videos showing the products; this builds awareness quickly on a small budget and allows two-way interaction and feedback.
parts.working: 1 mark for knowledge of the term/concept; up to 2 marks for explaining it in the context of the business (application).

stem: Kashmir Crafts makes handmade shawls and wooden boxes. It sells to three wholesalers, who sell to shops in tourist areas. It plans to start selling directly to consumers through its own website.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse two benefits to Kashmir Crafts of selling its products online directly to consumers instead of through wholesalers.
parts.answer: 1. Higher profit margins: without wholesalers and retailers taking a share, Kashmir Crafts can sell shawls at a lower price than shops while keeping more profit per item, increasing total profit. 2. Wider market and customer contact: a website and online marketplaces reach customers across Pakistan and abroad (diaspora, tourists), 24 hours a day, increasing sales; direct contact gives customer feedback on designs, helping product development and loyalty.
parts.working: Benefits: margins, control of brand and price, wider/international reach, customer data, lower costs of premises. Mark scheme: AO1 knowledge 2, AO2 application 2, AO3 analysis 4. Level 2 (5–8): two developed chains of analysis, each clearly applied to this business. Level 1 (1–4): knowledge and/or application with undeveloped or generic analysis. Evaluation earns no extra marks.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Chai Express sells packaged tea across Pakistan, from loose-leaf black tea to green tea and single-serve tea sachets.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the term 'market segmentation'.
parts.answer: Dividing a market into distinct groups of consumers with similar characteristics or needs (e.g. by age, income, location, lifestyle) so that a business can target them with a suitable marketing mix.
parts.working: 1 mark: dividing the market into groups; 1 mark: similar characteristics/needs; 1 mark: purpose — target with tailored marketing mix.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two ways Chai Express could segment the market for its tea products.
parts.answer: 1. Demographic (age/income): offer premium loose-leaf tea for higher-income older customers and cheaper single-serve sachets for students. 2. Geographic: stronger, milky tea blends for Punjab and green (kahwa) tea for Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and the northern areas, reflecting regional tastes.
parts.working: For each of two methods: 1 mark method identified, 1 mark applied to tea.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Lahore Looms uses 40 cones of cotton yarn a day. The supplier takes 5 days to deliver. Lahore Looms keeps a buffer inventory of 100 cones and always orders 800 cones at a time.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the re-order level for cotton yarn at Lahore Looms.
parts.answer: 300 cones
parts.working: Re-order level = (daily usage × lead time) + buffer inventory (M1) = 40 × 5 + 100 = 300 cones (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the maximum inventory level.
parts.answer: 900 cones
parts.working: Buffer + re-order quantity = 100 + 800 = 900 (B1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one cost to Lahore Looms of holding inventory.
parts.answer: Storage cost: yarn must be kept in a dry warehouse and insured; the space and insurance cost money and the cash tied up in 900 cones of yarn cannot be used elsewhere (opportunity cost). Also accept: damage/deterioration, theft, obsolescence.
parts.working: 1 mark for knowledge of the term/concept; up to 2 marks for explaining it in the context of the business (application).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term 'just-in-time (JIT) inventory management'.
parts.answer: A system in which materials and components are delivered just when they are needed for production, and finished goods are produced to meet orders, so little or no inventory (and no buffer) is held.
parts.working: 1 mark: supplies arrive exactly when needed / produce to order; 1 mark: minimal or zero inventory held.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one disadvantage of JIT for a bakery that supplies bread to supermarkets every morning.
parts.answer: If the flour supplier's delivery is late (e.g. because of a road closure or strike), the bakery has no buffer inventory and cannot bake, so it fails to deliver bread to supermarkets that morning, losing revenue and possibly the contract.
parts.working: 1 mark for knowledge of the term/concept; up to 2 marks for explaining it in the context of the business (application). Accept: higher ordering/delivery costs, loss of bulk-buying discounts, cannot meet sudden rises in demand.

stem: Rehman Motors runs car repair workshops. It imports brake pads from Thailand. It holds 3,600 brake pads and uses 450 a week. Shipping times have varied between 3 and 9 weeks this year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many weeks Rehman Motors' current inventory of brake pads will last.
parts.answer: 8 weeks

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the term 'supply chain management'.
parts.answer: Managing the flow of materials, components, information and finance from suppliers through production to the customer, coordinating all the businesses involved to minimise cost and delays. For Rehman Motors this includes managing the overseas brake-pad supplier, shipping and its workshops' needs.
parts.working: 1 mark: flow of goods/information from suppliers to customer; 1 mark: coordination to improve efficiency/reduce cost or delay; 1 mark: application.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one reason why Rehman Motors might choose to hold more inventory than usual.
parts.answer: Its brake pads are imported and shipping times are uncertain (delays at ports); holding extra inventory means workshops do not run out and lose customers who need urgent repairs. Also accept: expected price rises/depreciation of the rupee, bulk discounts.
parts.working: 1 mark for knowledge of the term/concept; up to 2 marks for explaining it in the context of the business (application).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: GreenBasket is an online grocery retailer in Karachi. Customers complain of missing items and late deliveries. Analyse two ways better supply chain management could improve GreenBasket's competitiveness.
parts.answer: 1. Accurate, shared information with suppliers: linking its ordering system to farmers and wholesalers means fresh produce is ordered according to real-time demand, so fewer items are out of stock and less produce is wasted; customers receive complete orders, improving loyalty against rival apps. 2. Faster, coordinated logistics: planning delivery routes and warehouse picking with supply chain software shortens order-to-delivery time and lowers fuel cost per order; GreenBasket can promise reliable delivery slots and compete on convenience and price.
parts.working: Ways: supplier relationships, information sharing, demand forecasting, logistics, reduced waste, lower cost, reliability. Mark scheme: AO1 knowledge 2, AO2 application 2, AO3 analysis 4. Level 2 (5–8): two developed chains of analysis, each clearly applied to this business. Level 1 (1–4): knowledge and/or application with undeveloped or generic analysis. Evaluation earns no extra marks.

stem: SmartTel assembles mobile phones in Pakistan using components imported from China and South Korea. It holds about 10 weeks of components, worth Rs 1.2 billion. In 2025, delays at the port stopped production for 2 weeks. New phone models are launched every 9 months.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether SmartTel should change to a just-in-time (JIT) system for its phone components.
parts.answer: For: SmartTel holds 10 weeks of components; JIT would release working capital (Rs 1.2 billion) and cut storage costs; phone components become obsolete quickly as models change, so less inventory means less write-off; encourages efficiency and quality. Against: components are imported from China and South Korea with long, unreliable lead times; the 2025 port delays stopped production for 2 weeks even with inventory; exchange-rate swings make frequent small orders more expensive; JIT needs reliable suppliers, close relationships and good transport, which SmartTel lacks. Judgement: a full JIT system is too risky given its international supply chain; SmartTel should reduce inventory gradually (e.g. lower buffer for components sourced locally, JIT for packaging) and develop local suppliers before adopting JIT more widely.
parts.working: Benefits vs risks of JIT in context of imported components and supply disruption; partial adoption; judgement. Mark scheme: AO1 knowledge 2, AO2 application 2, AO3 analysis 2, AO4 evaluation 6. Level 3 (9–12): developed analysis in context plus a supported judgement that answers the question for this business (e.g. 'it depends on…' weighed, with a clear conclusion). Level 2 (5–8): developed analysis with some, limited or unsupported evaluation. Level 1 (1–4): knowledge and some application; little or no analysis.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term 'sustainable production'.
parts.answer: Producing goods and services in ways that minimise harm to the environment and use resources (energy, water, materials) efficiently, so that the needs of future generations are not compromised.
parts.working: 1 mark: minimise environmental impact / efficient use of resources; 1 mark: without compromising future generations / long-term.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one way a hotel could make its operations more sustainable.
parts.answer: Install solar water heaters and low-flow showers; this cuts gas and water use per guest, reducing costs and the hotel's environmental impact, which can also attract environmentally aware guests. Also accept: recycling, reusing towels, local food suppliers.
parts.working: 1 mark for knowledge of the term/concept; up to 2 marks for explaining it in the context of the business (application).

parts.label: a
