parts.answer: Faster decisions: branch managers can approve small farm loans within days rather than waiting weeks for head office, so farmers needing seed and fertiliser before sowing choose Kisan rather than rival lenders, increasing loan volume. Local knowledge and motivation: branch managers know local farmers and crop conditions, so lending decisions are better informed (lower defaults), and having authority motivates managers, reducing turnover.
parts.working: Indicative content: speed of response; local knowledge; motivation/empowerment of branch managers; frees head office for strategy; development of future senior managers. Marks: Knowledge 2, Application 2, Analysis 4. Analysis Level 2 (3–4): two developed chains of cause and effect applied to a bank lending to farmers across 300 branches; Level 1 (1–2): undeveloped or generic chains. Exactly two points are credited; no credit for evaluation.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse one way a flat organisational structure could improve communication at a technology start-up with 40 employees.
parts.answer: With only two levels, developers can talk directly to the founders; messages are not distorted as they pass through layers, so customer feedback reaches decision-makers quickly and product changes are made faster than rivals.
parts.working: Indicative content: fewer levels → shorter chain of command; faster, less distorted messages; more two-way communication. Marks: Knowledge 1, Application 1, Analysis 3. Analysis Level 2 (2–3): a developed chain of cause and effect linked to a small, fast-moving technology start-up; Level 1 (1): a simple statement of effect. Only one point is required; no credit for evaluation.

stem: AgriGrow (an invented company) makes fertilisers in Pakistan. It is organised by function: production, marketing, finance and HR, all based in Lahore. Exports to East Africa and Central Asia now provide 35 % of sales, and each region has different crops, soils and product registration rules. The board plans to reorganise into three regional divisions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse two effects on AgriGrow of changing from a functional structure to a geographical structure.
parts.answer: Better response to local markets: each regional division (Pakistan, East Africa, Central Asia) has its own marketing and sales teams that understand local crops, soils and regulations, so product registration and promotion fit local farmers, increasing sales. Duplication and coordination problems: each region needs its own finance, HR and marketing staff, raising overhead costs, and regions may compete for resources or develop inconsistent brands.
parts.working: Indicative content: local responsiveness; accountability of regional managers; duplication of functions/higher costs; loss of functional specialist expertise; coordination problems. Marks: Knowledge 2, Application 2, Analysis 4. Analysis Level 2 (3–4): two developed chains of cause and effect applied to a fertiliser company expanding into new regions; Level 1 (1–2): undeveloped or generic chains. Exactly two points are credited; no credit for evaluation.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether a flat organisational structure is the most suitable structure for a growing chain of private schools.
parts.answer: Flat: fewer layers, faster communication between principals and owners, lower management costs, more empowered principals. But as the chain grows from 5 to 25 schools, owners would have too wide a span; quality and curriculum standards may vary; teachers need clear progression routes (heads of department, deputy principals), which a taller structure provides. Judgement: a flat structure suits a small chain, but growth needs an extra layer (e.g. regional academic directors) and some centralised quality control; the best structure depends on the size and how standardised the chain wants its schools to be.
parts.working: Indicative content: features of flat vs tall structures; span of control; communication; control and consistency; career paths; cost. Evaluation: a contingent judgement that changes with size. Marks: Knowledge 2, Application 2, Analysis 2, Evaluation 6. Evaluation Level 3 (5–6): judgements weighed throughout and a supported conclusion specific to the business; Level 2 (3–4): a judgement with some support in context; Level 1 (1–2): an unsupported or generic judgement.

stem: Al Baraka Hotels (an invented company) owns 18 hotels in Pakistan, from Karachi to Skardu. Each hotel manager buys supplies locally. Total purchasing is Rs 2.4 billion per year. An internal audit found that prices paid for identical items differed by up to 18 % between hotels. Central purchasing could gain bulk discounts of about 10 %, but a central purchasing team would cost Rs 45 million per year. About 30 % of purchasing is fresh food.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether Al Baraka Hotels should centralise purchasing for all its hotels.
parts.answer: For: data show prices paid for the same items vary by up to 18 % between hotels; central purchasing of Rs 2.4 billion a year could save about Rs 240 million if 10 % discounts are achieved (about Rs 195 million after the Rs 45 million team cost); better quality control and fewer frauds. Against: hotel managers lose authority and may be demotivated; local suppliers (fresh food) may be cheaper and fresher; deliveries to remote hotels (e.g. Skardu) may be slower; a new central team costs Rs 45 million a year. Judgement: centralise purchasing of standard items (linen, toiletries, equipment) where bulk discounts are largest, while leaving fresh food purchasing to local managers within agreed price limits.
parts.working: Indicative content: cost savings vs central team costs; consistency of quality; loss of local flexibility and motivation; logistics to remote hotels; partial centralisation. Evaluation: a reasoned decision using the data. Marks: Knowledge 2, Application 2, Analysis 2, Evaluation 6. Evaluation Level 3 (5–6): judgements weighed throughout and a supported conclusion specific to the business; Level 2 (3–4): a judgement with some support in context; Level 1 (1–2): an unsupported or generic judgement.

author: HomiLabs

stem: National Rail Freight (an invented state-owned business) has 9,000 employees and 7 levels of hierarchy. Customers complain that it takes weeks to agree new freight timetables. The board plans to remove two levels of middle management, cutting 350 posts.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether delayering will improve the performance of National Rail Freight.
parts.answer: Benefits: removing a layer (two of seven levels) shortens the chain of command so decisions on freight schedules are quicker; saves salaries; empowers depot managers. Problems: wider spans may overload managers in a safety-critical operation; loss of experienced managers' knowledge; lower morale and fear of further job cuts could lead to industrial action by unions; cost savings may be offset by redundancy payments. Judgement: delayering can improve speed and costs, but only if supported by training, IT systems and consultation with unions; in a safety-critical railway it should be phased.
parts.working: Indicative content: effects on communication, speed, costs, motivation, span of control, safety, workload; union reaction. Evaluation: conditional judgement for a large state-owned freight business. Marks: Knowledge 2, Application 2, Analysis 2, Evaluation 6. Evaluation Level 3 (5–6): judgements weighed throughout and a supported conclusion specific to the business; Level 2 (3–4): a judgement with some support in context; Level 1 (1–2): an unsupported or generic judgement.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Crescent Group (an invented conglomerate) has divisions in textiles, food, packaging and logistics.
Timeline:
2020: The group changes from a centralised functional structure to four decentralised divisions, each with its own finance, HR and IT.
2022: Divisions launch 14 new products; the food division opens in Saudi Arabia.
2024: Board centralises finance, IT and HR into a group shared-services centre; divisional managers keep control of production and marketing.
2025: Two senior managers in textiles resign, saying they have 'lost control of their budgets'.
Appendix 1: Group revenue – 2020 Rs 42 bn; 2023 Rs 61 bn; 2025 Rs 64 bn.
Appendix 2: Overheads as % of revenue – 2020 9 %; 2023 13 %; 2025 10 %.
Appendix 3: Textiles division revenue – 2023 Rs 18 bn; 2025 Rs 16.56 bn.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the effectiveness of the changes Crescent Group made to its organisational structure between 2020 and 2025.
parts.answer: 2020 decentralisation into 4 divisions: revenue grew (Appendix 1: Rs 42 bn to Rs 61 bn by 2023) and divisional managers launched new products, so it was effective for growth; but duplication raised overheads from 9 % to 13 % of revenue (Appendix 2) and the divisions competed with each other. 2024 recentralisation of finance, IT and HR into shared services cut overheads to 10 % by 2025 and improved control; however, the textiles division lost key managers and its revenue fell 8 % (Appendix 3), suggesting loss of autonomy hurt motivation. Overall judgement: the structural changes were partly effective – decentralisation drove growth and partial recentralisation of support functions restored cost control – but the 2024 change was poorly managed for textiles; effectiveness depends on whether the falls in textiles are caused by structure or by market conditions.
parts.working: Indicative content: knowledge of centralisation, decentralisation, divisional structure, shared services; interpretation of revenue and overhead data over time; impact on motivation and coordination; separating effects of structure from external factors. Evaluation: an overall judgement for 2020–2025 with evidence from both periods. Marks: Knowledge 3, Application 3, Analysis 6, Evaluation 8. Analysis needs three or four developed chains using the timeline and appendices. Evaluation Level 3 (6–8): a clear, justified decision that weighs the evidence and is specific to the business and the time period; Level 2 (3–5): a judgement with partial support; Level 1 (1–2): assertion only.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Bilal sells cars at Sky Motors (an invented dealership). He is paid a basic salary of Rs 60,000 per month plus commission of 3 % on the value of sales above a monthly target of Rs 2,000,000. In March his sales were Rs 3,400,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Bilal's total pay for March.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one disadvantage to Sky Motors of paying sales staff commission.
parts.answer: Staff may use high-pressure selling or offer unauthorised discounts to close deals, upsetting customers and damaging the dealership's reputation; teamwork suffers as staff compete for customers.
parts.working: 1 mark (knowledge): commission encourages quantity over quality / pressure selling / competition between staff / unstable pay; up to 2 marks (application/explanation): applied to a car dealership.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term 'job rotation'.
parts.answer: Moving employees between different tasks or jobs of a similar level at regular intervals.
parts.working: 1 mark: moving workers between tasks/jobs; 1 mark: of a similar level of skill/responsibility, at intervals.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how Maslow's hierarchy of needs could help the manager of an inter-city bus company motivate its drivers.
parts.answer: The manager should first meet lower-level needs – fair pay and safe rest facilities between long trips (physiological and safety); once met, recognition schemes such as 'driver of the month' satisfy esteem needs, motivating drivers to drive safely and punctually.
parts.working: 1 mark (knowledge): Maslow: needs in a hierarchy; lower needs must be met before higher ones motivate; up to 2 marks (application/explanation): applied to bus drivers' needs.

stem: Pak Box (an invented company) makes corrugated boxes. Machine operators are paid Rs 400 per hour for a basic 48-hour week. Overtime is paid at 1.5 times the basic hourly rate. All staff receive a free lunch. Last week Nadia, an operator, worked 56 hours.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify one non-financial method of motivation that Pak Box could use.
parts.answer: Job enrichment (also accept: job rotation, team working, empowerment, recognition).
parts.working: 1 mark for any valid non-financial method.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate Nadia's gross pay for the week.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain the term 'fringe benefits'.
parts.answer: Non-wage benefits given to employees in addition to their pay, such as free meals, medical insurance or transport; at Pak Box, the free lunch is a fringe benefit.
parts.working: 1 mark (knowledge): benefits in addition to pay/non-cash rewards; up to 2 marks (application/explanation): examples/applied to Pak Box.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term 'performance-related pay (PRP)'.
parts.answer: A payment system in which part of an employee's pay depends on how well they perform against agreed targets, usually assessed through appraisal.
parts.working: 1 mark: extra pay/bonus linked to individual performance; 1 mark: measured against targets/through appraisal.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one disadvantage of using performance-related pay for doctors in a public hospital.
parts.answer: Doctors' performance is hard to measure fairly: if pay is linked to patients seen per day, doctors may rush consultations, harming the quality of care; it may also damage teamwork between doctors.
parts.working: 1 mark (knowledge): problem of PRP (measurement, wrong incentives, teamwork, conflict); up to 2 marks (application/explanation): applied to doctors and patient care.

stem: Zenith Paints (an invented company) shares 8 % of its annual profit with its 250 employees, in proportion to each employee's salary. Last year profit was Rs 250 million and total salaries were Rs 500 million. Hira, a quality controller, earned a salary of Rs 1,200,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the profit share Hira will receive.
parts.working: Profit pool = 8 % × Rs 250 million = Rs 20 million (M1); Hira's share = 20,000,000 × 1,200,000 ÷ 500,000,000 (M1) = Rs 48,000 (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why profit sharing might not motivate Hira to work harder.
parts.answer: Hira is one of 250 staff; her own effort has little visible effect on company profit, and the payment comes once a year, so the link between effort and reward is weak (Vroom's expectancy theory).
parts.working: 1 mark (knowledge): weak link between individual effort and reward / delayed payment / profit affected by external factors; up to 2 marks (application/explanation): applied to Hira and the company.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse one way Taylor's scientific management could improve productivity at a parcel-sorting depot.
parts.answer: Managers could study each sorting task, time the movements and design one best method (e.g. layout of bins, scanner position); workers are trained in this method and paid a piece-rate bonus for parcels sorted, so output per hour rises and unit costs fall.
parts.working: Indicative content: work study, one best way, division of labour, training in standard methods, piece-rate pay. Marks: Knowledge 1, Application 1, Analysis 3. Analysis Level 2 (2–3): a developed chain of cause and effect linked to repetitive parcel-sorting tasks; Level 1 (1): a simple statement of effect. Only one point is required; no credit for evaluation.

stem: ConnectCall (an invented company) runs a call centre in Islamabad with 600 agents. Agents work alone at individual desks and are moved between shifts every week, so they rarely work with the same people. Absenteeism is 8 % and many agents say managers 'only speak to us when something goes wrong'.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse two ways that Mayo's findings could be used to improve motivation at ConnectCall.
parts.answer: Team working and social needs: Mayo found that workers are motivated by belonging to a group; organising agents into stable teams with team targets and team leaders would improve morale, so absence (now 8 %) falls. Management interest and communication: Mayo found that attention from managers raised productivity; regular one-to-one meetings and asking agents for ideas on improving calls would make them feel valued, raising call quality and reducing turnover.
parts.working: Indicative content: Hawthorne effect – attention from management; social/group needs; team working; communication and consultation; informal groups' norms. Marks: Knowledge 2, Application 2, Analysis 4. Analysis Level 2 (3–4): two developed chains of cause and effect applied to a call centre with isolated agents and high absence; Level 1 (1–2): undeveloped or generic chains. Exactly two points are credited; no credit for evaluation.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Kashmir Carpets (an invented company) employs 150 hand-weavers paid by piece rate per square metre. Its reject rate is 8 % and two export buyers have complained about quality. It plans to pay a daily time rate plus a team bonus if the team's reject rate is below 3 %.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse two effects on Kashmir Carpets of changing from piece rate to a time rate with a team quality bonus.
parts.answer: Quality improves: weavers no longer rush to finish more square metres, and the team bonus rewards low reject rates, so fewer carpets are rejected by export buyers, protecting the firm's reputation and prices. Output may fall: without pay per square metre, some weavers may work more slowly, so total output and on-time delivery may fall unless supervisors monitor performance; labour cost per unit may rise.
parts.working: Indicative content: effects on quality, output, labour cost per unit, teamwork, security of income for workers, supervision costs. Marks: Knowledge 2, Application 2, Analysis 4. Analysis Level 2 (3–4): two developed chains of cause and effect applied to a carpet exporter with a high reject rate; Level 1 (1–2): undeveloped or generic chains. Exactly two points are credited; no credit for evaluation.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether Herzberg's two-factor theory is more useful than Maslow's hierarchy of needs for motivating sales staff at a car showroom.
parts.answer: Herzberg: separates hygiene factors (salary, conditions, supervision) which prevent dissatisfaction from motivators (recognition, responsibility, achievement); for sales staff it suggests ensuring a fair basic salary and good working conditions, then offering recognition and responsibility (e.g. managing key fleet clients). Maslow: needs in order; suggests ensuring secure income before esteem; less practical guidance and assumes a fixed order. Limitations: both are general theories; sales staff are often strongly motivated by commission, which Herzberg treats as a hygiene factor – this may not fit sales jobs. Judgement: Herzberg is more practical for designing jobs, but neither fully explains sales motivation; a combination with financial incentives and expectancy theory is most useful.
parts.working: Indicative content: explanation of both theories; application to sales roles; limitations of each; role of money; individual differences. Evaluation: justified comparison specific to car sales staff. Marks: Knowledge 2, Application 2, Analysis 2, Evaluation 6. Evaluation Level 3 (5–6): judgements weighed throughout and a supported conclusion specific to the business; Level 2 (3–4): a judgement with some support in context; Level 1 (1–2): an unsupported or generic judgement.

stem:
Shalimar Weaves (an invented company) makes machine-tufted carpets.
Current scheme: piece rate of Rs 60 per m²; average output 40 m² per worker per day; 8 % of output is rejected.
Proposed scheme: time rate of Rs 2,000 per day plus a team bonus of Rs 400 per worker per day if the team's quality target is met (assume it is always met). Expected output 36 m² per worker per day; 2 % rejected.
The main export customer will pay a 10 % price premium for carpets with a certified reject rate below 3 %.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the labour cost per good square metre of carpet under the current piece-rate scheme and under the proposed scheme.
parts.answer: Piece rate: Rs 65.22 per good m²; proposed scheme: Rs 68.03 per good m².

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate whether Shalimar Weaves should introduce the proposed payment scheme.
parts.answer: Cost: labour cost per good m² rises by about Rs 2.81 (4.3 %), and total good output falls, so capacity and delivery dates may suffer. Benefits: rejects fall from 8 % to 2 %, cutting wasted wool and rework, and export buyers pay a 10 % premium for certified quality; more secure income may reduce turnover of skilled weavers; teamwork may improve. Risks: the forecasts are estimates; some weavers may prefer piece rate. Judgement: introduce the scheme if the quality premium and lower material waste outweigh the higher labour cost – with a 10 % price premium on exports this is likely, but trial it with one team first.
parts.working: Indicative content: interpretation of the calculations; quality vs output; material waste; customer requirements and price premium; motivation (security, teamwork); reliability of forecasts. Evaluation: decision using the data with a condition such as a trial. Marks: Knowledge 2, Application 2, Analysis 2, Evaluation 6. Evaluation Level 3 (5–6): judgements weighed throughout and a supported conclusion specific to the business; Level 2 (3–4): a judgement with some support in context; Level 1 (1–2): an unsupported or generic judgement.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Nexa Digital (an invented company) is listed on the stock exchange and employs 900 staff. It plans to give every employee shares worth 5 % of their salary each year, which they can sell only after 3 years. Its share price fell by 20 % last year. Labour turnover among senior developers is 25 %.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether the employee share ownership scheme will motivate staff at Nexa Digital.
parts.answer: For: staff become part-owners, aligning their interests with shareholders; long vesting (3 years) encourages retention of skilled developers; links to esteem/belonging needs. Against: share price is affected by markets, not individual effort, so the link between effort and reward is weak; for junior staff with low salaries the shares are of little value compared with a pay rise; if the share price falls (it fell 20 % last year), the scheme may demotivate. Judgement: likely to help retention of senior staff, less effective for juniors; combine with non-financial motivators and fair basic pay.
parts.working: Indicative content: how share ownership works; motivation theories (Vroom, Herzberg, Maslow); retention; share price volatility; differences between staff groups. Evaluation: conditional judgement for Nexa Digital. Marks: Knowledge 2, Application 2, Analysis 2, Evaluation 6. Evaluation Level 3 (5–6): judgements weighed throughout and a supported conclusion specific to the business; Level 2 (3–4): a judgement with some support in context; Level 1 (1–2): an unsupported or generic judgement.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Tezbite Eats (an invented company) runs a food-delivery app in 6 Pakistani cities.
Timeline:
2021: Launch; riders paid Rs 120 per delivery.
2023: 12,000 riders; per-delivery pay cut to Rs 100 to reduce losses.
2024: A rival app offers riders accident insurance.
2025: Operating loss of Rs 800 million; customer complaints about late, cold food rise by 40 %.
Appendix 1: Rider labour turnover 2023 – 38 %; 2025 – 65 %. Average customer rating fell from 4.5 to 3.9.
Appendix 2: Rider survey 2025 – unpredictable earnings 48 %; lack of respect/support from the company 27 %; safety 19 %; other 6 %.
Appendix 3: A guaranteed minimum of Rs 350 per hour worked would cost an estimated Rs 1.1 billion per year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Advise Tezbite Eats on how to improve the motivation of its delivery riders over the next two years.
parts.answer: Problem evidence: rider turnover 65 % (Appendix 1), ratings falling, survey shows unpredictable earnings (48 %) and lack of respect (27 %) as main complaints (Appendix 2). Options: (1) guaranteed minimum hourly earnings – tackles hygiene factor of insecure pay but costs about Rs 1.1 billion a year (Appendix 3); (2) tiered bonus for ratings and on-time delivery – stronger expectancy link (Vroom) but adds pressure and road-safety risks; (3) non-financial: rider hubs with rest areas, insurance, recognition, a path to supervisor roles. Recommendation: a modest guaranteed minimum at peak times plus accident insurance and rest hubs (Herzberg hygiene factors) first, then recognition and progression to motivate; avoid speed-based bonuses for safety reasons; judge success by turnover and ratings, depending on cash available after the 2025 loss.
parts.working: Indicative content: motivation theories applied to gig workers; financial vs non-financial methods; costs vs benefits from appendices; safety and reputation; competition for riders. Evaluation: clear advice with priorities and conditions. Marks: Knowledge 3, Application 3, Analysis 6, Evaluation 8. Analysis needs three or four developed chains using the timeline and appendices. Evaluation Level 3 (6–8): a clear, justified decision that weighs the evidence and is specific to the business and the time period; Level 2 (3–5): a judgement with partial support; Level 1 (1–2): assertion only.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term 'trade union'.
parts.answer: An organisation of workers that acts collectively to protect and improve its members' pay, working conditions and job security, e.g. by negotiating with employers.
parts.working: 1 mark: organisation/group of workers joining together; 1 mark: to protect/improve members' interests through collective negotiation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one benefit to workers at a sugar mill of being members of a trade union.
parts.answer: The union negotiates on behalf of all workers, giving them more bargaining power than individuals; during the crushing season it can secure overtime rates and safety equipment that individual seasonal workers could not win alone.
parts.working: 1 mark (knowledge): benefit: collective bargaining power, legal support, protection from unfair dismissal, safety; up to 2 marks (application/explanation): applied to sugar-mill workers.

stem: Workers at Lucky Star Cement (an invented company) went on strike for 3 days after a pay dispute. The plant normally sells 9,000 bags of cement per day at Rs 1,400 per bag. No cement was produced or sold during the strike. The two sides could not agree and the dispute was referred to arbitration.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify one form of industrial action, other than a strike.
parts.answer: Work-to-rule (also accept: overtime ban, go-slow, sit-in).
parts.working: 1 mark for any valid form.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the term 'arbitration'.
parts.answer: A way of settling an industrial dispute in which an independent third party listens to both sides and makes a decision, which may be binding on both, e.g. an arbitrator deciding the size of the pay rise at Lucky Star Cement.
parts.working: 1 mark (knowledge): independent third party decides the outcome of a dispute; up to 2 marks (application/explanation): binding/non-binding and/or applied to the cement dispute.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the sales revenue lost by Lucky Star Cement because of the strike.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term 'two-way communication'.
parts.answer: Communication in which the receiver can respond to the sender with feedback, so the message can be checked and discussed.
parts.working: 1 mark: message sent and receiver responds/gives feedback; 1 mark: allows checking of understanding/discussion.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one advantage to a chain of 40 pharmacies of using an intranet to communicate with its staff.
parts.answer: Updates on drug recalls and price changes can be posted once and read immediately by pharmacists in all 40 branches, so dangerous products are removed quickly and every branch charges the correct price.
parts.working: 1 mark (knowledge): intranet = internal network; fast, cheap, consistent, permanent record; up to 2 marks (application/explanation): applied to a pharmacy chain.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term 'no-strike agreement'.
parts.answer: An agreement between a union and an employer that the union will not call strikes, usually in exchange for benefits such as binding arbitration of disputes or better pay and conditions.
parts.working: 1 mark: union agrees not to take strike action; 1 mark: in return for something, e.g. arbitration, guaranteed pay increases.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one way a works council could improve employee relations at a car assembly plant.
parts.answer: A works council of elected workers and managers meets regularly to discuss changes such as new shift patterns before they are introduced; workers feel consulted, concerns are dealt with early, and the risk of disputes falls.
parts.working: 1 mark (knowledge): works council = forum for employee representatives and management to consult; up to 2 marks (application/explanation): applied to change at a car plant and its effect.

stem: Orbit Engineering (an invented company) designs oil and gas pipelines. It has 700 engineers in offices in Houston, Lahore, Kuala Lumpur, Dubai and Aberdeen. Most communication is by email. A project for a client in Oman was delayed by 6 weeks after a design change was misunderstood by one office.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse two barriers to effective communication at Orbit Engineering.
parts.answer: Time zones: with offices in Houston, Lahore and Kuala Lumpur, there are few overlapping working hours, so questions about a design may wait a day for a reply, delaying projects and frustrating clients. Language and cultural differences: technical instructions written in English may be misunderstood by staff for whom English is a second language, and cultural differences in how directly problems are raised mean errors may not be reported, leading to costly redesign work. (Also accept: too much email/information overload, technical failure, long chain of command.)
parts.working: Indicative content: time zones; language; culture; information overload; technical problems; lack of face-to-face contact; long chain of command. Marks: Knowledge 2, Application 2, Analysis 4. Analysis Level 2 (3–4): two developed chains of cause and effect applied to an engineering firm with teams in five countries; Level 1 (1–2): undeveloped or generic chains. Exactly two points are credited; no credit for evaluation.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse one benefit to the management of a large container port of collective bargaining with a trade union, rather than negotiating with each employee individually.
parts.answer: Managers negotiate pay and conditions for 3,000 dockworkers in one set of talks with union representatives, saving management time; agreed terms apply to all, so they are seen as fair and accepted, reducing disputes that could stop ship loading and cost the port fees.
parts.working: Indicative content: saves time and cost; consistent terms; union communicates and wins acceptance; reduced conflict. Marks: Knowledge 1, Application 1, Analysis 3. Analysis Level 2 (2–3): a developed chain of cause and effect linked to a large port with many dockworkers; Level 1 (1): a simple statement of effect. Only one point is required; no credit for evaluation.

stem: Gulf Star Airlines (an invented airline) wants to introduce new rosters that increase cabin crew flying hours by 10 %. The cabin crew union says this is unsafe and has threatened a strike during the Hajj season, the airline's busiest period. Talks between managers and the union have broken down.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse two ways that conciliation could help to resolve the dispute at Gulf Star Airlines.
parts.answer: A neutral conciliator meets both sides separately and together, reducing hostility and helping each understand the other's position, so talks restart and the threatened strike during Hajj season is avoided, protecting revenue. The conciliator can suggest compromises (e.g. phasing new rosters over 6 months with extra rest days), which both sides may accept without losing face, so the agreement lasts and future disputes are less likely.
parts.working: Indicative content: neutral third party; improves communication; suggests compromises; no imposed decision so both sides own it; cheaper/faster than strike or legal action. Marks: Knowledge 2, Application 2, Analysis 4. Analysis Level 2 (3–4): two developed chains of cause and effect applied to an airline facing a cabin-crew dispute at its busiest time; Level 1 (1–2): undeveloped or generic chains. Exactly two points are credited; no credit for evaluation.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Margalla Textiles (an invented company) has an annual wage bill of Rs 840 million. The union has claimed a pay rise of 18 %. Management has offered 10 %. Inflation is 12 %. Last year the company's profit rose by 25 %.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the difference in Margalla Textiles' annual wage bill between the union's claim and management's offer.
parts.working: Claim 18 % − offer 10 % = 8 % (M1); 8 % × Rs 840 million = Rs 67.2 million (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the change in workers' real wages under management's offer and under the union's claim. Give your answers to 2 decimal places.
parts.working: Offer: (1.10 ÷ 1.12 − 1) × 100 = −1.79 % (B1); claim: (1.18 ÷ 1.12 − 1) × 100 = +5.36 % (B1). Accept −2 % and +6 % (approximate subtraction method) for 1 mark only.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one reason why the union rejected management's offer.
parts.answer: With inflation at 12 %, a 10 % rise means workers can buy about 1.8 % less than before, so their living standards fall, while the company's profits rose by 25 % last year.
parts.working: 1 mark (knowledge): real wages fall / profits rising so firm can afford more; up to 2 marks (application/explanation): use of the data.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Al Shifa Hospital (an invented hospital) introduced a new electronic patient-records system. Staff were informed by an email sent one week before the launch, and training was a 30-minute video. In the first month, average patient waiting times rose from 40 to 75 minutes and nurses' absence doubled.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse two effects of poor communication on Al Shifa Hospital during the introduction of its new patient-records system.
parts.answer: Staff resistance and lower morale: nurses were told about the system by email a week before launch, so they felt ignored and anxious, leading to complaints and absence and making the change harder to implement. Errors and delays: without clear instructions and training, doctors could not find test results in the new system, so patients waited longer and the risk of treatment errors rose, damaging the hospital's reputation.
parts.working: Indicative content: resistance to change; low morale and trust; mistakes and patient safety risks; delays and inefficiency; rumours via grapevine. Marks: Knowledge 2, Application 2, Analysis 4. Analysis Level 2 (3–4): two developed chains of cause and effect applied to a hospital introducing a new IT system; Level 1 (1–2): undeveloped or generic chains. Exactly two points are credited; no credit for evaluation.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether a strong trade union is beneficial to the management of a large port.
parts.answer: Benefits: a single channel for negotiation and communication with thousands of dockworkers; unions can help win acceptance of change (e.g. automation) and enforce agreements; improved safety and morale. Costs: stronger bargaining power raises wages; strikes at a port are very costly (ships diverted, penalties); unions may resist automation, slowing productivity gains. Judgement: a strong union is beneficial if relations are cooperative (e.g. regular consultation, no-strike or arbitration agreements); where relations are adversarial, it can be very damaging; management's own approach largely decides which.
parts.working: Indicative content: roles of unions; collective bargaining; communication; change management; industrial action risks; costs. Evaluation: conditional judgement depending on the nature of employee relations. Marks: Knowledge 2, Application 2, Analysis 2, Evaluation 6. Evaluation Level 3 (5–6): judgements weighed throughout and a supported conclusion specific to the business; Level 2 (3–4): a judgement with some support in context; Level 1 (1–2): an unsupported or generic judgement.

stem: Lahore City Transit Company (an invented company) employs 700 staff, of whom 92 % are union members. It plans to install automatic ticket gates, which would remove the need for 140 ticket staff and save Rs 180 million per year. The union will accept the gates only if no employee is made redundant for 3 years. Labour turnover is 10 % per year. The service carries 200,000 passengers per day.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether Lahore City Transit Company should agree to the union's demand for a job guarantee in return for the union accepting automatic ticket gates.
parts.answer: For agreeing: the union represents 92 % of staff and a strike would stop services used by 200,000 passengers a day; natural wastage (labour turnover of 10 %, about 70 staff a year) means the 140 ticket staff jobs can be removed within about 2 years without redundancy; retraining staff as customer assistants maintains service and goodwill. Against: the guarantee limits flexibility if passenger numbers fall; savings of Rs 180 million a year are delayed; may set a precedent for future changes. Judgement: agree to a time-limited guarantee (e.g. 3 years) linked to retraining, because the cost of conflict exceeds the delayed savings, and natural wastage makes it affordable.
parts.working: Indicative content: cost of industrial action; savings from automation; natural wastage and redeployment; precedent; government/public stakeholder interest. Evaluation: a supported decision using the data. Marks: Knowledge 2, Application 2, Analysis 2, Evaluation 6. Evaluation Level 3 (5–6): judgements weighed throughout and a supported conclusion specific to the business; Level 2 (3–4): a judgement with some support in context; Level 1 (1–2): an unsupported or generic judgement.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Gulf Build (an invented company) employs 4,000 construction workers on 25 sites across the UAE. Workers speak at least five different languages and many have limited reading skills. Two serious accidents last year were linked to safety instructions that were misunderstood.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether face-to-face communication is the most effective method for Gulf Build to communicate with its site workers.
parts.answer: Face-to-face (site briefings, toolbox talks): immediate feedback, can check understanding with workers who speak Urdu, Hindi, Bengali or Tagalog, builds trust, vital for safety instructions. Limitations: time-consuming across 25 sites; messages may be changed as they pass from supervisors; no written record for legal/safety purposes. Alternatives: messaging apps with translated voice notes, posters with pictures, written procedures. Judgement: face-to-face is most effective for safety-critical and sensitive messages, but should be backed by written/visual records and digital messages for routine information; no single method is enough.
parts.working: Indicative content: features of face-to-face vs written/electronic communication; language barriers; safety; record keeping; cost and time. Evaluation: judgement for a multi-site construction firm with a multilingual workforce. Marks: Knowledge 2, Application 2, Analysis 2, Evaluation 6. Evaluation Level 3 (5–6): judgements weighed throughout and a supported conclusion specific to the business; Level 2 (3–4): a judgement with some support in context; Level 1 (1–2): an unsupported or generic judgement.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Chenab Airways (an invented airline) employs 3,500 staff.
Timeline:
2021: Losses after the pandemic; management cuts pay by 15 % without consulting unions.
2022: Pilots strike for 6 days; flights cancelled.
2023: New HR director sets up a joint consultative committee with unions and agrees that disputes will go to independent arbitration.
2024: Pay restored in two stages after negotiation; new fleet introduced with union agreement on training.
2025: Board announces, without consultation, that ground handling will be outsourced; union threatens a strike.
Appendix 1: Estimated cost of the 2022 strike Rs 2.4 bn.
Appendix 2: Days lost to industrial action – 2022: 18; 2023: 2; 2024: 0. On-time performance – 2022: 61 %; 2024: 82 %.
Appendix 3: Staff survey 'I trust senior management' – 2022: 22 %; 2024: 49 %.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the effectiveness of Chenab Airways' approach to employee relations between 2021 and 2025.
parts.answer: 2021–2022: management imposed pay cuts without consultation; the 2022 pilots' strike cost Rs 2.4 bn (Appendix 1) and punctuality fell to 61 % – ineffective. 2023: a new HR director set up a joint consultative committee and agreed an arbitration procedure; days lost to industrial action fell from 18 to 2 (Appendix 2), punctuality recovered to 82 %, staff survey trust rose from 22 % to 49 % – largely effective. 2025: the decision to outsource ground handling was announced without using the committee; the threatened strike suggests the new approach is not embedded. Judgement: the approach improved significantly after 2023 and was effective in reducing conflict and improving performance, but its inconsistent use in 2025 shows effectiveness depends on management's commitment to consultation for all major decisions.
parts.working: Indicative content: collective bargaining, consultation, arbitration, industrial action; evidence from timeline and appendices on costs, days lost, punctuality and trust; consistency of approach; external factors (fuel prices, demand). Evaluation: an overall judgement over the period, distinguishing phases. Marks: Knowledge 3, Application 3, Analysis 6, Evaluation 8. Analysis needs three or four developed chains using the timeline and appendices. Evaluation Level 3 (6–8): a clear, justified decision that weighs the evidence and is specific to the business and the time period; Level 2 (3–5): a judgement with partial support; Level 1 (1–2): assertion only.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Arcadia Generics (an invented company) makes medicines in Pakistan. It imports active ingredients from Germany. Each order costs €400,000. The exchange rate changed from €1 = Rs 300 to €1 = Rs 330.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cost in rupees of one order of raw materials before and after the change in the exchange rate.
parts.working: Before: 400,000 × 300 = Rs 120 million (M1 A1 shared); after: 400,000 × 330 = Rs 132 million (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one way Arcadia Generics could respond to the rise in its import costs.
parts.answer: It could find suppliers of active ingredients in Pakistan or a country whose currency has not risen, reducing exposure to the euro; or raise medicine prices, although government price controls on medicines may limit this.
parts.working: 1 mark (knowledge): valid response (raise price, change supplier, hedge/forward contract, cut other costs); up to 2 marks (application/explanation): applied to a medicine maker.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term 'recession'.
parts.answer: A period in which the economy's output (real GDP) falls, usually for at least two consecutive quarters, with falling incomes and rising unemployment.
parts.working: 1 mark: fall in real GDP/output/economic activity; 1 mark: for two consecutive quarters (or sustained period) / associated with rising unemployment.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one way a recession might affect a dealer selling luxury cars in Islamabad.
parts.answer: Luxury cars are income-elastic: as incomes and business profits fall, customers delay buying expensive new cars, so the dealer's sales and profit fall sharply; it may have to offer discounts to clear inventory.
parts.working: 1 mark (knowledge): effect of recession (lower incomes/demand, harder credit); up to 2 marks (application/explanation): applied to luxury cars with high income elasticity.

stem: Indus Auto (an invented company) assembles cars in Karachi. Steel accounts for 18 % of its production costs and almost all of it is imported. The government has introduced a 30 % tariff on imported steel to protect local steel mills.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify one government policy, other than tariffs, that could affect Indus Auto.
parts.answer: Interest rate changes (monetary policy) – also accept tax changes, subsidies, competition policy, environmental laws, import quotas.
parts.working: 1 mark for a valid policy.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the term 'tariff'.
parts.answer: A tax on imported goods, which raises their price in the domestic market; e.g. a 30 % tariff on imported steel raises the cost of steel sheets that Indus Auto buys from China.
parts.working: 1 mark (knowledge): tax on imports; up to 2 marks (application/explanation): effect on prices/protection and/or applied to Indus Auto.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one effect on Indus Auto of the new tariff on imported steel.
parts.answer: Steel makes up a large share of the cost of each car; the tariff raises costs, so Indus Auto must raise car prices (losing sales to imported cars) or accept lower profit margins.
parts.working: 1 mark (knowledge): higher input costs; up to 2 marks (application/explanation): consequences for prices/profit/competitiveness of a car maker.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Gulshan Furniture's sales revenue rose by 18 % in 2025 compared with 2024. During the same period, the rate of inflation was 24 %.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage change in Gulshan Furniture's real sales revenue in 2025. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.working: Real change = (1.18 ÷ 1.24 − 1) × 100 (M1 M1) = −4.84 % (A1). Accept −6 % (18 − 24) for 1 mark only.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why Gulshan Furniture's managers should not be satisfied with the 18 % rise in sales revenue.
parts.answer: Prices in the economy rose by 24 %, so in real terms revenue fell by about 4.8 %; if Gulshan raised its own prices in line with inflation, it is actually selling fewer units, suggesting it is losing market share.
parts.working: 1 mark (knowledge): nominal vs real – inflation exceeds growth; up to 2 marks (application/explanation): interpretation for Gulshan's sales volume/market share.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Capital University (an invented private university) in Islamabad charges annual fees of Rs 900,000. Unemployment in the city has risen from 6 % to 9 % in a year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse two effects of a rise in unemployment on Capital University.
parts.answer: Lower demand from fee-paying students: families who lose income cannot afford fees of Rs 900,000 a year, so enrolments fall and revenue drops; the university may need to offer scholarships or instalment plans. Easier recruitment of staff: with more people looking for work, the university can recruit qualified administrative staff and lecturers more easily and at lower salaries, reducing costs. (Also accept: more mature students seeking retraining, increasing demand for short courses.)
parts.working: Indicative content: fall in demand/ability to pay; counter-cyclical demand for retraining; easier, cheaper recruitment; bad debts from unpaid fees. Marks: Knowledge 2, Application 2, Analysis 4. Analysis Level 2 (3–4): two developed chains of cause and effect applied to a private university charging high fees; Level 1 (1–2): undeveloped or generic chains. Exactly two points are credited; no credit for evaluation.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Chai Junction (an invented company) runs 35 cafés in Karachi selling tea and snacks. BeanWorld, an international coffee chain with a strong brand and large marketing budget, plans to open 20 cafés in Karachi over the next year, many in the same shopping malls as Chai Junction.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse two effects on Chai Junction of the entry of BeanWorld into its market.
parts.answer: Loss of market share and pressure on prices: BeanWorld's strong international brand and modern cafés attract young customers, so Chai Junction's sales fall; to compete it may cut prices or run promotions, reducing profit margins. Pressure to improve: Chai Junction may need to refurbish branches, add loyalty apps and differentiate with local products (e.g. karak chai, desi snacks), raising costs in the short run but possibly strengthening its unique selling point. (Also accept: competition for staff and prime locations raising rents and wages.)
parts.working: Indicative content: loss of market share; price competition and lower margins; need to differentiate/innovate; competition for locations and staff. Marks: Knowledge 2, Application 2, Analysis 4. Analysis Level 2 (3–4): two developed chains of cause and effect applied to a local café chain facing a multinational rival; Level 1 (1–2): undeveloped or generic chains. Exactly two points are credited; no credit for evaluation.

author: HomiLabs

stem: CodeBridge (an invented company) provides software services from Lahore. 85 % of its revenue comes from clients in the USA and is paid in US dollars. Its costs are: salaries 60 % (paid in rupees); laptops, software licences and cloud services 25 % (priced in US dollars); office and other costs 15 % (in rupees). The exchange rate has changed from US$1 = Rs 280 to US$1 = Rs 310.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether CodeBridge will benefit overall from the depreciation of the Pakistani rupee.
parts.answer: Benefits: 85 % of revenue is earned in US dollars, so each dollar now brings more rupees (Rs 280 to Rs 310, +10.7 %); salaries (60 % of costs) are paid in rupees, so profit margins rise; it can cut its dollar prices to win more contracts. Costs: laptops and cloud subscriptions (25 % of costs) are priced in dollars and rise; depreciation often brings higher inflation in Pakistan, leading staff to demand pay rises and more engineers leaving for jobs abroad. Judgement: overall CodeBridge benefits, because its dollar revenue is much larger than its dollar costs, but the gain may shrink over time if inflation pushes up wages; it should use the gain to retain staff.
parts.working: Indicative content: effects on export revenue and price competitiveness; imported input costs; inflation and wage pressure; staff retention; time period. Evaluation: net judgement based on proportions of revenue and costs in each currency. Marks: Knowledge 2, Application 2, Analysis 2, Evaluation 6. Evaluation Level 3 (5–6): judgements weighed throughout and a supported conclusion specific to the business; Level 2 (3–4): a judgement with some support in context; Level 1 (1–2): an unsupported or generic judgement.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether changes in interest rates are the most important external influence on a house-building company.
parts.answer: Interest rates matter greatly: most buyers use mortgages, so higher rates raise monthly repayments and reduce demand; builders borrow to buy land, so higher rates raise costs. Other influences: incomes and employment (recession), government policy (planning permission, housing subsidies, taxes on property), raw material prices (cement, steel), exchange rates for imported materials, competition. Judgement: in economies where most buyers use mortgages, interest rates are often the most important; where few buyers use mortgages, incomes, inflation and building-material costs may matter more; the answer depends on how buyers finance homes and the company's own borrowing.
parts.working: Indicative content: effects of interest rates on demand and costs; alternative external influences; dependence on mortgage market and financing. Evaluation: a reasoned comparison and conclusion. Marks: Knowledge 2, Application 2, Analysis 2, Evaluation 6. Evaluation Level 3 (5–6): judgements weighed throughout and a supported conclusion specific to the business; Level 2 (3–4): a judgement with some support in context; Level 1 (1–2): an unsupported or generic judgement.

stem: Volta Bikes (an invented company) makes electric motorbikes in Lahore with capacity of 15,000 bikes a year. It sells them for Rs 320,000; a similar petrol motorbike costs Rs 250,000. The government has announced a subsidy of Rs 50,000 per electric motorbike for the next 3 years. Market research forecasts that Volta's demand will rise from 12,000 to 30,000 bikes a year. Doubling capacity would cost Rs 1.6 billion, borrowed at 17 % interest. Two Chinese manufacturers are considering entering the market.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether Volta Bikes should double its production capacity because of the new government subsidy.
parts.answer: For: the subsidy of Rs 50,000 cuts the effective price of a Volta e-bike from Rs 320,000 to Rs 270,000, now close to a petrol motorbike (Rs 250,000); market research forecasts demand rising from 12,000 to 30,000 units a year, beyond current capacity of 15,000; first-mover advantage. Against: the subsidy lasts only 3 years and may be withdrawn earlier if the government faces budget problems; doubling capacity costs Rs 1.6 billion at a 17 % interest rate; rivals from China may enter and also receive the subsidy; charging infrastructure is limited. Judgement: expand, but in phases (e.g. +50 % now, more if demand is confirmed), reducing the risk of spare capacity if the subsidy ends.
parts.working: Indicative content: effect of subsidy on price and demand; political risk/time limit; cost of finance; competition; infrastructure; phased expansion. Evaluation: conditional decision using the data. Marks: Knowledge 2, Application 2, Analysis 2, Evaluation 6. Evaluation Level 3 (5–6): judgements weighed throughout and a supported conclusion specific to the business; Level 2 (3–4): a judgement with some support in context; Level 1 (1–2): an unsupported or generic judgement.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term 'sustainability' in a business context.
parts.answer: Operating in a way that meets present needs without reducing the ability of future generations to meet their needs, e.g. by using renewable resources and limiting pollution.
parts.working: 1 mark: meeting current needs without harming future generations' ability to meet theirs; 1 mark: e.g. resource use, environment, long-term operation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one ethical issue a pharmaceutical company faces when setting the price of a new life-saving medicine.
parts.answer: A high price helps recover research costs and rewards shareholders, but may put the medicine out of reach of poor patients who will die without it; the company must balance profit against its duty to patients.
parts.working: 1 mark (knowledge): ethical issue: conflict between profit and access/fairness; up to 2 marks (application/explanation): applied to pricing of a life-saving medicine.

stem: Rang Dyeing (an invented company) dyes cotton fabric near Faisalabad. Local farmers complain that the water table is falling. After installing water-recycling equipment, the plant's water use fell from 180 litres to 117 litres per kilogram of fabric dyed. An environmental audit will be published next month.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify one stakeholder group affected by Rang Dyeing's water use.
parts.answer: Local community/farmers (also accept government, employees, customers, shareholders).
parts.working: 1 mark for any valid group.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the term 'environmental audit'.
parts.answer: An independent check of a business's impact on the environment, e.g. measuring Rang Dyeing's water use, waste-water quality and energy use, and comparing them with targets or legal limits.
parts.working: 1 mark (knowledge): independent assessment of environmental impact; up to 2 marks (application/explanation): what is measured and/or purpose, applied to the dyeing plant.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the percentage reduction in water used per kilogram of fabric.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term 'triple bottom line'.
parts.answer: A way of measuring business performance in three areas: profit (economic), people (social impact) and planet (environmental impact).
parts.working: 1 mark: measuring performance beyond profit; 1 mark: three elements: profit, people and planet.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one way a hotel in Nathia Gali could become more environmentally sustainable.
parts.answer: Install solar water heaters and ask guests to reuse towels; this cuts the use of gas and water, reducing carbon emissions and pressure on scarce mountain water supplies, and also lowers costs.
parts.working: 1 mark (knowledge): valid sustainable action; up to 2 marks (application/explanation): applied to a hill-station hotel and its effect.

stem: ConnectPak (an invented mobile network operator) is one of four networks in Pakistan, all charging similar prices. It will spend Rs 900 million over 3 years providing free internet to 2,000 rural schools in Sindh and Balochistan.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse two benefits to ConnectPak of its programme to provide free internet to rural schools.
parts.answer: Improved brand image: media coverage of children learning online makes customers see ConnectPak as a responsible company, increasing loyalty in a market where the four networks offer similar prices. Future customers and long-term growth: children and teachers in rural areas become familiar with ConnectPak's network, and the business builds towers in areas where rivals are weak, so it gains subscribers as rural incomes rise. (Also accept: staff motivation and recruitment, better relations with government regulators.)
parts.working: Indicative content: brand/reputation; customer loyalty; future market development; employee motivation; relationship with government/regulator. Marks: Knowledge 2, Application 2, Analysis 4. Analysis Level 2 (3–4): two developed chains of cause and effect applied to a mobile network in a price-competitive market; Level 1 (1–2): undeveloped or generic chains. Exactly two points are credited; no credit for evaluation.

author: HomiLabs

stem: FlyHigh Cargo (an invented airline) emits 48,000 tonnes of CO₂ per year. Carbon offsets cost US$12 per tonne of CO₂. The exchange rate is US$1 = Rs 280.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cost in rupees of offsetting all of FlyHigh Cargo's annual carbon emissions.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why buying carbon offsets may not make FlyHigh Cargo a sustainable business.
parts.answer: Offsets do not reduce FlyHigh's own emissions – the aircraft still burn the same fuel; some offset projects (e.g. tree planting) may not deliver the promised reductions, so critics may accuse the company of greenwashing.
parts.working: 1 mark (knowledge): offsets do not cut own emissions / unreliable projects / greenwashing; up to 2 marks (application/explanation): applied to a cargo airline.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse one reason why consumers may not believe the environmental claims made by a fast-fashion clothing brand.
parts.answer: The brand's business model relies on selling large volumes of cheap clothes that are worn a few times and thrown away; a small 'eco' range made from recycled polyester does not change this, so consumers see the claims as greenwashing – marketing designed to improve image – and may trust the brand less.
parts.working: Indicative content: greenwashing; conflict between business model and claims; lack of independent certification; past scandals. Marks: Knowledge 1, Application 1, Analysis 3. Analysis Level 2 (2–3): a developed chain of cause and effect linked to a fast-fashion brand; Level 1 (1): a simple statement of effect. Only one point is required; no credit for evaluation.

stem: TrendLine (an invented company) designs clothes in Karachi and sells them to retailers in Europe and Pakistan. It is considering requiring all its supplier factories to pay a living wage and pass independent safety audits, which would add 6 % to the cost of each garment. Two European retailers that buy 40 % of its output have said they will only use suppliers with independent audits from 2027.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether ethical behaviour will increase the long-term profit of TrendLine.
parts.answer: Increase: ethical sourcing audits protect against scandals that could lose contracts with European retailers; younger consumers increasingly prefer ethical brands; better conditions raise supplier productivity. Decrease: higher costs (living wages in supplier factories add 6 % to unit costs) in a price-competitive market where many customers buy on price; competitors may not follow. Judgement: ethical behaviour is likely to increase long-term profit if TrendLine can communicate it to customers and charge slightly higher prices or keep contracts with retailers that demand it; for price-sensitive segments the gain is uncertain.
parts.working: Indicative content: costs vs benefits of ethical sourcing; customer and retailer expectations; reputation risk; competition on price; time horizon. Evaluation: conditional judgement for TrendLine. Marks: Knowledge 2, Application 2, Analysis 2, Evaluation 6. Evaluation Level 3 (5–6): judgements weighed throughout and a supported conclusion specific to the business; Level 2 (3–4): a judgement with some support in context; Level 1 (1–2): an unsupported or generic judgement.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Silk Route Rugs (an invented company) exports hand-knotted rugs from Lahore. 25 % of its rugs come from a group of family workshops, the Bukhara workshops. A journalist has found that children under 14 work in some of these workshops. A US importer, which buys 30 % of Silk Route's rugs, says it will cancel orders if child labour is found in the supply chain. Finding new skilled suppliers would take about 9 months.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether Silk Route Rugs should stop buying from the Bukhara workshops.
parts.answer: For stopping: evidence of child labour is a serious ethical and legal issue; the US importer (30 % of sales) has threatened to cancel orders; a media scandal could damage the brand permanently. Against stopping immediately: the workshops supply 25 % of rugs with skills hard to replace; finding new suppliers takes 9 months; stopping may push children into worse work and hurt the community. Alternative: work with the workshops and an NGO to remove child labour within 3 months, pay for schooling, and audit regularly, cutting them off if they do not comply. Judgement: an immediate public commitment with a short, monitored improvement plan is best; if the workshops will not change, Silk Route must stop buying regardless of the cost.
parts.working: Indicative content: ethics vs profit; supplier dependence; customer/importer pressure; impact on children and community; options (stop, remediate, audit). Evaluation: a justified decision with conditions. Marks: Knowledge 2, Application 2, Analysis 2, Evaluation 6. Evaluation Level 3 (5–6): judgements weighed throughout and a supported conclusion specific to the business; Level 2 (3–4): a judgement with some support in context; Level 1 (1–2): an unsupported or generic judgement.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Sindh Sugar (an invented company) operates a sugar mill near Hyderabad.
Timeline:
2020: Mill fined for discharging untreated waste water into a canal.
2021: Invests Rs 6 bn in a co-generation plant that burns bagasse (sugar-cane waste) to make electricity; surplus sold to the national grid.
2022: Builds waste-water treatment plant.
2023: Launches drip-irrigation programme with 1,200 cane farmers, with loans for equipment.
2024: Fined again after a treatment-plant breakdown.
2025: Wins a national sustainability award.
Appendix 1: CO₂ emissions per tonne of sugar – 2020: 100 (index); 2025: 60.
Appendix 2: Revenue from electricity sales – 2022: Rs 0.6 bn; 2025: Rs 1.8 bn. Sugar revenue fell 5 % over the period.
Appendix 3: Participating farmers – water use per acre down 30 %, cane yield up 12 %; 140 small farmers stopped supplying the mill, saying they could not repay equipment loans.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the effectiveness of Sindh Sugar's sustainability strategy between 2020 and 2025.
parts.answer: Environmental: bagasse co-generation plant (2021) means the mill now sells surplus electricity, reducing fossil fuel use and CO₂ emissions per tonne of sugar by 40 % (Appendix 1); waste-water treatment ended fines. Economic: electricity sales rose to Rs 1.8 bn (Appendix 2), offsetting weaker sugar prices; investment of Rs 6 bn has a long payback. Social: the drip-irrigation programme for 1,200 farmers cut water use by 30 % and raised cane yields 12 %, securing supply, but smaller farmers could not afford the equipment and some stopped supplying the mill. Limitations: total water use is still high and the 2024 fine shows lapses. Judgement: largely effective – improved environmental performance and created a new income stream – but partly limited by uneven benefits for smaller farmers and long payback; effectiveness depends on future electricity tariffs paid by the grid.
parts.working: Indicative content: triple bottom line; data on emissions, water, revenue, yields; costs vs benefits; stakeholder effects; external factors (tariffs, sugar prices). Evaluation: an overall judgement over 2020–2025. Marks: Knowledge 3, Application 3, Analysis 6, Evaluation 8. Analysis needs three or four developed chains using the timeline and appendices. Evaluation Level 3 (6–8): a clear, justified decision that weighs the evidence and is specific to the business and the time period; Level 2 (3–5): a judgement with partial support; Level 1 (1–2): assertion only.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term 'backward vertical integration'.
parts.answer: When a business joins with or takes over a business at an earlier stage of the same supply chain, such as a supplier of its raw materials.
parts.working: 1 mark: merger/takeover of a business in the same industry/supply chain; 1 mark: at an earlier stage – a supplier.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why small businesses are important to the economy of Pakistan.
parts.answer: Small businesses employ a large share of the workforce, especially in towns and rural areas; for example, small workshops and shops provide jobs and incomes where large firms do not operate, reducing unemployment and poverty.
parts.working: 1 mark (knowledge): reason: employment, innovation, competition, supply large firms, entrepreneurship; up to 2 marks (application/explanation): applied to Pakistan's economy.

stem:
Three textile businesses in Faisalabad:
Asim Textiles: 1,200 employees; sales revenue Rs 4.8 bn; capital employed Rs 3.0 bn.
Faiz Fabrics: 450 employees; sales revenue Rs 3.6 bn; capital employed Rs 5.2 bn.
Mehran Mills: 2,100 employees; sales revenue Rs 6.3 bn; capital employed Rs 4.1 bn.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify which business is the largest when measured by sales revenue.
parts.answer: Mehran Mills.
parts.working: 1 mark: Mehran Mills (Rs 6.3 bn).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the term 'organic growth'.
parts.answer: Growth from within the business, by expanding its own capacity, opening new branches or launching new products, rather than by merging with or taking over other businesses; e.g. Asim Textiles building a new weaving shed.
parts.working: 1 mark (knowledge): internal growth, not via mergers/takeovers; up to 2 marks (application/explanation): method or example applied to the data.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate sales revenue per employee for each business and state which business has the highest.
parts.answer: Asim Textiles Rs 4 million; Faiz Fabrics Rs 8 million; Mehran Mills Rs 3 million. Faiz Fabrics has the highest.
parts.working: 4.8 bn ÷ 1,200 = Rs 4 m; 3.6 bn ÷ 450 = Rs 8 m; 6.3 bn ÷ 2,100 = Rs 3 m (M1 for method, A1 for all three); Faiz Fabrics highest (A1).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term 'merger'.
parts.answer: When two or more businesses agree to join together to form one new business, usually with shareholders of both owning the combined company.
parts.working: 1 mark: two businesses combine/join; 1 mark: by mutual agreement, forming one company.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why the owner of a successful family restaurant might choose to keep the business small.
parts.answer: The owner wants to keep personal control of food quality and the family atmosphere that customers value; expanding to more branches would mean relying on managers and borrowing, risking quality and family wealth.
parts.working: 1 mark (knowledge): reason: control, quality, personal service, risk, lifestyle, niche market; up to 2 marks (application/explanation): applied to a family restaurant.

stem: Fresh Squeeze (an invented company) runs 45 juice bars in Pakistan. Oranges are its main raw material. Wholesale orange prices rose by 35 % last year, and twice the business ran short of oranges. It plans to buy an orange orchard in Sargodha.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse two benefits to Fresh Squeeze of buying an orange orchard in Sargodha.
parts.answer: Security and quality of supply: Fresh Squeeze controls its own fruit, so it is protected from shortages and can choose varieties and picking times, giving fresher juice and a consistent taste that customers value. Lower costs and higher margins: it no longer pays the wholesaler's mark-up, which has been rising, so cost per cup falls and profit margins rise. (Also accept: control over sustainability claims; selling surplus fruit.)
parts.working: Indicative content: backward vertical integration; security of supply; quality control; removal of supplier margins; differentiation/traceability. Marks: Knowledge 2, Application 2, Analysis 4. Analysis Level 2 (3–4): two developed chains of cause and effect applied to a juice-bar chain dependent on oranges; Level 1 (1–2): undeveloped or generic chains. Exactly two points are credited; no credit for evaluation.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse one problem that might arise when a cement manufacturer takes over a chain of private hospitals (a conglomerate takeover).
parts.answer: The cement company's directors have no experience of healthcare; they may make poor decisions about staffing or medical equipment, so patient care and the hospitals' reputation suffer, leading to falling revenue and a lower return on the large sum paid for the takeover.
parts.working: Indicative content: lack of expertise; different cultures; diseconomies of scale/management difficulties; diversion of management attention from core business. Marks: Knowledge 1, Application 1, Analysis 3. Analysis Level 2 (2–3): a developed chain of cause and effect linked to a cement maker running hospitals; Level 1 (1): a simple statement of effect. Only one point is required; no credit for evaluation.

stem: Delta Foods plc (an invented company) has agreed to take over Bahar Biscuits, a family-owned business with a loyal customer base in Punjab. Delta paid a 35 % premium over the estimated value of Bahar. Delta expects cost savings of Rs 900 million per year from combining the two companies' factories and distribution.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse two reasons why the takeover of Bahar Biscuits may fail to increase value for Delta Foods' shareholders.
parts.answer: Clash of cultures: Bahar is a family firm with paternalistic management, Delta is a hierarchical plc; Bahar's experienced managers may leave, losing knowledge of its distributors, so sales fall. Overpayment and diseconomies: Delta paid a high premium, and integrating factories and IT is costly; if planned savings (Rs 900 million a year) are not achieved, return on the investment will be low. (Also accept: competition authority conditions; loss of customer loyalty to the Bahar brand.)
parts.working: Indicative content: culture clash; loss of key staff; overpayment/premium; integration costs; diseconomies of scale; synergies not achieved. Marks: Knowledge 2, Application 2, Analysis 4. Analysis Level 2 (3–4): two developed chains of cause and effect applied to a plc taking over a family biscuit maker; Level 1 (1–2): undeveloped or generic chains. Exactly two points are credited; no credit for evaluation.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Taj Telecom (an invented company) has an 18 % share of the market for home broadband. It has offered Rs 84 per share for all 50 million shares of Metrolink Plus (an invented company), which has an 11 % market share. Metrolink Plus's share price before the offer was Rs 70.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage premium that Taj Telecom is offering over Metrolink Plus's current share price.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total cost of the takeover and the combined market share of the two businesses.
parts.answer: Total cost Rs 4.2 bn; combined market share 29 %.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one reason why the competition authority might investigate the takeover.
parts.answer: With 29 % of the market the combined business would be one of the largest operators and could reduce competition, raising prices or reducing service for consumers; the authority may block the takeover or set conditions.
parts.working: 1 mark (knowledge): competition policy aims to prevent abuse of market power; up to 2 marks (application/explanation): applied using the 29 % share.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether franchising is the best way for a successful burger restaurant brand in Lahore to grow into other countries.
parts.answer: For franchising: franchisees provide the capital and local knowledge, so growth is fast with low financial risk; franchise fees and royalties provide income. Against: less control over quality and brand image abroad; profits shared; finding good franchisees takes time; legal costs in different countries. Alternatives: company-owned branches (more control, more capital and risk), joint ventures with local firms, master franchise. Judgement: franchising (possibly through a master franchisee in each country) is usually best for a restaurant brand with limited capital wanting fast growth, provided strict operating standards and inspection are in place; company-owned outlets may suit one or two flagship cities.
parts.working: Indicative content: franchising pros/cons; alternatives; brand control; capital; local knowledge; risk. Evaluation: a supported judgement on the best method. Marks: Knowledge 2, Application 2, Analysis 2, Evaluation 6. Evaluation Level 3 (5–6): judgements weighed throughout and a supported conclusion specific to the business; Level 2 (3–4): a judgement with some support in context; Level 1 (1–2): an unsupported or generic judgement.

stem:
PakSky Airlines (an invented airline) flies to 12 destinations from Karachi and Lahore. It wants to offer passengers more destinations in Asia.
Option A: a strategic alliance with Kelana Air (an invented Malaysian airline): shared flight codes on 40 routes, shared lounges and maintenance. Set-up cost Rs 2 bn.
Option B: buy six new aircraft and open 8 routes itself. Cost Rs 45 bn; delivery in 3 years; financed by loans at 17 % interest.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether PakSky Airlines should form a strategic alliance with Kelana Air rather than grow organically by buying more aircraft.
parts.answer: Alliance: code-sharing gives PakSky passengers access to 40 routes in Asia without buying aircraft; shared lounges and maintenance cut costs; low capital need (Rs 2 bn vs Rs 45 bn for six aircraft), which matters with high interest rates. Risks: less control over service quality, revenue shared, dependence on a partner that could leave. Organic growth: full control and keeps all profit but high cost, slow (aircraft delivery 3 years) and risky if demand falls. Judgement: the alliance is better now given limited capital and high interest rates, provided the agreement protects PakSky's brand and allows it to leave; organic growth can follow once demand on new routes is proven.
parts.working: Indicative content: methods of growth compared; capital and interest costs; speed; control; risk; synergies. Evaluation: decision using the case data. Marks: Knowledge 2, Application 2, Analysis 2, Evaluation 6. Evaluation Level 3 (5–6): judgements weighed throughout and a supported conclusion specific to the business; Level 2 (3–4): a judgement with some support in context; Level 1 (1–2): an unsupported or generic judgement.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
MediPlus (an invented company) runs pharmacies in Pakistan.
Timeline:
2019: 40 pharmacies; market share 6 %.
2021: 70 pharmacies after opening new branches funded from retained profit.
2022: Takes over rival CureWell (110 branches), funded by a large bank loan.
2023: New IT system fails for 3 weeks; many CureWell managers resign.
2024: Closes 25 branches where MediPlus and CureWell branches were close together; centralises purchasing.
2025: 155 pharmacies; market share 19 %.
Appendix 1: Operating profit margin – 2019: 9 %; 2021: 9 %; 2023: 4 %; 2025: 7 %. Gross margin rose by 2 percentage points after 2022.
Appendix 2: Labour turnover – 2021: 15 %; 2023: 34 %; 2025: 20 %.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the effectiveness of MediPlus's growth strategy between 2019 and 2025.
parts.answer: Organic growth 2019–2021 (from 40 to 70 pharmacies) was profitable: operating margin stable at 9 % (Appendix 1). The 2022 takeover of CureWell (110 branches) more than doubled its branch network quickly and gave buying power with suppliers (gross margin up 2 points), but integration problems followed: IT systems failed in 2023, labour turnover rose to 34 % (Appendix 2), and operating margin fell to 4 %. Diseconomies of scale and culture clash reduced the benefits. 2024–2025 closing 25 overlapping branches and centralising purchasing improved margins to 7 %. Judgement: the strategy was effective in increasing size and market share (from 6 % to 19 %), but less effective in terms of profitability and staff – the takeover was too large and fast to integrate; its long-term success depends on whether margins return to 9 %.
parts.working: Indicative content: organic vs external growth; economies and diseconomies of scale; integration; culture; evidence from margins, market share and turnover; different success criteria. Evaluation: an overall judgement over the period. Marks: Knowledge 3, Application 3, Analysis 6, Evaluation 8. Analysis needs three or four developed chains using the timeline and appendices. Evaluation Level 3 (6–8): a clear, justified decision that weighs the evidence and is specific to the business and the time period; Level 2 (3–5): a judgement with partial support; Level 1 (1–2): assertion only.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
