parts.text: Define the term 'business plan'.
parts.answer: A written document that sets out a business's objectives and how it intends to achieve them, including marketing, operations and financial forecasts.
parts.working: 1 mark: written document/report about a (new) business; 1 mark: objectives/strategies plus forecasts, e.g. market research, cash-flow and profit forecasts.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one risk a software engineer faces when leaving a salaried job to start her own IT company.
parts.answer: She gives up a regular income; if the company does not win enough clients in its first year she may be unable to pay her bills, and if she used her savings or (as a sole trader) has unlimited liability, she could lose personal assets.
parts.working: 1 mark (knowledge): risk: loss of income, loss of capital/savings, unlimited liability, failure; up to 2 marks (application/explanation): applied to the engineer starting an IT business.

stem: Areeba is starting a business in Multan selling homemade mango and lime pickles in glass jars, under the brand 'Nani's Kitchen'. Her business plan forecasts first-year sales of 18,000 jars at Rs 450 each. Variable costs are Rs 210 per jar and fixed costs are Rs 2,880,000 per year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify one source of support available to a new entrepreneur such as Areeba.
parts.answer: A government small-business support agency (also accept: business incubator, bank small-business adviser, microfinance lender, mentors, chamber of commerce).
parts.working: 1 mark for any valid source.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the term 'enterprise'.
parts.answer: The ability and willingness to take risks and use initiative to set up and run a business, combining resources to produce goods or services; Areeba showed enterprise by turning her mother's recipes into a branded product.
parts.working: 1 mark (knowledge): taking risks/initiative to start a business and organise resources; up to 2 marks (application/explanation): applied to Areeba's pickle business.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the forecast profit for Areeba's business in its first year.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two sections that a business plan for a new café would usually contain.
parts.answer: Any two of: executive summary/business description; market research and target market; marketing plan; operations (location, equipment, suppliers); staffing; financial forecasts (cash flow, profit, break-even); sources of finance.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid sections.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why a bank asks for a business plan before lending to a new café owner.
parts.answer: The bank needs evidence that the café can repay; the plan's market research and cash-flow forecast show whether expected revenue will cover loan repayments and the risk of default, helping the bank decide how much to lend and at what interest rate.
parts.working: 1 mark (knowledge): reason: assess risk/ability to repay, viability; up to 2 marks (application/explanation): applied to a café loan decision.

stem: A university business incubator in Peshawar helped 240 new businesses to start. Three years later, 78 of them were still trading.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of businesses started at the incubator that were no longer trading after three years.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the term 'opportunity cost' for an entrepreneur starting a business.
parts.answer: The next best alternative given up when making a choice; for a graduate starting a business at the incubator, it is the salary they could have earned in a job instead.
parts.working: 1 mark (knowledge): next best alternative forgone; up to 2 marks (application/explanation): applied to an entrepreneur's choice.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one reason why many new businesses fail in their first three years.
parts.answer: Poor cash-flow management: new businesses often give credit to customers while paying suppliers immediately, so they run out of cash even when sales are growing, and cannot pay wages or rent.
parts.working: 1 mark (knowledge): reason: cash flow, poor market research, lack of experience, competition, insufficient finance; up to 2 marks (application/explanation): explained with its consequence.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Bilal, a 24-year-old graduate, plans to start KhetiLink, an app that lets small farmers in Sindh order seeds and fertiliser and sell their crops directly to buyers. He has Rs 1.5 million of savings and needs Rs 12 million to develop the app and set up delivery. Most farmers currently deal with local middlemen.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse two challenges Bilal might face in starting KhetiLink.
parts.answer: Low trust and digital skills among customers: many small farmers have basic phones and are wary of buying through an app, so adoption is slow and revenue grows more slowly than the business plan forecasts. Raising finance: with no track record and an untested idea, banks may refuse to lend without collateral, so Bilal must use his own savings or seek investors who will take a share of ownership, limiting growth or his control. (Also accept: competition from established middlemen, building a delivery network in rural areas.)
parts.working: Indicative content: finance; customer adoption/trust; lack of experience; competition from middlemen; logistics in rural areas; cash flow. Marks: Knowledge 2, Application 2, Analysis 4. Analysis Level 2 (3–4): two developed chains of cause and effect applied to an agritech start-up in rural Sindh; Level 1 (1–2): undeveloped or generic chains. Exactly two points are credited; no credit for evaluation.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse one way a government could support entrepreneurs.
parts.answer: The government could offer low-interest start-up loans or loan guarantees; because new businesses often lack collateral, this makes finance available, so more viable businesses can start and invest in equipment, creating jobs and tax revenue.
parts.working: Indicative content: finance (loans, grants, guarantees); training and advice; incubators; tax relief; reduced regulation. Marks: Knowledge 1, Application 1, Analysis 3. Analysis Level 2 (2–3): a developed chain of cause and effect linked to entrepreneurs who lack finance or experience; Level 1 (1): a simple statement of effect. Only one point is required; no credit for evaluation.

stem: Pani Pure (an invented social enterprise) runs 60 solar-powered water filtration plants in Tharparkar, where groundwater is salty. It sells filtered water at Rs 2 per litre, just enough to cover costs, and trains local women to run the plants. A private company has offered to buy Pani Pure.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse two ways in which the objectives of Pani Pure, as a social enterprise, are likely to differ from those of a private-sector water company.
parts.answer: Social objectives come first: Pani Pure measures success by the number of families with safe water and the fall in waterborne illness, so it sells water at cost even in the poorest villages, whereas a private company would focus on profitable areas. Use of surpluses: Pani Pure reinvests surpluses in more filtration plants rather than paying dividends to shareholders, so it expands into new villages even when returns are low. (Also accept: employing local women as plant operators as an objective; financial sustainability rather than profit maximisation.)
parts.working: Indicative content: social/environmental objectives vs profit; reinvestment of surplus; pricing; target communities; measures of success. Marks: Knowledge 2, Application 2, Analysis 4. Analysis Level 2 (3–4): two developed chains of cause and effect applied to a water social enterprise in Tharparkar; Level 1 (1–2): undeveloped or generic chains. Exactly two points are credited; no credit for evaluation.

author: HomiLabs

stem: StyleBox (an invented start-up) sends a monthly box of clothing accessories to subscribers in Karachi. It has Rs 18 million cash in the bank. Its costs are Rs 2.6 million per month and its revenue is Rs 1.1 million per month. Its business plan forecast 4,000 subscribers by month 6, but it has only 1,400.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many months StyleBox's current cash will last if its monthly costs and revenue stay at their current levels.
parts.answer: 12 months.
parts.working: Net monthly outflow = 2.6 m − 1.1 m = Rs 1.5 million (M1); 18 m ÷ 1.5 m (M1) = 12 months (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one limitation of the sales forecast in StyleBox's business plan.
parts.answer: The forecast assumed 4,000 subscribers by month 6, but it was based on a small online survey of friends and family, so it was too optimistic; actual revenue is much lower, and decisions based on it (e.g. hiring staff) increased costs.
parts.working: 1 mark (knowledge): forecasts are estimates/based on assumptions or limited research; up to 2 marks (application/explanation): applied to StyleBox.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether the personal qualities of the entrepreneur are the most important factor in the success of a new restaurant.
parts.answer: Qualities such as resilience, hard work, creativity and willingness to take risks help an owner survive the long hours and early losses; leadership affects staff and service quality. Other factors: location and footfall; access to finance and cash-flow management; market research and choice of target market; competition; skills of the chef; economic conditions such as inflation in food prices. Judgement: personal qualities are necessary, but without a good location, sound finances and a product customers want, even an excellent entrepreneur may fail; the most important factor depends on the market – in a crowded restaurant area, location and differentiation may matter most.
parts.working: Indicative content: entrepreneurial qualities; alternative factors (finance, location, planning, competition, economy); interaction between factors. Evaluation: a supported conclusion on relative importance. Marks: Knowledge 2, Application 2, Analysis 2, Evaluation 6. Evaluation Level 3 (5–6): judgements weighed throughout and a supported conclusion specific to the business; Level 2 (3–4): a judgement with some support in context; Level 1 (1–2): an unsupported or generic judgement.

stem: Hunar Sisters (an invented social enterprise) trains 200 women in Hunza and Chitral to make embroidered goods, which it sells online at fair prices. It makes a small surplus that it uses to train more women. An investor offers Rs 50 million for a 40 % share if the business becomes a private limited company with a target return of 20 % a year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether Hunar Sisters should accept the investor's offer to convert into a profit-making private limited company.
parts.answer: For: Rs 50 million of investment would let the business open in three cities and train 600 more women, increasing social impact; professional management may improve online marketing. Against: the investor wants 40 % ownership and a target return of 20 % a year, which may push up prices or reduce payments to artisans, conflicting with the social mission; founders lose some control; grant funders may withdraw. Judgement: accept only if the shareholder agreement protects the social objective (e.g. minimum payments to artisans, founders keep a majority and veto), otherwise seek alternative finance such as impact investors or grants; growth that abandons the mission would destroy the business's main selling point.
parts.working: Indicative content: social enterprise vs profit-making company; finance for growth; control; conflict between objectives; brand built on social mission; alternatives. Evaluation: a conditional decision for Hunar Sisters. Marks: Knowledge 2, Application 2, Analysis 2, Evaluation 6. Evaluation Level 3 (5–6): judgements weighed throughout and a supported conclusion specific to the business; Level 2 (3–4): a judgement with some support in context; Level 1 (1–2): an unsupported or generic judgement.

author: HomiLabs

stem: FitFuel (an invented start-up) makes high-protein snacks in Lahore. Its business plan, used to raise Rs 40 million from investors, forecast that 70 % of revenue would come from selling through gyms. After 12 months: gyms provide 25 % of revenue; online subscriptions provide 60 % and are growing by 15 % per month; supermarkets provide 15 %. The gym sales team costs Rs 1.2 million per month.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether the founders of FitFuel should follow their original business plan or change their strategy.
parts.answer: Data: the plan forecast 70 % of revenue from gym sales, but gyms provide only 25 %; online subscriptions are 60 % and growing 15 % a month. Sticking to the plan: investors approved it, and gym partnerships may still grow; but evidence shows demand is elsewhere. Changing (pivot): focus on online subscriptions, cut the costly gym sales team; risks – depends on delivery partners, competitors may copy, investors need to agree. Judgement: a business plan is a guide, not a fixed rule; the founders should revise the plan around online subscriptions, using the new evidence, and explain the change to investors with updated forecasts.
parts.working: Indicative content: purpose and limitations of business plans; interpretation of data; flexibility; investors' expectations; risks of change. Evaluation: decision based on the data with conditions. Marks: Knowledge 2, Application 2, Analysis 2, Evaluation 6. Evaluation Level 3 (5–6): judgements weighed throughout and a supported conclusion specific to the business; Level 2 (3–4): a judgement with some support in context; Level 1 (1–2): an unsupported or generic judgement.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term 'mixed economy'.
parts.answer: An economy in which resources are allocated partly by the private sector through markets and partly by the government (public sector).
parts.working: 1 mark: both private sector and public sector; 1 mark: allocate resources/produce goods and services.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one difference between a co-operative and a private limited company.
parts.answer: In a co-operative, members (e.g. dairy farmers) each have one vote regardless of the money they invest and profits are shared according to use; in a private limited company, votes and dividends depend on the number of shares owned.
parts.working: 1 mark (knowledge): valid difference: ownership/control (one member one vote), purpose, distribution of profit; up to 2 marks (application/explanation): explained/illustrated.

stem: Hamid has opened a tutoring centre in Rawalpindi under the brand of Smart Tutors (an invented company). He paid an initial fee of Rs 2,500,000 and must pay a royalty of 6 % of sales revenue each year. He expects sales revenue of Rs 54,000,000 in his first year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the type of business organisation used by Hamid.
parts.answer: Franchise (Hamid is a franchisee; also accept sole trader operating a franchise).
parts.working: 1 mark: franchise/franchisee.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the term 'franchise'.
parts.answer: An agreement in which a franchisor allows a franchisee to use its brand name, products and business methods in return for an initial fee and ongoing royalties; Hamid runs a Smart Tutors centre using its name and teaching materials.
parts.working: 1 mark (knowledge): right to use another business's brand/format in exchange for fees/royalties; up to 2 marks (application/explanation): applied to Hamid and Smart Tutors.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the total amount Hamid must pay to Smart Tutors in his first year.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term 'multinational company'.
parts.answer: A business that has its headquarters in one country and production or service operations (not just sales) in two or more countries.
parts.working: 1 mark: business operating in more than one country; 1 mark: production/operations facilities abroad, not just exporting.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one benefit to Pakistan of a multinational car maker opening an assembly plant near Karachi.
parts.answer: It creates thousands of direct jobs and more at local parts suppliers, raising incomes; workers learn new technology and quality methods, which spreads to Pakistani firms.
parts.working: 1 mark (knowledge): benefit: jobs, skills/technology transfer, tax revenue, exports, investment; up to 2 marks (application/explanation): applied to a car plant in Pakistan.

stem: Pak Power Distribution (an invented company) is owned by the government and distributes electricity to 4 million homes. It loses Rs 60 billion a year, mainly because of electricity theft and unpaid bills. The government plans to sell it to private investors.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the form of ownership of Pak Power Distribution at present.
parts.answer: Public sector (state-owned; government-owned also accepted).
parts.working: 1 mark: public sector / owned by the government.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the term 'privatisation'.
parts.answer: Transferring ownership of a business from the public sector (government) to the private sector, e.g. by selling shares in Pak Power Distribution to private investors.
parts.working: 1 mark (knowledge): transfer of ownership from public to private sector; up to 2 marks (application/explanation): method or example applied.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one possible disadvantage to consumers of privatising Pak Power Distribution.
parts.answer: A private owner aims to make a profit; it may raise electricity prices or stop investing in unprofitable rural areas, so poorer consumers pay more or receive worse supply, especially if it remains a local monopoly.
parts.working: 1 mark (knowledge): disadvantage: higher prices, cuts to unprofitable services, private monopoly; up to 2 marks (application/explanation): applied to electricity consumers.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Zaiqa Foods Ltd (an invented company) has 10 million shares, of which the Qureshi family owns 8 million. It plans to become a public limited company and sell 6 million new shares on the stock exchange.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of Zaiqa Foods' shares the Qureshi family will own after the share issue.
parts.working: Total shares after issue = 10 m + 6 m = 16 m (M1); family 8 m ÷ 16 m (M1) × 100 = 50 % (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the term 'divorce of ownership and control'.
parts.answer: In a public limited company the shareholders who own the company are often different from the directors and managers who control it day to day; after the share issue Zaiqa's new shareholders will own half the company but the managers will make decisions, and their objectives may differ.
parts.working: 1 mark (knowledge): owners (shareholders) separate from those who control (directors/managers); up to 2 marks (application/explanation): consequence (different objectives) applied to Zaiqa.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Green Leaf Tea Ltd (an invented company) is a family-owned private limited company that blends and packs tea. It wants Rs 3 billion to build a new packing plant. The family is considering converting it into a public limited company and selling shares on the stock exchange.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse two disadvantages to Green Leaf Tea of converting to a public limited company.
parts.answer: Loss of control: new shareholders can buy shares and vote, and the family's share would fall below 50 %; outside shareholders may push for short-term profit and oppose the family's long-term investment in tea gardens, or a rival could build up a stake and take over. Cost and disclosure: listing costs (underwriters, legal and accounting fees) are high, and annual accounts must be published, so competitors learn about Green Leaf's margins and plans; meeting stock-exchange rules raises administration costs.
parts.working: Indicative content: loss of control/takeover risk; short-termism; flotation costs; disclosure of information; regulation; divorce of ownership and control. Marks: Knowledge 2, Application 2, Analysis 4. Analysis Level 2 (3–4): two developed chains of cause and effect applied to a family-owned tea company; Level 1 (1–2): undeveloped or generic chains. Exactly two points are credited; no credit for evaluation.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse one advantage to two architects of forming a partnership rather than each working as a sole trader.
parts.answer: They pool skills: one specialises in residential design and the other in commercial buildings, so the partnership can bid for larger mixed-use projects that neither could win alone, increasing revenue and sharing workload and decision-making.
parts.working: Indicative content: more capital; shared skills; shared workload and decisions; cover for holidays/illness; shared risk of losses. Marks: Knowledge 1, Application 1, Analysis 3. Analysis Level 2 (2–3): a developed chain of cause and effect linked to two architects working together; Level 1 (1): a simple statement of effect. Only one point is required; no credit for evaluation.

stem: The National Water Board (an invented organisation) supplies water to 20 million people. It has made losses for ten years and many pipes leak. Some politicians want it sold to private investors.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse two reasons why the government might keep the National Water Board in the public sector.
parts.answer: Water is an essential service: a private owner would aim for profit and might raise prices or not supply poor areas, so keeping it public ensures everyone has access at affordable prices, improving public health. It is a natural monopoly: building rival pipe networks would waste resources, and a private monopoly could exploit consumers, so public ownership (or strict regulation) protects consumers and lets the government invest for the long term, e.g. in reservoirs during droughts.
parts.working: Indicative content: essential/merit good; natural monopoly; strategic importance; social objectives vs profit; long-term investment; employment. Marks: Knowledge 2, Application 2, Analysis 4. Analysis Level 2 (3–4): two developed chains of cause and effect applied to a national water supplier; Level 1 (1–2): undeveloped or generic chains. Exactly two points are credited; no credit for evaluation.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether a co-operative is the most suitable form of business organisation for 300 mango growers in Multan who want to export their fruit.
parts.answer: Co-operative: growers pool resources to buy cold storage, packing and certification that no single small farmer could afford; one member one vote keeps control with farmers; profits shared by quantity supplied. Problems: slow democratic decisions; difficulty raising large amounts of capital; members may lack marketing and export expertise; disputes over quality. Alternatives: a private limited company owned by the growers (easier to raise finance, appoint professional managers), or selling to an established exporter. Judgement: a co-operative is suitable because members' main aim is a fair price and shared facilities, provided it hires professional managers for exporting; a company may be better if large external finance is needed.
parts.working: Indicative content: features of co-operatives; finance; control; decision-making; expertise; alternatives. Evaluation: a supported recommendation for the growers. Marks: Knowledge 2, Application 2, Analysis 2, Evaluation 6. Evaluation Level 3 (5–6): judgements weighed throughout and a supported conclusion specific to the business; Level 2 (3–4): a judgement with some support in context; Level 1 (1–2): an unsupported or generic judgement.

stem: Sadia runs Sadia's Bakes, a successful cake business in Islamabad, as a sole trader. She plans to open a central bakery supplying 20 cafés, which needs a bank loan of Rs 15 million. Her brother is willing to invest Rs 5 million if he can have a share in the business. She owns her house.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether Sadia should change Sadia's Bakes from a sole trader to a private limited company.
parts.answer: For: limited liability protects her house if the Rs 15 million loan cannot be repaid; a company may find it easier to borrow and to bring in her brother as a shareholder; better image with corporate clients. Against: registration and accounting costs; accounts must be filed and are available to the public; she must share profits and some control with any new shareholders; banks may still ask for a personal guarantee, reducing the protection of limited liability. Judgement: forming a private limited company is sensible because she is taking on large debt and planning to grow, but she should be aware that a personal guarantee would weaken the benefit.
parts.working: Indicative content: limited vs unlimited liability; finance; control; costs and disclosure; personal guarantee; growth plans. Evaluation: decision for Sadia's Bakes. Marks: Knowledge 2, Application 2, Analysis 2, Evaluation 6. Evaluation Level 3 (5–6): judgements weighed throughout and a supported conclusion specific to the business; Level 2 (3–4): a judgement with some support in context; Level 1 (1–2): an unsupported or generic judgement.

author: HomiLabs

stem: GreenFields Co-operative (an invented dairy co-operative) is owned by 1,800 farmers in Punjab, each with one vote. It wants to build a milk-powder plant costing Rs 900 million. Banks have refused to lend the full amount. Nordic Dairy (an invented foreign company) has offered Rs 600 million for 45 % of the shares if GreenFields becomes a private limited company.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether GreenFields Co-operative should convert into a private limited company to finance its expansion.
parts.answer: For: Rs 900 million needed for a milk-powder plant; banks have refused to lend the full amount; a company could sell shares to an investor (Nordic Dairy has offered Rs 600 million for 45 %) and appoint professional managers. Against: the 1,800 farmer-members would lose 'one member one vote' and could be outvoted; a profit-seeking investor may pay farmers lower milk prices; members' loyalty may fall and supply could drop. Judgement: convert only if the farmers keep majority ownership (55 %) and a guaranteed fair milk price is written into the shareholder agreement; otherwise look for alternatives such as a joint venture for the powder plant only, leaving the co-operative intact.
parts.working: Indicative content: co-operative principles; access to finance; control and objectives; members' interests; alternative structures (joint venture). Evaluation: conditional judgement using the data. Marks: Knowledge 2, Application 2, Analysis 2, Evaluation 6. Evaluation Level 3 (5–6): judgements weighed throughout and a supported conclusion specific to the business; Level 2 (3–4): a judgement with some support in context; Level 1 (1–2): an unsupported or generic judgement.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term 'internal stakeholder'.
parts.answer: A person or group inside the organisation with an interest in its activities, such as employees, managers and (often) shareholders/owners.
parts.working: 1 mark: group with an interest in the business; 1 mark: from within the organisation – employees, managers, owners.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one way the local community could be affected by the expansion of an airport near Islamabad.
parts.answer: More flights mean more noise and air pollution for nearby villages, disturbing sleep and reducing house prices; however, residents may also gain jobs in airport services.
parts.working: 1 mark (knowledge): valid effect (noise, pollution, traffic, jobs, land loss); up to 2 marks (application/explanation): applied to an airport expansion.

stem: Hyper Bazaar (an invented company) runs 8 hypermarkets in Karachi. It wants to extend payment to its suppliers from 30 days to 60 days. A local pressure group, 'Clean Karachi', is campaigning against its use of plastic bags.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify one external stakeholder of Hyper Bazaar.
parts.answer: Suppliers (also accept: customers, local community, government, pressure groups, banks).
parts.working: 1 mark for any external stakeholder.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the term 'pressure group'.
parts.answer: An organisation that tries to influence the decisions of businesses or governments on a particular issue, e.g. the 'Clean Karachi' group campaigning against Hyper Bazaar's plastic bags through social media and protests.
parts.working: 1 mark (knowledge): organised group aiming to influence decisions on an issue; up to 2 marks (application/explanation): methods/example applied to Hyper Bazaar.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one way Hyper Bazaar's suppliers could influence its decisions.
parts.answer: Large food manufacturers supply popular brands that customers expect to find; if Hyper Bazaar demands longer credit periods, these suppliers could refuse to deliver, so Hyper Bazaar may have to accept their terms.
parts.working: 1 mark (knowledge): supplier influence: power of key brands, credit terms, prices, quality; up to 2 marks (application/explanation): applied to a hypermarket.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two responsibilities a business has to its employees.
parts.answer: Any two of: pay at least the legal minimum wage on time; provide a safe and healthy workplace; treat employees fairly without discrimination; provide training; follow employment contracts and laws.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid responsibilities.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one responsibility a bank has to its customers.
parts.answer: To keep customers' money and personal data secure, e.g. protecting online banking from fraud; if it fails, customers lose savings and trust, and the bank faces fines and loss of business.
parts.working: 1 mark (knowledge): valid responsibility (security, fair charges, honest information, privacy); up to 2 marks (application/explanation): applied to bank customers.

stem: Pak Glass (an invented company): total dividends paid to shareholders rose from Rs 120 million in 2024 to Rs 165 million in 2025. The average monthly wage of production workers rose from Rs 48,000 to Rs 51,600 over the same period. Inflation was 12 %.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in total dividends and the percentage increase in average wages at Pak Glass between 2024 and 2025.
parts.answer: Dividends +37.5 %; average wages +7.5 %.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one possible conflict between Pak Glass's shareholders and employees shown by these data.
parts.answer: Shareholders' dividends rose five times faster than wages, while inflation was 12 %, so employees' real wages fell; employees may feel profits are being paid to owners rather than workers and demand higher pay, which would reduce future dividends.
parts.working: 1 mark (knowledge): conflict over distribution of profit; up to 2 marks (application/explanation): use of data including inflation.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Crown Tobacco (an invented company) makes cigarettes in Pakistan. The government wants to reduce smoking for health reasons but also receives large tax revenues from cigarette sales.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse two ways in which the government, as a stakeholder, can influence Crown Tobacco.
parts.answer: Taxation: raising excise duty on cigarettes increases prices, reducing sales volume; Crown may cut costs or move into other products. Regulation: laws requiring large health warnings and banning advertising limit Crown's ability to promote its brands, so it loses new young customers and must rely on packaging and distribution. (Also accept: minimum age laws, restrictions on where smoking is allowed, action on illegal cigarettes.)
parts.working: Indicative content: taxes and duties; advertising/packaging laws; age restrictions; smoking bans; enforcement against illegal trade; licensing. Marks: Knowledge 2, Application 2, Analysis 4. Analysis Level 2 (3–4): two developed chains of cause and effect applied to a cigarette manufacturer; Level 1 (1–2): undeveloped or generic chains. Exactly two points are credited; no credit for evaluation.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse one way customers can influence the decisions of a mobile phone manufacturer.
parts.answer: Customers post reviews and complaints on social media; when many buyers complained about a phone overheating, the reviews spread quickly and sales fell, so the manufacturer was forced to recall the model and change its design to protect its brand.
parts.working: Indicative content: purchasing decisions/boycott; social media reviews; feedback and market research; consumer protection groups. Marks: Knowledge 1, Application 1, Analysis 3. Analysis Level 2 (2–3): a developed chain of cause and effect linked to a phone maker sensitive to reviews; Level 1 (1): a simple statement of effect. Only one point is required; no credit for evaluation.

stem: Sky Pak Airlines (an invented company) made losses for five years. A new owner has bought 70 % of its shares and plans to cut 1,200 of its 7,000 jobs, outsource catering and close 6 domestic routes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse two reasons why the objectives of shareholders and employees at Sky Pak Airlines may conflict during its restructuring.
parts.answer: Shareholders want a return to profit quickly, so they support cutting 1,200 jobs and outsourcing catering, which reduces costs; employees want job security and fair pay, so they oppose the cuts, and may take industrial action that disrupts flights. Shareholders want to sell old aircraft and lease newer ones on fewer routes; employees on cancelled routes lose jobs or must relocate. The more the plan benefits shareholders, the more employees lose, creating conflict.
parts.working: Indicative content: profit vs job security; pay restraint vs dividends; outsourcing; route cuts; short-term vs long-term interests. Marks: Knowledge 2, Application 2, Analysis 4. Analysis Level 2 (3–4): two developed chains of cause and effect applied to an airline restructuring with job cuts; Level 1 (1–2): undeveloped or generic chains. Exactly two points are credited; no credit for evaluation.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Coastal Highways (an invented company) has a government contract to build a coastal road near Gwadar. The planned route crosses land used by fishing villages to reach the beach. Villagers have protested and blocked the site twice, delaying work by 5 weeks.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse two ways Coastal Highways could reduce conflict with the local community over the new road.
parts.answer: Consultation: holding meetings with fishing communities and adjusting the route to keep access to the beach would show residents they are listened to, reducing protests that could delay construction and increase costs. Compensation and benefits: paying fair compensation for land and employing local workers on construction gives the community a share of the benefits, so opposition falls and the project finishes on time.
parts.working: Indicative content: consultation and communication; compensation; local jobs; changing plans to reduce harm; community projects (schools, clinics). Marks: Knowledge 2, Application 2, Analysis 4. Analysis Level 2 (3–4): two developed chains of cause and effect applied to a road builder near fishing villages; Level 1 (1–2): undeveloped or generic chains. Exactly two points are credited; no credit for evaluation.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether a mining company operating in Balochistan can satisfy the objectives of all its stakeholders.
parts.answer: Stakeholder objectives: shareholders want profit; employees want safe jobs and fair pay; local community wants jobs, water and a clean environment; government wants royalties and development; environmental groups want limited damage. Some objectives can be met together (local hiring, safety improves productivity, community projects secure a 'social licence to operate'). But conflicts are often unavoidable – e.g. water use for processing versus village supply, profit versus environmental restoration costs. Judgement: the company cannot satisfy all fully; it must prioritise and compromise, using consultation and CSR to reduce conflict; the balance depends on the power and interest of each group and on legal requirements.
parts.working: Indicative content: different stakeholder objectives; areas of overlap and conflict; stakeholder power; CSR and consultation; trade-offs. Evaluation: a supported conclusion – cannot fully satisfy all, but can manage. Marks: Knowledge 2, Application 2, Analysis 2, Evaluation 6. Evaluation Level 3 (5–6): judgements weighed throughout and a supported conclusion specific to the business; Level 2 (3–4): a judgement with some support in context; Level 1 (1–2): an unsupported or generic judgement.

stem: NovaSoft (an invented company) develops banking software in Lahore. It employs 300 developers; labour turnover is 30 %. One bank client provides 35 % of its revenue. It is funded by a venture capital firm that owns 40 % of its shares.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether employees are the most important stakeholder group for NovaSoft.
parts.answer: Employees: NovaSoft's product is software built by skilled developers; with 30 % turnover, losing developers delays projects and loses clients; their knowledge is the main asset. Customers: generate all revenue; a key client provides 35 % of sales. Shareholders: venture capital investors control funding and can replace management. Judgement: for a software business employees are probably the most important because without them NovaSoft cannot serve customers or create value for shareholders; but the importance of each group changes – when funding is needed, investors dominate; the key client also has great power.
parts.working: Indicative content: roles and power of employees, customers, shareholders/investors; interdependence; changes over time. Evaluation: judgement specific to NovaSoft. Marks: Knowledge 2, Application 2, Analysis 2, Evaluation 6. Evaluation Level 3 (5–6): judgements weighed throughout and a supported conclusion specific to the business; Level 2 (3–4): a judgement with some support in context; Level 1 (1–2): an unsupported or generic judgement.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Al Hamd Garments (an invented company) employs 1,100 workers in a town near Lahore. It could move to a new special economic zone 40 km away, where it would pay no corporate tax for 10 years and land is cheaper; profit would rise by about Rs 300 million a year. The union opposes the move. Al Hamd is the town's largest employer. Its European buyers prefer modern factories that pass social audits.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether Al Hamd Garments should move its factory to the special economic zone.
parts.answer: Shareholders: tax exemption for 10 years and lower land costs increase profit by about Rs 300 million a year. Employees: 1,100 workers would face a 40 km journey; the union opposes the move; many may leave, losing skills (turnover could rise). Community: the town loses its largest employer; the new zone gains jobs. Customers: newer factory improves compliance with buyers' audits. Judgement: the move offers clear financial benefits, but the business should proceed only if it provides free transport and relocation help to keep skilled workers; otherwise the loss of experienced machinists may cancel the savings.
parts.working: Indicative content: costs and benefits for each stakeholder group; power of union/buyers; conflict; measures to reduce conflict. Evaluation: a decision with conditions using the data. Marks: Knowledge 2, Application 2, Analysis 2, Evaluation 6. Evaluation Level 3 (5–6): judgements weighed throughout and a supported conclusion specific to the business; Level 2 (3–4): a judgement with some support in context; Level 1 (1–2): an unsupported or generic judgement.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Skyline Developers (an invented company) is building a 40-storey apartment complex in Karachi.
Timeline:
2021: Construction starts; residents of nearby streets complain about traffic and water shortages.
2022: Residents' association wins a court order stopping work for 9 months.
2023: New CEO creates a community liaison committee; the company funds a water treatment plant and adds a public park to the design. Work restarts.
2024: Cash shortages; two building contractors stop work after not being paid for 4 months.
2025: Project 80 % complete.
Appendix 1: Extra costs from the 2022 stoppage – Rs 1.2 bn.
Appendix 2: Apartments pre-sold – 2022: 30 %; 2025: 85 %.
Appendix 3: Dividends paid – none 2023–2025.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate how effectively Skyline Developers managed its stakeholders between 2021 and 2025.
parts.answer: 2021–2022: the company ignored residents' concerns about traffic and water; protests and a court case stopped work for 9 months, adding Rs 1.2 bn in costs (Appendix 1) – ineffective. 2023: new CEO set up a community liaison committee, funded a water treatment plant and changed the design to add a park; protests ended and construction restarted; buyers' confidence returned (pre-sales up from 30 % to 85 %, Appendix 2). 2024–2025: suppliers paid late due to cash shortages – two contractors stopped work; shareholders received no dividend for 3 years. Judgement: management of the community became effective after 2023, but other stakeholders (suppliers, shareholders) were less well managed, partly because of the earlier delays; overall the company learned to manage key stakeholders, but too late to avoid serious costs.
parts.working: Indicative content: stakeholder power and interest; conflict; consultation; CSR; effects on costs, sales and timing; different groups over different periods. Evaluation: overall judgement with evidence across the period. Marks: Knowledge 3, Application 3, Analysis 6, Evaluation 8. Analysis needs three or four developed chains using the timeline and appendices. Evaluation Level 3 (6–8): a clear, justified decision that weighs the evidence and is specific to the business and the time period; Level 2 (3–5): a judgement with partial support; Level 1 (1–2): assertion only.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term 'mission statement'.
parts.answer: A short written statement of the purpose and values of an organisation, explaining what it is trying to achieve in broad, qualitative terms.
parts.working: 1 mark: statement of purpose/aims of the organisation; 1 mark: qualitative/values, not measurable targets.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one benefit to a charity hospital in Lahore of having a mission statement.
parts.answer: It tells staff, donors and patients what the hospital stands for, e.g. 'free quality care for all'; this helps attract donations from people who share its values and guides doctors' decisions.
parts.working: 1 mark (knowledge): benefit: shared purpose, motivation, guides decisions, communicates to stakeholders/donors; up to 2 marks (application/explanation): applied to a charity hospital.

stem: Al Noor Foods (an invented company) set a corporate objective of increasing sales revenue by 15 % in 2025. Its revenue was Rs 320 million in 2024 and Rs 361.6 million in 2025.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify one objective other than profit that Al Noor Foods might have.
parts.answer: Growth (also accept: survival, market share, CSR/ethical objective, customer satisfaction).
parts.working: 1 mark for any valid objective.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the term 'corporate objective'.
parts.answer: A target for the whole business, set by senior management, which guides departmental objectives; e.g. Al Noor's target to increase revenue by 15 % a year.
parts.working: 1 mark (knowledge): objective for the organisation as a whole; up to 2 marks (application/explanation): link to departmental objectives/example.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate whether Al Noor Foods achieved its sales revenue objective in 2025.
parts.answer: Revenue grew by 13 %, so the 15 % objective was not achieved (it fell short by 2 percentage points).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term 'satisficing'.
parts.answer: Aiming for a satisfactory or acceptable level of profit (or other outcome) rather than the maximum possible, often to balance the owner's other aims or stakeholders' interests.
parts.working: 1 mark: aiming for an acceptable/satisfactory level rather than the maximum; 1 mark: e.g. of profit, balancing other goals.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why survival might be the main objective of a new restaurant.
parts.answer: In its first year the restaurant has high start-up costs and few regular customers, so cash is tight; it must focus on covering costs and building a customer base to avoid closing, rather than making large profits.
parts.working: 1 mark (knowledge): new businesses face high failure risk; up to 2 marks (application/explanation): applied to a new restaurant (cash, customers, competition).

stem: Sunrise Paints (an invented company) set an objective of a 20 % share of the decorative paint market by 2025. In 2025 the total market was worth Rs 12.5 billion and Sunrise Paints' sales revenue was Rs 2.35 billion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Sunrise Paints' market share in 2025 and state whether it achieved its objective.
parts.answer: 18.8 %; the objective of 20 % was not achieved.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the term 'hierarchy of objectives'.
parts.answer: The way objectives are linked from the top of the organisation downwards: the mission leads to corporate objectives (e.g. 20 % market share), which lead to departmental objectives (e.g. marketing to open 300 new retailers) and individual targets.
parts.working: 1 mark (knowledge): objectives at different levels linked to each other; up to 2 marks (application/explanation): example from Sunrise Paints.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one reason why Sunrise Paints' departmental objectives must be consistent with its corporate objective.
parts.answer: If the production department aims to cut costs by reducing output while marketing aims to increase market share, the two will conflict: shops will run out of paint and the 20 % target will be missed.
parts.working: 1 mark (knowledge): coordination – all departments work towards same goal; up to 2 marks (application/explanation): applied to Sunrise Paints.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two objectives a social enterprise might have.
parts.answer: Any two of: a social objective (e.g. employing disadvantaged people); an environmental objective; making a surplus to reinvest; financial sustainability/covering costs; growth to help more people.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid objectives.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one way a business could communicate its objectives to its employees.
parts.answer: Through team meetings and the intranet at the start of each year, managers explain the corporate objective and each team's targets; staff understand how their work contributes, so they are more motivated and decisions are consistent.
parts.working: 1 mark (knowledge): valid method (meetings, intranet, appraisal/MBO, newsletters); up to 2 marks (application/explanation): explained with its effect.

stem: The Peshawar City Transit Authority (an invented organisation) is owned by the provincial government. It charges a flat fare of Rs 30 and receives a government subsidy of Rs 2 billion a year. Private bus companies in the city charge Rs 50–80.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse two reasons why the objectives of the Peshawar City Transit Authority are likely to differ from those of a private bus company.
parts.answer: Public service objective: the authority aims to provide affordable transport for all citizens, so it keeps fares low (Rs 30) even if this means losses, whereas a private company would set fares to make a profit. Wider social objectives: the authority aims to reduce traffic congestion and pollution and to serve poorer areas, so it runs routes that are not profitable; a private operator would cut these routes to raise profit.
parts.working: Indicative content: public vs private sector; social objectives; affordability; externalities (congestion, pollution); political influence; funded by subsidies vs profit motive. Marks: Knowledge 2, Application 2, Analysis 4. Analysis Level 2 (3–4): two developed chains of cause and effect applied to a public metro bus service; Level 1 (1–2): undeveloped or generic chains. Exactly two points are credited; no credit for evaluation.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse one benefit to a paint company of setting SMART objectives for its sales team.
parts.answer: A specific, measurable target such as 'increase sales to hardware shops in Punjab by 12 % by December' lets managers check progress monthly; salespeople know exactly what is expected, so they focus effort, and managers can take action early if targets are being missed, improving sales performance.
parts.working: Indicative content: clear focus; measurement and control; motivation; links to appraisal/MBO; coordination. Marks: Knowledge 1, Application 1, Analysis 3. Analysis Level 2 (2–3): a developed chain of cause and effect linked to a paint company's sales team; Level 1 (1): a simple statement of effect. Only one point is required; no credit for evaluation.

stem: Desi Dairy (an invented company) was owned by one family for 40 years. The family aimed for 'steady profits and fair treatment of our 2,000 supplying farmers'. It has been bought for Rs 8 bn by a multinational food company listed on the London Stock Exchange.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse two ways the takeover by a multinational may change Desi Dairy's objectives.
parts.answer: Profit and shareholder value: the multinational's shareholders expect a return on its Rs 8 bn purchase, so Desi Dairy may move from the family's satisficing objectives to profit targets, e.g. cutting less profitable products and raising prices. Growth and standardisation: the new owner may set objectives for national market share and exports, using its brands and global standards, while CSR objectives (e.g. paying farmers above market price) may change to fit group policy, possibly harming relations with farmers.
parts.working: Indicative content: from satisficing to profit maximisation/shareholder value; growth and market share targets; standardisation; CSR changes; short-term targets. Marks: Knowledge 2, Application 2, Analysis 4. Analysis Level 2 (3–4): two developed chains of cause and effect applied to a family dairy taken over by a multinational; Level 1 (1–2): undeveloped or generic chains. Exactly two points are credited; no credit for evaluation.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Nexus Retail (an invented company) had revenue of Rs 4 billion in 2025. Its corporate objective is to double revenue to Rs 8 billion by 2030 (in 5 years). Last year its revenue grew by 9 %.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the average annual growth rate in revenue that Nexus Retail needs to achieve its objective. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: 14.87 % per year.
parts.working: Required growth factor over 5 years = 8 ÷ 4 = 2 (M1); annual factor = 2^(1/5) (M1) = 1.1487 (M1); growth rate = 14.87 % (A1). Do not accept 20 % (simple division 100 % ÷ 5).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why Nexus Retail might not achieve this objective.
parts.answer: Its revenue grew by only 9 % last year; a recession or new competitors (e.g. online retailers) could reduce demand further, making 14.87 % a year unrealistic without acquisitions.
parts.working: 1 mark (knowledge): valid internal/external reason; up to 2 marks (application/explanation): applied to Nexus Retail and the data.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether growth should be the main objective of a family-owned chain of 12 pharmacies.
parts.answer: For growth: economies of scale in buying medicines; stronger position against national chains; more career opportunities for staff; long-term family wealth. Against: growth needs finance and management skills; the family may lose control or the personal service that customers value; risk of overtrading and cash-flow problems; regulation of pharmacies requires qualified pharmacists who are scarce. Alternative objectives: profitability, survival, customer service, ethical objectives. Judgement: moderate growth may be appropriate if the chain is threatened by larger rivals, but it should be balanced with profitability and quality; the right objective depends on the family's aims, finance and the competitive environment.
parts.working: Indicative content: benefits and risks of growth; alternative objectives; family control; competition; finance; changing objectives over time. Evaluation: a supported conclusion for the pharmacy chain. Marks: Knowledge 2, Application 2, Analysis 2, Evaluation 6. Evaluation Level 3 (5–6): judgements weighed throughout and a supported conclusion specific to the business; Level 2 (3–4): a judgement with some support in context; Level 1 (1–2): an unsupported or generic judgement.

stem: AquaClear (an invented company) sells bottled water in Pakistan. Its objectives are: (1) increase profit by 10 % a year; (2) by 2028, 40 % of bottles to be glass or recycled plastic; (3) provide free drinking water to 500 schools. The packaging objective will add Rs 350 million a year to costs. The government is discussing a tax on single-use plastic.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether AquaClear's CSR objectives conflict with its profit objective.
parts.answer: Conflict: plastic reduction (switching 40 % of bottles to glass and recycled plastic) raises costs by Rs 350 million a year; free water for schools gives away product. Complementary: CSR builds brand image and customer loyalty in a crowded bottled-water market; may avoid future plastic taxes; supermarkets favour sustainable suppliers; motivates staff. Judgement: in the short run the objectives conflict because costs rise; in the long run they are largely complementary if consumers reward the brand and regulation tightens; the degree of conflict depends on whether AquaClear can charge a small premium.
parts.working: Indicative content: costs of CSR; benefits to revenue and reputation; regulation; short vs long term; competitors. Evaluation: conditional judgement for AquaClear. Marks: Knowledge 2, Application 2, Analysis 2, Evaluation 6. Evaluation Level 3 (5–6): judgements weighed throughout and a supported conclusion specific to the business; Level 2 (3–4): a judgement with some support in context; Level 1 (1–2): an unsupported or generic judgement.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
QuickMart (an invented company) runs convenience stores in Pakistan.
Number of stores: 2022 – 60; 2025 – 140.
Market share: 2022 – 9 %; 2025 – 17 %.
Operating profit margin: 2022 – 8 %; 2025 – 2 %.
Gearing: 2022 – 35 %; 2025 – 62 %.
New stores take about 3 years to break even. Interest rates are 17 %. Two rival chains are opening stores rapidly.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether the board of QuickMart should change its main objective from growth to profitability.
parts.answer: Evidence for change: store numbers rose from 60 to 140 in three years, but operating profit margin fell from 8 % to 2 %; new stores take 3 years to break even; gearing has risen to 62 %, and interest rates are 17 %, so further debt-financed growth is risky. Evidence against: market share rose from 9 % to 17 %, giving buying power; rivals are expanding, so stopping growth could let them take prime locations. Judgement: shift the focus to profitability for the next 2 years – close or improve loss-making stores and reduce gearing – while allowing selective growth only where returns are proven; the change protects the business's survival given high gearing and interest rates.
parts.working: Indicative content: interpretation of data (margins, gearing, market share); risks of growth; benefits of consolidation; competitor response; time horizon. Evaluation: a reasoned decision using the data. Marks: Knowledge 2, Application 2, Analysis 2, Evaluation 6. Evaluation Level 3 (5–6): judgements weighed throughout and a supported conclusion specific to the business; Level 2 (3–4): a judgement with some support in context; Level 1 (1–2): an unsupported or generic judgement.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
LearnSmart (an invented company) is an online learning app for school students in Pakistan.
Timeline:
2020: Founded by two teachers; mission 'quality learning for every child'.
2022: Raises US$10 million from venture capital investors; offers most content free to attract users.
2024: Expands into Bangladesh and Egypt.
2025: Investors say no more funding will be provided unless the business shows a clear path to profit within 2 years.
Appendix 1: Registered users – 2021: 0.4 m; 2025: 3.2 m. Annual loss – 2021: Rs 0.2 bn; 2025: Rs 1.5 bn.
Appendix 2: Cash balance end of 2025 – Rs 1.75 bn.
Appendix 3: Paying subscribers – 4 % of users at Rs 6,000 per year. A rival app has 6 % paying subscribers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Advise the founders of LearnSmart on the objectives the business should set for the next three years.
parts.answer: Current position: users grew from 0.4 m to 3.2 m (Appendix 1) but losses rose to Rs 1.5 bn; cash covers about 14 months (Appendix 2); investors now demand a path to profit. Options: (1) continue user growth – maintains market leadership, but cash runs out; (2) switch to profitability – raise subscription conversion from 4 % to 8 % (Appendix 3), cut marketing; risks slowing growth and letting a rival catch up; (3) social objectives (free access for government schools) – supports mission and reputation, may attract grants, but costs money. Recommendation: set SMART objectives combining break-even within 24 months (conversion rate 8 %, cut marketing cost per user by 30 %), keep moderate growth in Pakistan only, and a limited social objective funded by partners; review every 6 months. Success depends on how price-sensitive parents are.
parts.working: Indicative content: growth, profit, survival and social objectives; data on users, losses, cash and conversion; investors' and other stakeholders' expectations; SMART objectives; risks. Evaluation: clear advice with priorities, measurable targets and conditions. Marks: Knowledge 3, Application 3, Analysis 6, Evaluation 8. Analysis needs three or four developed chains using the timeline and appendices. Evaluation Level 3 (6–8): a clear, justified decision that weighs the evidence and is specific to the business and the time period; Level 2 (3–5): a judgement with partial support; Level 1 (1–2): assertion only.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term 'buffer inventory'.
parts.answer: The minimum level of inventory a business plans to hold at all times to cover unexpected demand or late deliveries.
parts.working: 1 mark: inventory held as a safety reserve; 1 mark: to cover unexpected demand/delays in delivery (minimum level).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why a hospital pharmacy holds buffer inventory of insulin.
parts.answer: Insulin is needed urgently by patients and running out could endanger lives, so a buffer protects against late deliveries or sudden rises in demand.
parts.working: 1 mark: reason (cover late delivery / sudden rise in demand); 1 mark: application to insulin/hospital patients; 1 mark: development (cost of stock-out is very high – patient safety, reputation – so higher holding cost is justified).

stem: BuildRight Hardware sells bags of cement in Multan. Its inventory control data: maximum inventory 2,400 bags; buffer inventory 400 bags; average daily sales 150 bags; lead time 4 days. A delivery always brings inventory back up to the maximum level.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the re-order quantity.
parts.answer: 2,000 bags
parts.working: Max − buffer = 2,400 − 400 = 2,000 bags (B1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the re-order level.
parts.answer: 1,000 bags
parts.working: Buffer + (daily usage × lead time) = 400 + (150 × 4) M1 = 1,000 bags A1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate how many days, to the nearest day, each delivery lasts if sales stay at the average rate.
parts.answer: 13 days

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain one reason why BuildRight's actual inventory levels might not follow this pattern.
parts.answer: Demand for cement is seasonal/uneven (e.g. building slows in the monsoon), so daily usage varies and the re-order level is reached earlier or later than planned.
parts.working: 1 mark: reason (variable demand, late or early deliveries, supplier shortages); 1 mark: applied to cement/building trade; 1 mark: consequence (stock-out or excess inventory).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Speedy Spares distributes car spare parts to 300 garages in Peshawar. Garages expect parts to be delivered the same day they are ordered.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify one cost of holding too little inventory.
parts.answer: Lost sales / lost customers (stock-out costs).
parts.working: 1 mark for any valid cost: lost sales, loss of goodwill, cost of emergency orders, idle production.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the term 'stock-out'.
parts.answer: A stock-out is when a business has no inventory of an item when a customer wants it, so the order cannot be met.
parts.working: 1 mark: inventory runs out/zero; 1 mark: customer demand cannot be met; 1 mark: example or consequence (garage goes to a rival).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one reason why Speedy Spares might hold a high level of inventory even though this is expensive.
parts.answer: Garages need the part the same day; if Speedy Spares does not have it, the garage will order from a competitor and may switch permanently, so the lost sales and goodwill cost more than holding inventory.
parts.working: 1 mark: reason; 1 mark: applied to same-day delivery/garages; 1 mark: developed consequence.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Rainbow Paints holds an average of Rs 6.0 million of raw materials. Its annual holding cost (storage, insurance, damage and the opportunity cost of capital) is 22 % of the average value of inventory. With a just-in-time (JIT) system, average inventory would fall to Rs 1.5 million, but more frequent deliveries would add Rs 600,000 a year to transport costs.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the net annual saving to Rainbow Paints from introducing JIT.
parts.working: Reduction in average inventory = 6.0 − 1.5 = Rs 4.5m M1; holding cost saved = 4.5 × 0.22 = Rs 990,000 M1; net saving = 990,000 − 600,000 = Rs 390,000 A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one non-financial factor Rainbow Paints should consider before introducing JIT.
parts.answer: Reliability of suppliers: paint pigments may come from abroad, so a single late delivery could stop production because there is no buffer.
parts.working: 1 mark: factor (supplier reliability, quality of deliveries, relationship with suppliers, staff training); 1 mark: application; 1 mark: development.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: MediPlus runs 40 pharmacies across Karachi. Each branch orders its own medicines by telephone. Analyse two benefits to MediPlus of introducing a computerised inventory control system linked to all branches.
parts.answer: e.g. (1) automatic re-ordering when a medicine reaches its re-order level, so fewer stock-outs of essential medicines and higher customer loyalty; (2) real-time data allows stock to be moved between branches and slow-moving or near-expiry items identified, reducing waste and capital tied up in inventory.
parts.working: Content points (any two developed): automatic re-ordering and fewer stock-outs; accurate real-time inventory records; less waste of expired medicines; transfer of stock between branches; better data for bulk buying from suppliers (purchasing economies); less staff time spent counting and ordering. Level 2 (5–8): two points, each analysed with a developed chain of reasoning and applied to the context (top of band: both points fully developed and in context). Level 1 (1–4): knowledge of relevant points, with limited application or simple statements of effect. 0: no creditable content.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse one disadvantage for a fashion clothing retailer of holding large inventories.
parts.answer: Fashions change quickly, so large inventories risk becoming obsolete; unsold clothes must be heavily discounted, cutting profit margins, and the cash tied up cannot be used to buy new styles customers want.
parts.working: Knowledge/application 1–2, analysis 3–5. Content: risk of obsolescence as fashions change; markdowns reduce profit margin; capital tied up/opportunity cost; storage and insurance costs; less flexibility to stock new lines. Level 2 (3–5): developed chain of reasoning applied to the context. Level 1 (1–2): knowledge or a simple point with little context.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Karachi Grill is a chain of 12 restaurants. It buys about 4 tonnes of fresh chicken each week. Analyse two factors Karachi Grill should consider when choosing a supplier of fresh chicken.
parts.answer: e.g. (1) quality and food safety (cold chain, halal certification) – poor quality risks illness and brand damage; (2) reliability and delivery frequency – chicken is perishable, so daily reliable deliveries let the chain hold little inventory.
parts.working: Content points (any two developed): quality/food safety and hygiene standards; reliability and lead time; price and payment terms (credit period); flexibility to change order size; capacity to supply 4 tonnes a week; location (freshness, transport cost); ethical/animal welfare standards. Level 2 (5–8): two points, each analysed with a developed chain of reasoning and applied to the context (top of band: both points fully developed and in context). Level 1 (1–4): knowledge of relevant points, with limited application or simple statements of effect. 0: no creditable content.

stem: HomeNest sells flat-pack furniture online in Pakistan. It buys 20,000 chair frames a year from a supplier in Vietnam at Rs 2,000 each; lead time is 8 weeks and HomeNest holds an average inventory of 5,000 frames. A local supplier in Sialkot offers frames at Rs 2,300 each with a lead time of 1 week, so average inventory could fall to 1,200 frames. HomeNest's annual holding cost is 20 % of the value of average inventory. Customer reviews often mention 'out of stock' messages, and the Vietnamese supplier was late three times last year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the change in HomeNest's total annual cost (purchase cost plus holding cost) if it switches to the Sialkot supplier.
parts.answer: Total annual cost rises by Rs 4,552,000.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate whether HomeNest should switch to the Sialkot supplier.
parts.answer: Judgement depends on whether faster, more reliable supply wins enough extra sales to cover the Rs 4.552m higher cost.
parts.working: Arguments for/against: For: 1-week lead time gives flexibility and fewer stock-outs (reviews show lost sales); less capital tied up; lower risk of shipping delays and exchange-rate changes; 'made in Pakistan' may appeal. Against: annual cost rises by about Rs 4.55m; unknown quality/capacity of Sialkot supplier; Vietnamese supplier may lower price or improve reliability; could use both suppliers. Judgement: e.g. switch if extra contribution from avoided stock-outs exceeds Rs 4.55m a year, or trial a dual-sourcing arrangement first. Level 3 (9–12): a supported, contextual judgement that weighs the arguments (e.g. 'it depends on…'), built on developed analysis of both sides. Level 2 (5–8): developed analysis applied to the context, with at most a simple or unsupported judgement. Level 1 (1–4): knowledge and limited application; points listed, not developed. 0: no creditable content.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether effective supply chain management is the most important factor in the success of a large supermarket chain.
parts.answer: Supply chain management is vital (availability, freshness, low costs) but its importance relative to location, pricing, staff and brand depends on the chain's strategy.
parts.working: Arguments for/against: For: availability of products and freshness drive customer loyalty; bulk purchasing and logistics keep prices low in a low-margin business; reduced waste; data sharing with suppliers. Against: location and convenience, pricing strategy, customer service, online ordering and marketing also matter; a strong supply chain cannot rescue a poor store location or offer. Judgement: e.g. most important for a low-price, high-volume chain; less dominant for a premium chain competing on service. Level 3 (9–12): a supported, contextual judgement that weighs the arguments (e.g. 'it depends on…'), built on developed analysis of both sides. Level 2 (5–8): developed analysis applied to the context, with at most a simple or unsupported judgement. Level 1 (1–4): knowledge and limited application; points listed, not developed. 0: no creditable content.

stem:
Pak Spice Exports (PSE) packs ground spices and spice mixes in Lahore and sells them to supermarkets in the UK, Gulf states and Pakistan.
Timeline:
2021: PSE buys chillies, turmeric and cumin from about 200 small farmers through middlemen; quality varies.
2022: A UK customer rejects a Rs 40 million shipment because of high aflatoxin levels in chilli powder.
2023: PSE starts to buy directly from 60 farmer groups and trains them in drying and storage; it now holds 4 months of raw spices.
2025: A competitor launches a JIT system with one large supplier and cuts prices by 8 %.
Appendix 1: raw spice inventory Rs 180 million (2025); annual holding cost 18 % of inventory value; spice prices vary by up to 35 % between harvest and off-season.
Appendix 2: on-time delivery to customers 2023: 88 %; 2025: 95 %. Customer rejections: 2022: 6 shipments; 2025: 1 shipment.
Appendix 3: the directors are considering (A) moving to JIT purchasing from two large suppliers or (B) building a temperature- and humidity-controlled warehouse to hold harvest-season stock.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Advise the directors of PSE on their inventory and supply chain strategy for the next three years.
parts.answer: Likely recommendation: keep buying at harvest and invest in controlled storage (B), with closer direct links to farmer groups, because seasonal prices and food safety make JIT risky; reconsider JIT only for packaging materials.
parts.working: Points to use: Seasonal supply means JIT for raw spices is risky and would lose harvest-time price advantage (up to 35 %); holding cost Rs 32.4m a year (18 % × Rs 180m); food-safety rejections cost Rs 40m – direct sourcing and controlled storage reduce aflatoxin risk; improved on-time delivery (88 % → 95 %) shows current strategy is working; competitor price cut (8 %) puts pressure on costs; option B needs capital but protects quality; option A cuts holding cost but increases dependence on two suppliers; JIT may suit packaging/ non-seasonal items. Judgement: A clear recommendation with conditions (e.g. B plus supplier contracts; review if spice prices stabilise). Level 5 (17–20): developed, evidence-based evaluation throughout, using several pieces of case data, leading to a justified overall judgement/recommendation for this business. Level 4 (13–16): developed evaluation of several points, judgement supported but less complete. Level 3 (9–12): developed analysis using case data, with some evaluative comment. Level 2 (5–8): limited analysis with some application. Level 1 (1–4): knowledge only. 0: no creditable content.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term 'process innovation'.
parts.answer: Introducing a new or much improved method of producing a good or delivering a service.
parts.working: 1 mark: new/improved method or process; 1 mark: of production/delivery (not a new product).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one way process innovation could help a bank reduce its costs.
parts.answer: Introducing app-based account opening with digital identity checks reduces the staff time per new customer, so the bank needs fewer branch staff and its cost per account falls.
parts.working: 1 mark: example of process innovation; 1 mark: application to a bank; 1 mark: link to lower costs.

stem: Shaheen Bricks runs a brick kiln near Gujranwala. In 2024 it made 12 million bricks and burned 1,500 tonnes of coal. In 2025, after converting to a zigzag kiln, it made 14 million bricks and burned 1,260 tonnes of coal. Coal costs Rs 45,000 per tonne.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many tonnes of coal Shaheen Bricks saved in 2025 compared with making 14 million bricks at the 2024 rate of coal use.
parts.answer: 490 tonnes
parts.working: 2024 rate = 1,500 ÷ 12 = 125 tonnes per million bricks M1; 14 × 125 = 1,750 tonnes; saving = 1,750 − 1,260 = 490 tonnes A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the value of this saving.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one benefit to Shaheen Bricks, other than lower costs, of reducing its coal use.
parts.answer: Lower smoke emissions help it meet government air-pollution rules, so it is less likely to be closed during smog-season bans.
parts.working: 1 mark: benefit (meet regulations, avoid closure, better reputation, attract buyers wanting greener materials); 1 mark: application; 1 mark: development.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term 'operational flexibility'.
parts.answer: The ability of a business's operations to change the volume or variety of output quickly in response to changes in demand.
parts.working: 1 mark: ability to change/adapt operations; 1 mark: volume and/or product mix in response to demand.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why a small restaurant might find it difficult to make its operations more environmentally sustainable.
parts.answer: Solar panels, energy-efficient kitchens or biodegradable packaging cost more, and a small restaurant has limited finance and thin profit margins, so it may not be able to afford them.
parts.working: 1 mark: reason (cost, lack of finance, limited expertise, customers unwilling to pay more); 1 mark: application; 1 mark: development.

parts.label: a
parts.text: TrendLine is a fast-fashion retailer with 60 stores. It orders most of its clothes six months ahead from factories in Bangladesh. Analyse two ways TrendLine could make its operations more flexible.
parts.answer: e.g. (1) use local suppliers with short lead times for part of its range, so it can reorder best-sellers within weeks; (2) multi-skilled workforce/flexible staff contracts so stores and warehouses can respond to busy periods.
parts.working: Content points (any two developed): nearer/local suppliers and shorter lead times; smaller, more frequent orders; flexible contracts/temporary staff; multi-skilling; flexible machinery at suppliers; outsourcing peaks; better demand data (ERP/sales data) to adjust orders. Level 2 (5–8): two points, each analysed with a developed chain of reasoning and applied to the context (top of band: both points fully developed and in context). Level 1 (1–4): knowledge of relevant points, with limited application or simple statements of effect. 0: no creditable content.

parts.label: a
parts.text: RideGo rents cars to tourists in Islamabad and the northern areas. It is considering replacing its petrol fleet with electric cars. Analyse two ways this change could affect RideGo's operations.
parts.answer: e.g. (1) charging time and limited range in mountain areas require new route planning and charging points, which may reduce how many hires each car can make; (2) lower fuel and maintenance costs per km reduce unit costs and support a 'green tourism' image.
parts.working: Content points (any two developed): charging infrastructure and range limits; lower running/maintenance costs; high capital cost; staff training; changes to scheduling and capacity; environmental image; dependence on electricity supply/load-shedding. Level 2 (5–8): two points, each analysed with a developed chain of reasoning and applied to the context (top of band: both points fully developed and in context). Level 1 (1–4): knowledge of relevant points, with limited application or simple statements of effect. 0: no creditable content.

stem: StrideFit makes sports shoes. It now offers 'mass customised' shoes: customers choose colours and add their name on the company website. Customised shoes sell for Rs 18,000 a pair with variable costs of Rs 11,500; standard shoes sell for Rs 9,000 with variable costs of Rs 5,400. Last month StrideFit sold 600 customised pairs and 4,000 standard pairs.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the term 'mass customisation'.
parts.answer: Producing goods in large volumes using flexible (often computer-controlled) systems while allowing each item to be tailored to the individual customer.
parts.working: 1 mark: large-scale/efficient production; 1 mark: products tailored to individual customers; 1 mark: example/use of flexible technology.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total contribution from each type of shoe last month.
parts.answer: Customised Rs 3,900,000; standard Rs 14,400,000

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one operational problem StrideFit may face in offering customised shoes.
parts.answer: Each order is different, so production lines must change settings often; this slows output and raises the risk of errors (wrong name/colour), increasing lead times.
parts.working: 1 mark: problem (complexity, changeovers, errors, longer lead time, more inventory of colours); 1 mark: application; 1 mark: development.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Cocoa Crown makes premium hand-finished chocolates sold in gift boxes for weddings and Eid. Analyse how Cocoa Crown's operations strategy should support its marketing strategy.
parts.answer: e.g. (1) a premium price needs consistently high quality – so operations should focus on quality assurance and skilled staff rather than lowest cost; (2) demand peaks at Eid and wedding season, so operations need flexibility (temporary staff, batch planning) to meet these peaks without loss of quality.
parts.working: Content points (any two developed): quality focus supporting premium positioning/brand; flexibility for seasonal peaks; customised packaging/personalisation; small batch production; reliable delivery for events; costs controlled but not at the expense of quality; sustainable sourcing of cocoa supporting brand image. Level 2 (5–8): two points, each analysed with a developed chain of reasoning and applied to the context (top of band: both points fully developed and in context). Level 1 (1–4): knowledge of relevant points, with limited application or simple statements of effect. 0: no creditable content.

stem: Northern Cement Ltd makes 2 million tonnes of cement a year. Electricity is its second-largest cost. The directors are considering a waste-heat recovery plant that would cost Rs 2,700 million.
