It would generate 30 million kWh (units) of electricity a year, which currently costs Rs 28 per kWh from the grid. Annual maintenance would be Rs 90 million. The company's banks have started to offer lower interest rates on 'green' loans, and a large export customer has asked all its suppliers to cut carbon emissions by 30 % by 2030.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the annual net saving and the payback period of the waste-heat recovery plant. Give the payback period in years and months.
parts.answer: Net saving Rs 750 million a year; payback 3 years 7.2 months (about 3 years 7 months).
parts.working: Gross saving = 30m × Rs 28 = Rs 840m M1; net = 840 − 90 = Rs 750m A1; payback = 2,700 ÷ 750 = 3.6 years M1 = 3 years 7.2 months A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate whether Northern Cement Ltd should invest in the waste-heat recovery plant.
parts.answer: Likely yes: 3.6-year payback, protection from rising electricity prices and meeting customer carbon targets, provided finance (green loan) is available and output stays high.
parts.working: Arguments for/against: For: payback 3.6 years on a long-life asset; reduces exposure to grid tariff rises and load-shedding; helps meet export customer's 30 % carbon target (keeps sales); cheaper green finance; reputation. Against: large capital cost and opportunity cost; saving depends on kiln running at high capacity (lower output → less waste heat); maintenance/technical risk; tariff may fall; payback ignores time value of money. Judgement: e.g. invest, using a green loan, if forecast output is stable; the customer requirement makes it strategic, not just a cost decision. Level 3 (9–12): a supported, contextual judgement that weighs the arguments (e.g. 'it depends on…'), built on developed analysis of both sides. Level 2 (5–8): developed analysis applied to the context, with at most a simple or unsupported judgement. Level 1 (1–4): knowledge and limited application; points listed, not developed. 0: no creditable content.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Raahi Motors (an invented company) makes electric motorbikes in Karachi.
Timeline:
2021: Starts by assembling 3,000 bikes a year from imported Chinese kits; job-shop style assembly by 40 workers.
2022: Sets up a flow-production line; output 12,000 bikes. Battery packs still imported.
2023: Opens battery-swap stations in 25 petrol pumps so riders do not wait to charge.
2024: Begins making battery packs locally with a Korean partner; government reduces sales tax on electric bikes.
2025: Introduces a battery recycling scheme; output 30,000 bikes; a rival imports cheaper bikes.
Appendix 1: average cost per bike: 2021 Rs 310,000; 2023 Rs 245,000; 2025 Rs 228,000. Selling price 2025: Rs 265,000; rival's price Rs 239,000.
Appendix 2: warranty claims per 1,000 bikes: 2022: 64; 2025: 21. Battery-swap stations: 25 (2023), 140 (2025).
Appendix 3: capacity utilisation 2025: 75 %. Share of components made in Pakistan: 2021: 10 %; 2025: 55 %.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the success of Raahi Motors' operations strategy between 2021 and 2025.
parts.answer: Largely successful: costs fell 26 %, quality improved and the swap network adds value, but price still above rival and 75 % capacity utilisation leave room to improve.
parts.working: Points to use: Move to flow production → economies of scale, unit cost from Rs 310,000 to Rs 228,000 (−26 %); quality: warranty claims down from 64 to 21 per 1,000; battery-swap network as an operations-led USP; localisation to 55 % reduces import and exchange-rate risk and benefits from tax cut; recycling scheme supports sustainability; but price Rs 26,000 above rival, margin only Rs 37,000 per bike; 75 % capacity utilisation raises unit fixed costs; dependence on Korean partner; external factors (tax cut) also helped. Judgement: Overall judgement about success, weighing cost/quality evidence against competitive price gap, and which elements mattered most. Level 5 (17–20): developed, evidence-based evaluation throughout, using several pieces of case data, leading to a justified overall judgement/recommendation for this business. Level 4 (13–16): developed evaluation of several points, judgement supported but less complete. Level 3 (9–12): developed analysis using case data, with some evaluative comment. Level 2 (5–8): limited analysis with some application. Level 1 (1–4): knowledge only. 0: no creditable content.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether making operations more environmentally sustainable will always increase costs for a fast-food restaurant chain.
parts.answer: Not always: some changes (energy efficiency, waste reduction) cut costs over time, while others (sustainable packaging, ethical sourcing) raise costs; the result depends on time-scale and the change chosen.
parts.working: Arguments for/against: Increase costs: biodegradable packaging, certified ingredients, new equipment, staff training, monitoring. Reduce costs: LED lighting and efficient fryers lower energy bills; less food waste; reusing oil; government incentives; customers may pay more or visit more often (revenue), avoiding fines. Judgement: e.g. short-run costs rise, but long-run costs may fall; depends on scale of chain (bulk buying of green packaging) and on customer attitudes. Level 3 (9–12): a supported, contextual judgement that weighs the arguments (e.g. 'it depends on…'), built on developed analysis of both sides. Level 2 (5–8): developed analysis applied to the context, with at most a simple or unsupported judgement. Level 1 (1–4): knowledge and limited application; points listed, not developed. 0: no creditable content.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify one method of lean production.
parts.answer: e.g. kaizen (continuous improvement), JIT, cell production, kanban, simultaneous engineering.
parts.working: 1 mark for any valid lean method.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the term 'benchmarking'.
parts.answer: Comparing a business's processes or performance with those of the best-performing businesses in the industry, in order to find and copy better practices.
parts.working: 1 mark: comparing performance/processes; 1 mark: with the best/leading firms; 1 mark: purpose – to identify improvements/set targets.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one reason why a garment factory might use quality control by inspection rather than quality assurance.
parts.answer: Inspection is simple and cheap to start: inspectors check finished garments for faults before shipping, so a small factory with an untrained workforce can still stop faulty goods reaching the buyer.
parts.working: 1 mark: reason; 1 mark: application to garments; 1 mark: development.

stem: Moonlight Garments makes 25,000 shirts a month. Faults are found in 4 % of shirts and each faulty shirt costs Rs 350 to repair (rework). The production manager says that a quality assurance system would cut the fault rate to 1.5 %.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the monthly cost of rework at the current fault rate.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the monthly saving in rework costs if the fault rate falls to 1.5 %.
parts.working: New faulty = 375 shirts; cost Rs 131,250 M1; saving = 350,000 − 131,250 = Rs 218,750 A1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one benefit to Moonlight Garments of a lower fault rate, other than lower rework costs.
parts.answer: Fewer faulty shirts reach buyers, so fewer orders are rejected by export customers and Moonlight's reputation for quality improves, helping it win repeat orders.
parts.working: 1 mark: benefit (reputation, fewer returns, more output from same resources, motivation); 1 mark: application; 1 mark: development.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term 'quality circle'.
parts.answer: A small group of workers from the same area who meet regularly to identify and solve quality problems.
parts.working: 1 mark: small group of employees meeting regularly; 1 mark: to discuss/solve quality or work problems.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one benefit of quality circles for a call centre.
parts.answer: Call agents know the common customer complaints, so their suggestions can shorten call scripts or fix recurring problems, improving customer satisfaction; being involved also motivates them.
parts.working: 1 mark: benefit; 1 mark: application to a call centre; 1 mark: development.

stem: Velo Cycles assembles bicycles on a long production line where each worker repeats one task, such as fitting brakes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the term 'cell production'.
parts.answer: Production is organised into small teams (cells), each responsible for making a complete product or a complete part of the process, rather than one long line of single tasks.
parts.working: 1 mark: teams/cells; 1 mark: each cell makes a whole unit/major stage; 1 mark: team responsible for quality/output.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one benefit to Velo Cycles of changing to cell production.
parts.answer: Workers in a cell do several tasks and see a whole bicycle built, so they are more motivated and take responsibility for quality, reducing faults.
parts.working: 1 mark: benefit (motivation, quality, flexibility, multi-skilling); 1 mark: application; 1 mark: development.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Shifa Care is a private hospital in Rawalpindi. Its patient-satisfaction scores have fallen for two years. Analyse two benefits to Shifa Care of benchmarking against leading hospitals.
parts.answer: e.g. (1) comparing waiting times and procedures with the best hospitals shows exactly where Shifa Care is weak and gives realistic targets; (2) learning from proven practices (patient booking systems, hygiene routines) is faster and cheaper than developing its own.
parts.working: Content points (any two developed): identifies gaps in performance; sets realistic targets; learns proven best practice; quicker/cheaper improvement; improves competitiveness and reputation; motivates staff with clear standards. Level 2 (5–8): two points, each analysed with a developed chain of reasoning and applied to the context (top of band: both points fully developed and in context). Level 1 (1–4): knowledge of relevant points, with limited application or simple statements of effect. 0: no creditable content.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse one disadvantage for a food-canning factory of relying on inspection of finished cans to control quality.
parts.answer: Faults are found only at the end, after ingredients, energy and labour have been used, so faulty batches are wasted; and inspection checks only a sample, so contaminated cans might still reach customers, risking recalls and damage to the brand.
parts.working: Knowledge/application 1–2, analysis 3–5. Content: waste of resources as faults are found late; cost of inspectors; sample checks may miss faults – health risk and recall; workers do not take responsibility for quality. Level 2 (3–5): developed chain of reasoning applied to the context. Level 1 (1–2): knowledge or a simple point with little context.

stem: Zest Bottlers changes its filling line between flavours 6 times a day. Each changeover takes 45 minutes. Using lean techniques, it has cut each changeover to 15 minutes. When running, the line fills 80 crates an hour. Each crate earns a contribution of Rs 120. The factory works 300 days a year and can sell all extra output.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the extra annual contribution from the faster changeovers.
parts.working: Time saved per day = 6 × 30 = 180 min = 3 hours M1; extra crates per day = 3 × 80 = 240 A1; per year = 240 × 300 = 72,000 crates M1; × Rs 120 = Rs 8,640,000 A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why the extra contribution may be lower than calculated.
parts.answer: The calculation assumes all extra crates can be sold at the same contribution; if Zest must cut prices or demand is seasonal, the extra output may not be sold, and workers may not achieve 15-minute changeovers every time.
parts.working: 1 mark: reason (demand may not exist, price cuts, changeovers not always achieved, breakdowns, extra variable costs); 1 mark: application; 2 marks: developed explanation of the effect on contribution.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: SkyMeals prepares 18,000 in-flight meals a day for airlines at Lahore airport. The managers plan to introduce total quality management (TQM). Analyse two problems SkyMeals might face when introducing TQM.
parts.answer: e.g. (1) TQM needs every worker to accept responsibility for quality; staff used to supervisors' checks may resist, so training and culture change take time and money; (2) the costs of training and new procedures come before the benefits, reducing short-term profit, and airline contracts may still demand inspection.
parts.working: Content points (any two developed): cultural change/resistance from staff and supervisors; training costs and time; need for management commitment; benefits slow to appear; bureaucracy/paperwork; difficulty in measuring quality across shifts. Level 2 (5–8): two points, each analysed with a developed chain of reasoning and applied to the context (top of band: both points fully developed and in context). Level 1 (1–4): knowledge of relevant points, with limited application or simple statements of effect. 0: no creditable content.

stem: FixFast repairs mobile phones in 30 shops. It does 18,000 repairs a year. 6 % of repaired phones are returned because the fault comes back; each return costs FixFast Rs 2,500 (staff time, parts and a free accessory to apologise). A rival chain has a return rate of 2 %. FixFast's manager wants to introduce kaizen groups in every shop; most technicians are paid per repair and staff turnover is 40 % a year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate FixFast's annual cost of returns now and the annual saving if it reduces its return rate to 2 %.
parts.answer: Cost now Rs 2,700,000; saving Rs 1,800,000

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate whether kaizen is the best way for FixFast to improve the quality of its repairs.
parts.answer: Kaizen can help, but high staff turnover and piece-rate pay undermine it; better training, quality checks and pay that rewards quality may be needed first.
parts.working: Arguments for/against: For kaizen: technicians closest to problems suggest improvements; low cost; continuous small gains; motivation through involvement; potential saving of Rs 1.8m. Against/alternatives: 40 % turnover means knowledge is lost; per-repair pay encourages speed over quality; may need training, testing every phone before return, better parts suppliers, benchmarking against rival (2 %). Judgement: e.g. kaizen works only alongside changes to pay and training; best combined approach. Level 3 (9–12): a supported, contextual judgement that weighs the arguments (e.g. 'it depends on…'), built on developed analysis of both sides. Level 2 (5–8): developed analysis applied to the context, with at most a simple or unsupported judgement. Level 1 (1–4): knowledge and limited application; points listed, not developed. 0: no creditable content.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Green Valley Dairy (GVD) collects milk from 5,000 farmers in central Punjab and sells packaged milk, yoghurt and butter.
Timeline:
2022: Quality checks only at the factory gate; 7 % of milk rejected for adulteration or high bacteria.
2023: Food authority closes two competitors for selling adulterated milk; consumer trust in packaged milk falls.
2024: GVD installs chilling centres in 40 villages; testing done at collection.
2025: A large hotel chain asks GVD to gain an international food-safety certification within two years.
Appendix 1: rejected milk 2022: 7 %; 2025: 3.5 %. Cost of quality testing per year: 2022 Rs 15 million; 2025 Rs 42 million.
Appendix 2: customer complaints per million packs: 2022: 48; 2025: 19. Best competitor: 8.
Appendix 3: options: (A) introduce TQM with training for all 900 staff and farmer groups, cost Rs 60 million over two years; (B) gain the certification by adding more laboratory testing, cost Rs 25 million a year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Advise GVD's directors on the best quality strategy for the next three years.
parts.answer: Probably A (TQM, building quality in at farm and factory) combined with the certification, because the hotel contract and low consumer trust make quality a competitive advantage, but justify against cost.
parts.working: Points to use: Rejections halved and complaints down 60 % since chilling centres – quality assurance at source works; still worse than best competitor (19 vs 8); testing costs nearly tripled; option B is inspection-based – recurring cost and does not prevent faults; option A changes culture, involves farmers, long-term savings, supports certification; risks of A: time, resistance, 5,000 farmers hard to train; hotel contract requires certification within two years; consumer trust after competitor closures gives opportunity to differentiate. Judgement: A justified recommendation, e.g. A with targeted testing to secure certification on time. Level 5 (17–20): developed, evidence-based evaluation throughout, using several pieces of case data, leading to a justified overall judgement/recommendation for this business. Level 4 (13–16): developed evaluation of several points, judgement supported but less complete. Level 3 (9–12): developed analysis using case data, with some evaluative comment. Level 2 (5–8): limited analysis with some application. Level 1 (1–4): knowledge only. 0: no creditable content.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether lean production is suitable for a business with highly seasonal demand, such as a manufacturer of school uniforms.
parts.answer: Partly: lean techniques such as kaizen and waste reduction suit any business, but JIT and minimal inventory are risky when almost all demand comes in a few weeks before the school year.
parts.working: Arguments for/against: For: reduced waste and costs; kaizen and cell production improve quality and productivity all year; flexible workforce matches output to demand. Against: production must build inventory before the peak (JIT cannot meet a sudden surge with limited capacity); suppliers also face peaks; temporary workers may not support kaizen culture. Judgement: e.g. adopt selected lean methods (quality, waste reduction) but keep planned seasonal inventory; depends on lead times and capacity. Level 3 (9–12): a supported, contextual judgement that weighs the arguments (e.g. 'it depends on…'), built on developed analysis of both sides. Level 2 (5–8): developed analysis applied to the context, with at most a simple or unsupported judgement. Level 1 (1–4): knowledge and limited application; points listed, not developed. 0: no creditable content.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term 'labour-intensive production'.
parts.answer: Production that uses a high proportion of labour compared with capital (machinery) to make a product.
parts.working: 1 mark: high proportion/ratio of labour; 1 mark: relative to capital/machinery.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one disadvantage of flow production for a car manufacturer.
parts.answer: Flow production lines are very expensive to set up and inflexible, so changing to a new model or a smaller volume is costly; a fault at one stage can stop the whole line.
parts.working: 1 mark: disadvantage; 1 mark: application to cars; 1 mark: development.

stem: ColourCraft makes paint in batches. Its mixing plant works 16 hours a day. It makes 2 colour changes a day, and each change (cleaning tanks and pipes) takes 3 hours.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify one example of a business that would use batch production.
parts.answer: e.g. a bakery making different types of bread, a paint maker, a clothing factory.
parts.working: 1 mark: any valid example.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the working day ColourCraft loses to colour changes.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one way ColourCraft could reduce the time lost to colour changes.
parts.answer: Plan the order of batches from light to dark colours so tanks need less cleaning between batches, and make larger batches so fewer changes are needed.
parts.working: 1 mark: method (scheduling, larger batches, dedicated tanks for popular colours, quick-changeover techniques); 1 mark: application; 1 mark: development.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Timber Tales is a workshop of six carpenters in Chiniot that makes carved beds and dining tables to each customer's own design.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the term 'capital-intensive production'.
parts.answer: Production in which machinery and equipment make up a high proportion of the inputs compared with labour, e.g. automated lines.
parts.working: 1 mark: high proportion of capital/machines; 1 mark: relative to labour; 1 mark: example or consequence (high fixed costs, low variable costs).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why Timber Tales uses job production.
parts.answer: Each customer wants a unique carved design, so every item must be made individually to the specification; job production allows this and the business can charge a premium price for craftsmanship.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse one advantage of batch production for a bakery that makes six kinds of bread.
parts.answer: Batch production lets the bakery use the same ovens and staff for several bread types in turn, so it can offer variety to shops without buying a separate line for each type, keeping fixed costs per loaf low.

stem: Saba Soaps is deciding how to wrap bars of soap. Manual wrapping: fixed costs Rs 1,200,000 a month; variable cost Rs 300 per carton. Robotic wrapping: fixed costs Rs 4,500,000 a month; variable cost Rs 150 per carton. Output varies between 15,000 and 30,000 cartons a month.

parts.text: Calculate the monthly output at which both methods have the same total cost.
parts.answer: 22,000 cartons

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why Saba Soaps might choose manual wrapping even if average output is above this level.
parts.answer: Output sometimes falls to 15,000 cartons, when the robot's high fixed costs make it more expensive; manual wrapping is more flexible and avoids a large capital outlay and the risk of breakdowns.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Juicy Delight makes 15 flavours of fruit juice in batches. Its sales of mango and orange juice have tripled. Analyse two factors Juicy Delight should consider before using flow production for these two flavours.

stem: Prime Uniforms makes white school shirts. Using batch production it made 40,000 shirts a month at a total cost of Rs 18 million. After moving to flow production it makes 60,000 shirts a month at a total cost of Rs 22.80 million.

parts.text: Calculate the percentage change in the average cost per shirt. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.text: Explain one risk to Prime Uniforms of having moved to flow production.

stem: SmileWorks Dental Lab makes crowns and bridges by hand for 150 dental clinics. It employs 10 skilled technicians. A CAD/CAM milling system costs Rs 24 million. It would replace 4 technicians, each costing Rs 1,800,000 a year, and reduce wasted materials by Rs 2,400,000 a year, but would cost Rs 1,000,000 a year to maintain. Crowns would be ready in 2 days instead of 6. Some dentists say hand-finished crowns look more natural. The lab has Rs 10 million in cash.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the annual net saving and the payback period of the CAD/CAM system (in years, to 2 decimal places).
parts.answer: Net saving Rs 8,600,000; payback 2.79 years
parts.working: Labour saving = 4 × 1.8m = Rs 7.2m M1; total savings 7.2 + 2.4 = 9.6m; less maintenance 1.0m = Rs 8.60m A1; payback = 24 ÷ 8.6 M1 = 2.79 years A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate whether SmileWorks Dental Lab should invest in the CAD/CAM system.
parts.answer: Likely yes if finance is available and quality is accepted: payback under 3 years and faster delivery are strong, but the reaction of dentists and staff and the Rs 14m funding gap need care.
parts.working: Arguments for/against: For: payback 2.79 years; faster delivery (2 vs 6 days) is a competitive advantage; consistent accuracy; less waste; ability to grow. Against: Rs 24m vs Rs 10m cash – needs a loan/lease; some dentists prefer hand-finished look (could keep hand finishing); redundancy affects morale; technology risk and training; savings estimates may be optimistic. Judgement: e.g. invest (perhaps by leasing) and keep skilled technicians for finishing premium crowns. Level 3 (9–12): a supported, contextual judgement that weighs the arguments (e.g. 'it depends on…'), built on developed analysis of both sides. Level 2 (5–8): developed analysis applied to the context, with at most a simple or unsupported judgement. parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether flow production is always the most efficient production method for a bicycle manufacturer.
parts.answer: Flow production gives the lowest unit cost for high, stable volumes of standard bicycles, but batch or cell production can be more efficient for varied models or lower volumes.

stem:
Indus Spinning Mills (ISM) spins cotton yarn in Faisalabad and sells it to weavers in Pakistan and China.
Timeline:
2020: 1,100 workers; 60 % of machines over 25 years old; output 18,000 tonnes.
2021: Buys automatic winding machines and starts replacing old ring frames.
2022: 350 workers made redundant; strike for 10 days; union agrees a deal including retraining.
2023: Installs software that monitors every spindle; maintenance becomes predictive.
2024: Electricity prices rise 45 %; output 24,000 tonnes.
2025: Exports to China fall 20 % because of competition from Vietnamese mills.
Appendix 1: yarn faults per tonne: 2020: 12; 2025: 4. Labour productivity (tonnes per worker): 2020: 16.4; 2025: 32.0.
Appendix 2: cost per kg of yarn 2020: Rs 610; 2025: Rs 690 (energy is now 38 % of cost, was 24 %). Capital spending 2021–2024: Rs 4.2 billion, financed mostly by loans; gearing 2025: 62 %.
Appendix 3: staff survey 2025: 58 % satisfied (2021: 41 %).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the effectiveness of ISM's automation strategy between 2020 and 2025.
parts.answer: Partly effective: productivity doubled and quality improved, but unit costs still rose because of energy prices, debt is high and export sales fell; overall judgement depends on whether the mill would have been worse without automation.
parts.working: Points to use: Productivity 16.4 → 32.0 t/worker (+95 %); faults down from 12 to 4 per tonne; output +33 %; predictive maintenance; but cost per kg up 13 % mainly due to 45 % electricity rise; automation increases energy dependency; gearing 62 % from loan-financed Rs 4.2bn – interest risk; redundancies and strike harmed relations but satisfaction now improved (41 % → 58 %); exports to China down 20 % – automation did not create a cost advantage over Vietnam; external factors vs strategy. Judgement: Supported overall judgement, e.g. effective in operations terms but not yet in financial/competitive terms. Level 5 (17–20): developed, evidence-based evaluation throughout, using several pieces of case data, leading to a justified overall judgement/recommendation for this business. Level 4 (13–16): developed evaluation of several points, judgement supported but less complete. Level 3 (9–12): developed analysis using case data, with some evaluative comment. parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the term 'economies of scale'.
parts.answer: The reductions in average (unit) cost that a business gains as it increases its scale of operation.
parts.working: 1 mark: fall in average/unit cost; 1 mark: as scale/output increases; 1 mark: example or type (purchasing, technical, financial, managerial).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one technical economy of scale a large cement company might gain.
parts.answer: A large kiln costs less than twice as much as a kiln of half the size but produces twice the output, so the capital cost per tonne of cement is lower.
parts.working: 1 mark: technical economy (larger/more efficient machinery, specialised equipment, law of increased dimensions); 1 mark: application; 1 mark: effect on unit cost.

stem: Fresh Farm Foods plans a distribution warehouse for 120,000 cartons a year. Site A is in a rural area: annual rent Rs 8 million; transport cost to customers Rs 90 per carton. Site B is on the edge of Lahore: annual rent Rs 13 million; transport cost Rs 40 per carton.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total annual cost of rent and transport at each site and state which site is cheaper.
parts.answer: Site A Rs 18,800,000; Site B Rs 17,800,000; Site B is cheaper by Rs 1,000,000.

parts.text: Define the term 'reshoring'.
parts.answer: Moving production or services back to the business's home country after they had been located abroad.

parts.label: b

stem: AquaPure bottles mineral water. Its old plant made 200,000 cases a year at a total cost of Rs 30 million. Its new, larger plant makes 500,000 cases a year at a total cost of Rs 60 million.

parts.answer: Old Rs 150; new Rs 120; fall 20 %

stem:
Lakeview Hotels is choosing a site for a new hotel. It uses weighted scoring (scores out of 10).
Factor (weight): access to tourists (0.35); land and building cost (0.25); availability of staff (0.2); local infrastructure (0.2).
Site A Murree: 7, 8, 5, 6. Site B Naran: 9, 5, 6, 7. Site C Skardu: 6, 7, 9, score for infrastructure not yet decided.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the weighted score for Site A and Site B.
parts.answer: Site A 6.65; Site B 7.00

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the lowest infrastructure score Site C would need to have the highest weighted score. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: Site C needs an infrastructure score above 6.75 to beat Site B (7.00), so the lowest score to 1 decimal place is 6.8 (a whole-number score of 7 would also work).
parts.working: C without infrastructure = 0.35×6 + 0.25×7 + 0.2×9 = 5.65 M1; needs > 7.00 so 0.2x > 1.35 M1; x > 6.75, i.e. a score of at least 6.8 A1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one reason why Lakeview Hotels should not rely only on this method.
parts.answer: The weights and scores are subjective – a manager who prefers one site can choose numbers that favour it – and the method leaves out costs and risks such as road closures in winter.
parts.working: 1 mark: limitation (subjective weights/scores, excludes some factors, ignores financial data, false precision); 1 mark: application; 1 mark: development.

stem: ShopNow is an online retailer delivering 1,500,000 parcels a year across Pakistan. Option 1: one national warehouse in Lahore, fixed costs Rs 60 million a year; average delivery cost Rs 85 per parcel; average delivery time 3 days. Option 2: three regional warehouses (Karachi, Lahore, Islamabad), fixed costs Rs 26 million a year each; average delivery cost Rs 52 per parcel; average delivery time 1.5 days. parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total annual cost of each option.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate whether ShopNow should use three regional warehouses instead of one national warehouse.

stem:
Sunrise Juices (an invented company) makes fruit juices in Multan and exports 40 % of output to the Gulf states.
Timeline:
2021: One factory, capacity 50 million litres; utilisation 70 %.

Appendix 3: exchange rate PKR per AED: 2021: 43; 2025: 76.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Advise the directors of Sunrise Juices on where to locate their new factory.
parts.answer: Either can be justified; a strong answer weighs cost advantages of Multan (labour, fruit, weak rupee aiding exports) against UAE's speed and contract requirement, and makes a conditional recommendation.
parts.working: Points to use: Capacity pressure (96 %) – expansion needed; contract requires 10-day delivery – Multan (12–18 days) fails unless logistics improve; UAE plant meets delivery and avoids rising shipping of finished goods but concentrate still shipped; UAE costs Rs 1.3bn more, higher wages, tax holiday; weak rupee makes Pakistan-made exports cheaper (AED 43 → 76) but makes UAE investment costlier in rupees; risk of single contract; Multan option adds more capacity (30m vs 20m) and serves domestic growth; intangible factors – control, management at distance. parts.text: Evaluate whether the benefits of economies of scale always outweigh the diseconomies of scale for a fast-growing airline.

stem: Daily Bread bakery employed 12 bakers who made 9,600 loaves a day. After buying a larger oven it employs 10 bakers who make 10,500 loaves a day.

parts.answer: Before 800 loaves per baker; after 1,050; increase 31.25 %

parts.text: Explain one reason why higher labour productivity may not lead to higher profit for Daily Bread.

stem: Grand Palace Hotel in Islamabad has 180 rooms, two restaurants and a conference hall.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify one input used in Grand Palace Hotel's transformation process.
parts.answer: e.g. staff (labour), food ingredients, electricity, the building, management skill.
parts.working: 1 mark for any valid input.

parts.text: Explain the term 'transformation process'.
parts.answer: The process by which a business converts inputs (land, labour, capital, enterprise, materials) into outputs of goods or services that are worth more to customers.

stem: Royal Tailors makes men's suits. Each suit sells for Rs 32,000. Cloth, lining and buttons for each suit cost Rs 14,000. The owner wants to increase added value to Rs 20,000 per suit.

parts.answer: Rs 34,000; increase 6.25 %

stem: ConnectPlus runs a customer-service call centre for a mobile network. In week 1, 40 agents handled 14,400 calls in a 6-day week. After new software was introduced, 36 agents handled 15,120 calls in a 6-day week. Customer complaints about 'problem not solved' rose by 15 %.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of calls per agent per day before and after the change, and the percentage change. Give the percentage to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: Before 60; after 70; increase 16.7 %

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the difference between efficiency and effectiveness, using ConnectPlus as an example.
parts.answer: Efficiency is producing output with the fewest resources (more calls per agent); effectiveness is meeting the objective (solving customers' problems). ConnectPlus is more efficient but less effective, because more problems are left unsolved.

stem: Comfort Shoes makes sandals in Sialkot. Last year it paid 50 workers Rs 60,000 a month each and made 25,000 pairs a month. After raising pay to Rs 70,000 a month and introducing a team bonus, it now has 46 workers who make 28,000 pairs a month. Absenteeism fell from 9 % to 4 %. The owner wonders whether to raise pay again.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate labour productivity and the labour cost per pair before and after the change. Give answers to 2 decimal places where necessary.
parts.answer: Productivity 500 → 608.70 pairs per worker per month; labour cost per pair Rs 120.00 → Rs 115.00

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate whether paying higher wages is the best way for Comfort Shoes to improve its efficiency.
parts.answer: Higher pay has worked so far (labour cost per pair fell), but further rises may give diminishing returns; investment in equipment, training and better methods may be better next steps.
parts.working: Arguments for/against: For: productivity rose ~22 % and labour cost per pair fell from Rs 120 to Rs 115; lower absenteeism; team bonus links pay to output. Against: Herzberg – pay is a hygiene factor, further rises may not motivate; cost increases if output does not rise; other routes – training, new machines, better layout, lean methods, quality improvements; part of gain may be from bonus not wage. Judgement: e.g. not the best next step on its own – combine performance-related pay with capital investment and training. stem: Basmati Gold Mills sells 400,000 kg of rice a year in 50 kg sacks to wholesalers at Rs 300 per kg; paddy and processing inputs cost Rs 260 per kg. stem:
A school is building a new science laboratory. The activities are (durations in weeks):
A: 4 weeks, starts at once
B: 6 weeks, starts at once
C: 3 weeks, after A
D: 5 weeks, after A
E: 4 weeks, after B and C
F: 2 weeks, after D and E

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the critical path and the minimum time needed to complete the project.
parts.answer: Critical path A-C-E-F; 13 weeks
parts.working: Paths: A-D-F = 11; A-C-E-F = 13; B-E-F = 12 M1; critical path A-C-E-F, 13 weeks A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total float of activity B and activity D.
parts.answer: B: 1 week; D: 2 weeks
parts.working: Total float = LFT − duration − EST. B: LFT 7 − 6 − 0 = 1 B1; D: LFT 11 − 5 − 4 = 2 B1.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the term 'enterprise resource planning (ERP)'.
parts.answer: A single computer software system that integrates all a business's functions – purchasing, inventory, production, finance, HR, sales – using one shared database so information flows between departments in real time.
parts.working: 1 mark: software/IT system; 1 mark: integrates/links different functions/departments; 1 mark: shared data in real time/example of use.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one cost of introducing ERP for a small manufacturing business.
parts.answer: Buying the licences and paying consultants to set up the system is expensive, and staff must be trained, so output may fall while they learn – a large cost relative to a small firm's budget.
parts.working: 1 mark: cost (software, hardware, consultants, training, disruption); 1 mark: application to small firm; 1 mark: development.

stem:
Part of a network for opening a new restaurant (durations in days):
Activity P: duration 5, EST 0, LFT 9.
Activity Q: duration 4, EST 3, LFT 7.
Activity R: duration 6, EST 5, LFT 14.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total float for each activity.
parts.answer: P 4 days; Q 0 days; R 3 days
parts.working: Total float = LFT − duration − EST: P 9 − 5 − 0 = 4; Q 7 − 4 − 3 = 0; R 14 − 6 − 5 = 3 (B1 each).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which of these activities is on the critical path and explain why.
parts.answer: Q, because its total float is zero, so any delay to it delays the whole project.
parts.working: 1 mark: Q; 1 mark: zero float/any delay delays project completion.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
TechNest is installing a new IT network in an office building. Activities (durations in days):
A: 3 days, starts at once
B: 5 days, starts at once
C: 4 days, after A
D: 6 days, after A
E: 2 days, after B and C
F: 5 days, after C
G: 3 days, after D and E and F

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the earliest start time (EST) and latest finish time (LFT) for each activity.
parts.answer: A: EST 0, LFT 3; B: EST 0, LFT 10; C: EST 3, LFT 7; D: EST 3, LFT 12; E: EST 7, LFT 12; F: EST 7, LFT 12; G: EST 12, LFT 15
parts.working: Forward pass for EST (take the largest EFT of predecessors), backward pass for LFT (smallest LST of successors). 4 marks all correct; 3 marks for 5–6 activities correct; 2 marks for 3–4; 1 mark for a correct method shown.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the critical path and the project duration.
parts.answer: A-C-F-G; 15 days
parts.working: B1 path, B1 duration.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Activity E is delayed by 4 days. State the effect on the project and explain why.
parts.answer: The project is delayed by 1 day(s), to 16 days, because E has only 3 days of total float.
parts.working: E's total float = 12 − 2 − 7 = 3 days B1; delay beyond float delays project by 1 day B1.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Expo Events is organising a five-day international textile trade fair in Karachi with 400 exhibitors. Analyse two limitations of using critical path analysis to plan this project.
parts.answer: e.g. (1) durations are estimates – visa approvals for foreign exhibitors and customs clearance of display goods are uncertain, so the plan may be unrealistic; (2) CPA does not guarantee that resources (staff, contractors) are available or that work is done to the right quality.
parts.working: Content points (any two developed): estimated durations may be inaccurate; complex network with many activities; does not ensure resources available/cost; does not guarantee quality; external factors (security, weather, visas); needs constant updating; training/software cost. Level 2 (5–8): two points, each analysed with a developed chain of reasoning and applied to the context (top of band: both points fully developed and in context). Level 1 (1–4): knowledge of relevant points, with limited application or simple statements of effect. 0: no creditable content.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Stitch & Style exports garments to European fashion retailers, who now change orders at short notice. Analyse how an enterprise resource planning (ERP) system could help Stitch & Style respond to these changes.
parts.answer: e.g. (1) a changed order is instantly visible to purchasing and production, so fabric orders and production schedules are updated automatically, cutting lead times; (2) real-time data on capacity and inventory lets managers tell customers quickly and accurately whether a new delivery date is possible, improving customer service.
parts.working: Content points (any two developed): integrated real-time information; automatic adjustment of material requirements and schedules; better capacity planning; accurate delivery dates; reduced inventory and waste; costing of changes/pricing; links with suppliers and customers. Level 2 (5–8): two points, each analysed with a developed chain of reasoning and applied to the context (top of band: both points fully developed and in context). Level 1 (1–4): knowledge of relevant points, with limited application or simple statements of effect. 0: no creditable content.

stem:
BuildPro is fitting out a new shop. Activities (durations in days):
A: 5 days, starts at once
B: 3 days, starts at once
C: 6 days, after A
D: 4 days, after B
E: 3 days, after C and D
Some activities can be shortened by employing extra workers: A by up to 1 day at Rs 40,000 per day; C by up to 3 days at Rs 25,000 per day; D by up to 2 days at Rs 15,000 per day; E by up to 1 day at Rs 60,000 per day. The client will pay BuildPro a bonus of Rs 80,000 if the shop is ready 2 days early.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the critical path and the project duration.
parts.answer: A-C-E; 14 days
parts.working: Paths A-C-E = 14, B-D-E = 10 M1; A-C-E, 14 days A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the cheapest way to finish the project in 12 days, and whether it is worth doing to earn the bonus.
parts.answer: Shorten C by 2 days at a cost of Rs 50,000; B-D-E (10 days) is still not critical; net gain Rs 30,000, so it is worth doing.
parts.working: Only critical activities need shortening, so D is not considered M1; cheapest critical activity is C at Rs 25,000/day → 2 days = Rs 50,000 A1; bonus 80,000 − 50,000 = Rs 30,000 gain, worth doing A1.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Al-Hamd Foods is building a new frozen-food factory and wants it to open before the summer season. Activities (durations in weeks):
A: obtain planning approval, 2, starts at once
B: build factory shell, 6, after A
C: order freezing equipment from Italy, 4, after A
D: install electrics and cold rooms, 8, after B
E: ship equipment to Pakistan, 5, after C
F: install and test equipment, 3, after D and E
G: train staff, 2, after F
The managing director says, 'Now we have a critical path, the factory will open on time.' Shipping times from Italy have varied by up to 6 weeks in the past year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the minimum project duration and the total float of activities C and E.
parts.answer: 21 weeks; C float 5 weeks; E float 5 weeks
parts.working: Critical path A-B-D-F-G = 2+6+8+3+2 = 21 weeks M1 A1; C: LFT 11 − 4 − 2 = 5 B1; E: LFT 16 − 5 − 6 = 5 B1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate the managing director's view that critical path analysis will ensure the factory opens on time.
parts.answer: CPA helps planning but cannot ensure completion: the equipment route has only 5 weeks' float and shipping varies by up to 6 weeks; approvals, weather and contractor problems may also delay critical activities.
parts.working: Arguments for/against: For: shows critical activities (A, B, D, F, G) to monitor; shows float of 5 weeks on C/E so the shipping risk is mostly covered; helps schedule resources and identify where to add resources. Against: durations are estimates; shipping delay of 6 weeks plus any customs delay could exceed the float; planning approval depends on government; CPA does not manage quality or costs; plan must be updated and managed actively. Judgement: e.g. CPA improves the chance of opening on time but does not ensure it; needs contingency planning and close monitoring of the critical path. Level 3 (9–12): a supported, contextual judgement that weighs the arguments (e.g. 'it depends on…'), built on developed analysis of both sides. Level 2 (5–8): developed analysis applied to the context, with at most a simple or unsupported judgement. Level 1 (1–4): knowledge and limited application; points listed, not developed. 0: no creditable content.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Heritage Woodcraft exports furniture to 14 countries. Orders, inventory and production are recorded on separate spreadsheets, and orders are often delivered late. An ERP system would cost Rs 36 million to install. It is expected to reduce inventory-holding costs by Rs 9 million a year and administrative staff costs by Rs 7.50 million a year. Licence and support fees would be Rs 4.50 million a year. The firm has 220 employees and many have limited computer skills.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the payback period of the ERP system in years and months.
parts.answer: 3 years 0 months
parts.working: Annual net saving = 9 + 7.5 − 4.5 = Rs 12m M1 A1; payback = 36 ÷ 12 = 3.0 years M1 = 3 years 0 months A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate whether Heritage Woodcraft should introduce the ERP system.
parts.answer: Likely yes: a 3-year payback plus less tangible benefits (on-time delivery, better information) – provided training and implementation are well managed.
parts.working: Arguments for/against: For: 3-year payback; integrated data stops late deliveries (customer satisfaction across 14 countries); better inventory control; accurate costing. Against: estimates may be optimistic; staff with limited computer skills – training cost and resistance; implementation problems may disrupt orders; Rs 36m opportunity cost; ongoing fees; might start with cheaper modules. Judgement: e.g. introduce, phased, with strong training; the benefits beyond cost savings make it strategic. Level 3 (9–12): a supported, contextual judgement that weighs the arguments (e.g. 'it depends on…'), built on developed analysis of both sides. Level 2 (5–8): developed analysis applied to the context, with at most a simple or unsupported judgement. Level 1 (1–4): knowledge and limited application; points listed, not developed. 0: no creditable content.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Al-Shifa Pharma Group (an invented company) has three businesses: a medicine factory, a distribution company and 85 pharmacies.
Timeline:
2020: Each business has its own IT system; monthly stock counts done by hand in pharmacies.
2022: Two-week shortage of a popular children's medicine although the factory had 3 months' stock in its warehouse.
2023: The factory installs ERP; production planning improves.
2024: The drug regulator requires every medicine pack to be tracked by barcode from factory to patient by 2027.
2025: Distribution company loses a contract with a hospital chain after repeated late deliveries.
Appendix 1: factory inventory days 2022: 95; 2025: 60. Pharmacy stock-outs per month (all branches): 2022: 410; 2025: 380.
Appendix 2: extending ERP to the whole group would cost Rs 450 million over 2 years; group profit 2025: Rs 600 million.
Appendix 3: many pharmacy staff are part-time and staff turnover is 35 %.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Advise the directors of Al-Shifa Pharma Group whether to extend ERP to the whole group.
parts.answer: Likely recommendation: extend ERP group-wide, phased, because the regulator's tracking rule and supply chain failures require integrated information; manage cost and training risk.
parts.working: Points to use: ERP in factory cut inventory days 95 → 60 but pharmacy stock-outs barely fell (410 → 380) – the problem is lack of integration between businesses; 2022 shortage shows information gap; regulator's 2027 barcode tracking makes integration almost compulsory; lost hospital contract – distribution delays; cost Rs 450m = 75 % of one year's profit – finance and opportunity cost; staff turnover 35 % and part-time staff – training difficulty; phased roll-out reduces risk; alternatives (simpler barcode system). Judgement: Clear recommendation with conditions and timing to meet 2027 deadline. Level 5 (17–20): developed, evidence-based evaluation throughout, using several pieces of case data, leading to a justified overall judgement/recommendation for this business. Level 4 (13–16): developed evaluation of several points, judgement supported but less complete. Level 3 (9–12): developed analysis using case data, with some evaluative comment. Level 2 (5–8): limited analysis with some application. Level 1 (1–4): knowledge only. 0: no creditable content.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A television company is producing a 6-episode drama. Activities (durations in weeks):
A: 4 weeks, starts at once
B: 3 weeks, starts at once
C: 5 weeks, after A
D: 7 weeks, after B
E: 6 weeks, after C
F: 2 weeks, after D
G: 3 weeks, after E and F

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the project duration and the total float of activities B, D and F.
parts.answer: 18 weeks; B, D and F each have 3 weeks' float
parts.working: Paths: A-C-E-G = 4+5+6+3 = 18; B-D-F-G = 3+7+2+3 = 15 M1; duration 18 weeks A1; B, D, F all on the non-critical path with float 18 − 15 = 3 weeks A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Activity B is delayed by 2 weeks and activity F then takes 3 weeks longer than planned. Calculate the new project duration and state the new critical path.
parts.answer: 20 weeks; new critical path B-D-F-G
parts.working: B-D-F-G becomes 5 + 7 + 5 + 3 = 20 weeks M1, longer than A-C-E-G (18) A1; project 20 weeks, critical path B-D-F-G A1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the float of an activity is shared with other activities on the same path.
parts.answer: The float belongs to the whole non-critical path: if B uses 2 weeks of it, only 1 week is left for D and F, because they follow B in sequence.
parts.working: 1 mark: float is on the path/sequence; 1 mark: using it earlier reduces float for later activities (example).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Seaview Hotel in Karachi has 120 rooms. In June (30 days) it sold 2,592 room-nights.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Seaview Hotel's capacity utilisation in June.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one way Seaview Hotel could increase its capacity utilisation in June.
parts.answer: Offer discounted packages to local families or companies for conferences during the quieter month of June, filling rooms that would otherwise be empty.
parts.working: 1 mark: method (promotions/price discounts, new market segments, events, partnerships with travel agents, reduce capacity); 1 mark: application; 1 mark: development.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term 'outsourcing'.
parts.answer: Using another business (a third party) to carry out a task or produce a part of the product that was, or could be, done within the business.
parts.working: 1 mark: using an external business/third party; 1 mark: for an activity previously done or able to be done in-house.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one disadvantage for a private school of outsourcing its payroll.
parts.answer: The school loses direct control of a sensitive task; if the payroll firm makes errors or pays late, teachers' motivation falls and confidential salary data may be at risk.
parts.working: 1 mark: disadvantage (loss of control, quality/reliability, confidentiality, dependence, cost of contract); 1 mark: application; 1 mark: development.

stem: QuickPrint has fixed costs of Rs 4,800,000 a month and a maximum capacity of 20,000 print jobs a month. It currently completes 12,000 jobs a month.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the fixed cost per job at the current output and at an output of 16,000 jobs.
parts.answer: Rs 400 and Rs 300

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the capacity utilisation at each of these outputs.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why higher capacity utilisation can improve QuickPrint's competitiveness.
parts.answer: Fixed costs are spread over more jobs, so unit cost falls (from Rs 400 to Rs 300 fixed cost per job); QuickPrint can cut prices or earn a higher margin than rivals.
parts.working: 1 mark: fixed costs spread over more output; 1 mark: lower unit cost (using data); 1 mark: lower prices/higher margin → competitiveness.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Fresh Pack makes cardboard boxes. It made 13,500 boxes last week, when its capacity utilisation was 75 %.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Fresh Pack's maximum weekly capacity.
parts.answer: 18,000 boxes

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the extra output needed each week to reach 90 % capacity utilisation.
parts.answer: 2,700 boxes

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain the term 'excess capacity'.
parts.answer: Excess capacity exists when a business's actual output is below its maximum possible output, so some resources (machines, staff, space) are under-used.
parts.working: 1 mark: output below maximum/capacity; 1 mark: resources under-used; 1 mark: consequence (higher unit fixed costs) or example.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Wheels Up makes bicycles. It needs 10,000 saddles a year. Making them itself would need a new machine and a supervisor, adding fixed costs of Rs 1,500,000 a year, with variable costs of Rs 640 per saddle. A supplier in China offers to supply the saddles for Rs 760 each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the annual cost of making the saddles and of buying them in, and state which is cheaper.
parts.answer: Make Rs 7,900,000; buy Rs 7,600,000; buying in is cheaper by Rs 300,000.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of saddles a year above which making them would be cheaper.
parts.answer: Above 12,500 saddles

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one non-financial factor Wheels Up should consider before outsourcing the saddles.
parts.answer: Quality and reliability of the Chinese supplier: late shipments would stop bicycle assembly, and poor saddles would harm Wheels Up's brand.
parts.working: 1 mark: factor (quality, reliability/lead time, control, confidentiality of designs, effect on employees, exchange rate risk); 1 mark: application; 1 mark: development.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: StarScreen owns a six-screen cinema in Faisalabad. On weekday afternoons, only 15 % of seats are sold. Analyse two ways StarScreen could increase its capacity utilisation.
parts.answer: e.g. (1) lower weekday afternoon prices or student/senior discounts – the extra revenue from otherwise empty seats adds to contribution because costs are mostly fixed; (2) use screens for other purposes – school film trips, corporate presentations, live sports or gaming events.
parts.working: Content points (any two developed): off-peak price discrimination; new segments (schools, seniors); alternative uses (events, conferences, gaming); promotions/loyalty schemes; partnerships; reduce capacity at off-peak (close screens) to cut costs. Level 2 (5–8): two points, each analysed with a developed chain of reasoning and applied to the context (top of band: both points fully developed and in context). Level 1 (1–4): knowledge of relevant points, with limited application or simple statements of effect. 0: no creditable content.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Indus Air is a domestic airline that prepares its own in-flight meals in a kitchen at Karachi airport. Analyse two benefits to Indus Air of outsourcing its in-flight catering to a specialist catering company.
parts.answer: e.g. (1) the specialist has economies of scale from serving many airlines, so cost per meal may fall and Indus Air avoids the fixed costs of its kitchen; (2) managers can focus on core activities (flying, safety, customer service), and the airline gains flexibility to change meal numbers with demand.
parts.working: Content points (any two developed): lower cost per meal (specialist's economies of scale); fixed costs become variable; focus on core activities; specialist expertise and quality/hygiene certification; flexibility; frees capital (kitchen space/equipment); less HR management. Level 2 (5–8): two points, each analysed with a developed chain of reasoning and applied to the context (top of band: both points fully developed and in context). Level 1 (1–4): knowledge of relevant points, with limited application or simple statements of effect. 0: no creditable content.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse one way a car manufacturer could be harmed by rationalisation (permanently reducing its capacity).
parts.answer: If it closes a plant and demand later recovers, it cannot meet orders; customers may switch to rivals, and reopening or building capacity takes years and costs more than keeping the plant.
parts.working: Knowledge/application 1–2, analysis 3–5. Content: inability to meet a recovery in demand/lost sales; redundancy costs and lower morale of remaining staff; loss of skilled workers; damage to reputation and community relations. Level 2 (3–5): developed chain of reasoning applied to the context. Level 1 (1–2): knowledge or a simple point with little context.

stem: Royal Ceramics has 3 factories, each with a capacity of 40,000 sinks a year. Total output is 72,000 sinks a year. Each factory has fixed costs of Rs 6 million a year. The directors plan to close one factory and move its output to the other two.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the capacity utilisation before and after the closure.
parts.answer: 60 % before; 90 % after

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the fall in fixed cost per sink, assuming output is unchanged.
parts.answer: Rs 83.33 per sink (from Rs 250 to Rs 166.67)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one risk to Royal Ceramics of operating at the higher capacity utilisation.
parts.answer: With 90 % utilisation there is little spare time for maintenance, so machine breakdowns become more likely and urgent orders cannot be met.
parts.working: 1 mark: risk (no slack for peaks, maintenance, staff stress, quality falls); 1 mark: application; 1 mark: development.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Golden Bakers delivers bread and cakes every morning to 1,500 shops using its own fleet of 35 vans. The fleet costs Rs 54 million a year in fixed costs (drivers' salaries, insurance, depreciation) and Rs 62 per km in fuel and maintenance; the vans travel 1,200,000 km a year. A logistics company offers to make all deliveries for Rs 105 per km. Shops have complained about late deliveries on 8 % of days. The logistics company's contracts are for 3 years; it serves several competing bakeries.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the annual cost of the in-house fleet and the annual saving (or extra cost) if Golden Bakers outsources deliveries.
parts.answer: In-house Rs 128,400,000; outsourced Rs 126,000,000; saving Rs 2,400,000 a year

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate whether Golden Bakers should outsource its deliveries.
parts.answer: Saving is about Rs 2.4m a year (under 2 %), small compared with the risks of losing control of time-critical fresh deliveries; decision depends on service guarantees.
parts.working: Arguments for/against: For: saving Rs 2.4m; specialist may improve punctuality (8 % late now); frees capital (could sell vans); focus on baking. Against: small saving; loss of control over early-morning delivery and freshness; logistics firm serves competitors – priority and confidentiality; 3-year lock-in; drivers' redundancy and morale; drivers may also sell/take orders from shops (customer relationships). Judgement: e.g. only outsource if the contract includes punctuality guarantees and penalties; otherwise improve in-house scheduling. Level 3 (9–12): a supported, contextual judgement that weighs the arguments (e.g. 'it depends on…'), built on developed analysis of both sides. Level 2 (5–8): developed analysis applied to the context, with at most a simple or unsupported judgement. Level 1 (1–4): knowledge and limited application; points listed, not developed. 0: no creditable content.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Elegance Furniture can make 2,400 sofas a year and is working at 96 % capacity utilisation. Sales are forecast to grow by 12 % next year. It can either build an extension (cost Rs 45 million, adding 1,000 sofas of capacity, ready in 10 months) or outsource the extra sofas to a smaller workshop at Rs 6,000 more per sofa than its own variable cost. Elegance has a reputation for high-quality hand-finished sofas.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the forecast demand for next year, and the number of sofas Elegance Furniture would need to outsource if it does not expand.
parts.answer: Demand 2580 sofas; outsource 180 sofas

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the extra cost of outsourcing these sofas for one year.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Evaluate whether Elegance Furniture should outsource production or build an extension.
parts.answer: Short term outsourcing is needed anyway (extension takes 10 months); long term the extension may be better if growth continues, protecting quality.
parts.working: Arguments for/against: Outsource: low extra cost (about Rs 1.08m a year) vs Rs 45m investment; flexible if growth is uncertain; available now. Against: quality/reputation risk for hand-finished sofas; dependence on a small workshop; capacity of workshop. Extension: control over quality; capacity for further growth (but would cut utilisation to about 75 %, raising unit fixed costs); finance needed; 10 months delay. Operating at near 100 % also causes stress and no time for maintenance. Judgement: e.g. outsource in the short term with strict quality checks; build extension if forecasts beyond next year confirm growth. Level 3 (9–12): a supported, contextual judgement that weighs the arguments (e.g. 'it depends on…'), built on developed analysis of both sides. Level 2 (5–8): developed analysis applied to the context, with at most a simple or unsupported judgement. Level 1 (1–4): knowledge and limited application; points listed, not developed. 0: no creditable content.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether high capacity utilisation is always beneficial for a hotel.
parts.answer: High utilisation spreads fixed costs and raises profit, but near 100 % it can reduce service quality, leave no flexibility and wear out facilities; the ideal level is high but below full capacity.
parts.working: Arguments for/against: Benefits: fixed costs per room fall; higher revenue and profit; signals popularity. Problems: staff overworked, lower service quality; no rooms for loyal or high-paying guests; no time for maintenance/refurbishment; may have achieved it through heavy discounts (low profit per room); overbooking. Judgement: e.g. not always – depends on how it is achieved (price), staff capacity and the hotel's positioning. Level 3 (9–12): a supported, contextual judgement that weighs the arguments (e.g. 'it depends on…'), built on developed analysis of both sides. Level 2 (5–8): developed analysis applied to the context, with at most a simple or unsupported judgement. stem:
BrightTech (an invented company) designs and sells smart home devices (doorbells, cameras) in Pakistan and the Middle East.
Timeline:
2021: All devices assembled in BrightTech's own factory in Islamabad; capacity utilisation 55 %.
2022: Outsources assembly of cameras to a Chinese contract manufacturer; closes half its factory.
2023: Also outsources customer support to a call centre in the Philippines.
2024: A batch of 20,000 cameras has a software fault; recall costs Rs 160 million. Customer satisfaction falls.
2025: Brings customer support back in-house; considers outsourcing doorbell assembly too.
Appendix 1: average cost per camera: 2021 Rs 7,800; 2025 Rs 5,900. Gross profit margin: 2021 22 %; 2025 31 %.
Appendix 2: time from new design to product launch: 2021: 9 months; 2025: 14 months.
Appendix 3: customer satisfaction score (out of 10): 2021: 8.1; 2023: 6.4; 2025: 7.2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the effectiveness of BrightTech's outsourcing strategy between 2021 and 2025.
parts.answer: Mixed: outsourcing cut costs (camera cost −24 %, margin up 9 points), but quality, speed to market and customer satisfaction suffered; support outsourcing failed and was reversed.
parts.working: Points to use: Cost per camera down 24 %; gross margin 22 % → 31 %; reduced idle capacity (55 % utilisation) and fixed costs; but recall Rs 160m – loss of quality control; launch time longer (9 → 14 months) – harms competitiveness in fast-moving tech; satisfaction 8.1 → 6.4, partly recovered to 7.2 after reshoring support; strategic core (design, software, customer relationship) should stay in-house; implications for doorbell decision. Judgement: Overall judgement on effectiveness, e.g. effective for cost but not for quality/innovation; outsourcing manufacturing acceptable with stronger quality control, support should stay in-house. Level 5 (17–20): developed, evidence-based evaluation throughout, using several pieces of case data, leading to a justified overall judgement/recommendation for this business. Level 4 (13–16): developed evaluation of several points, judgement supported but less complete. Level 3 (9–12): developed analysis using case data, with some evaluative comment. Level 2 (5–8): limited analysis with some application. Level 1 (1–4): knowledge only. 0: no creditable content.

author: HomiLabs

stem: PrintPoint is a copy shop near a university. Its monthly costs are: rent Rs 150,000; staff salaries Rs 220,000; paper Rs 4 per page; ink and toner Rs 1.5 per page. Its electricity bill has a fixed monthly charge plus a charge for each unit used. Last month it printed 80,000 pages.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate PrintPoint's total cost and average cost per page last month, excluding electricity.
parts.answer: Total cost Rs 810,000; average cost Rs 10.125 (about Rs 10.13) per page

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the term 'semi-variable cost', using PrintPoint's electricity as an example.
parts.answer: A cost with a fixed element that must be paid whatever the output and a variable element that rises with output; PrintPoint pays a fixed monthly charge plus more for each unit used as it prints more.
parts.working: 1 mark: fixed element; 1 mark: variable element that changes with output; 1 mark: application to electricity.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term 'margin of safety'.
parts.answer: The amount by which a business's current (or planned) output or sales exceeds its break-even output.
parts.working: 1 mark: difference between actual/planned output (sales); 1 mark: and break-even output.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why a new gym would want a large margin of safety.
parts.answer: Gym memberships can fall quickly if a rival opens nearby; a large margin of safety means sales can fall a long way before the gym makes a loss, giving time to respond.
parts.working: 1 mark: reason (protection against falling sales/rising costs, reassures lenders); 1 mark: application; 1 mark: development.

stem: Crunchy Bites makes packets of nimko (savoury snacks). Each packet sells for Rs 250 and has variable costs of Rs 140. In May it sold 18,000 packets. Fixed costs are Rs 1,500,000 a month.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Crunchy Bites' total contribution and profit in May.
parts.answer: Total contribution Rs 1,980,000; profit Rs 480,000

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one way the contribution per packet could be useful to Crunchy Bites' managers.
parts.answer: It shows how much each extra packet adds towards fixed costs and profit, so managers can quickly judge whether a special order or price cut will increase profit.
parts.working: 1 mark: use (break-even, special orders, pricing, choosing between products); 1 mark: application; 1 mark: development.

author: HomiLabs

stem: FlexiMat makes yoga mats. When it makes 10,000 mats a month, its total costs are Rs 2,600,000. When it makes 15,000 mats a month, its total costs are Rs 3,400,000. Each mat sells for Rs 260. Assume fixed costs and variable cost per mat stay constant.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate FlexiMat's variable cost per mat and its fixed costs.
parts.answer: Variable cost Rs 160 per mat; fixed costs Rs 1,000,000 a month

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate FlexiMat's break-even output.
parts.answer: 10,000 mats a month

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one reason why FlexiMat's variable cost per mat may not stay constant.
parts.answer: As output grows FlexiMat may get bulk-buying discounts on rubber, so the variable cost per mat falls; or overtime pay at high output may raise it.
parts.working: 1 mark: reason (bulk discounts, overtime, input price changes, waste); 1 mark: application; 1 mark: effect on break-even accuracy.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Westline Clothing makes three products. Monthly data (Rs million):
Shirts: revenue 12.0; variable costs 7.2; share of fixed costs 3.0.
Trousers: revenue 9.0; variable costs 6.3; share of fixed costs 2.25.
Jackets: revenue 5.0; variable costs 4.2; share of fixed costs 1.25.
Fixed costs (Rs 6.5 million) are shared in proportion to revenue and would not change if one product were dropped. The finance director suggests dropping jackets because they make a loss.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the contribution and the profit or loss of each product using these figures.
parts.answer: Shirts: contribution Rs 4.80m, profit Rs 1.80m; Trousers: contribution Rs 2.70m, profit Rs 0.45m; Jackets: contribution Rs 0.80m, profit Rs -0.45m
parts.working: Contribution = revenue − variable costs (B1 for all three); profit = contribution − share of fixed costs (B1); jackets loss of Rs 0.45m shown (B1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate Westline's total monthly profit now and if jackets are dropped.
parts.answer: Now Rs 1.80m; without jackets Rs 1.00m
parts.working: Total profit = 4.8 + 2.7 + 0.8 − 6.5 = Rs 1.80m B1; without jackets 4.8 + 2.7 − 6.5 = Rs 1.00m B1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the finance director's suggestion may be wrong.
parts.answer: Jackets have a positive contribution of Rs 0.8m; the fixed costs remain if they are dropped, so total profit would fall by Rs 0.8m. The loss is only caused by how fixed costs were allocated.
parts.working: 1 mark: jackets make a positive contribution; 1 mark: fixed costs unchanged/reallocated to other products; 1 mark: total profit falls (using data).

author: HomiLabs

stem: SunGlow sells solar lanterns. Fixed costs are Rs 2,400,000 a month, price Rs 1,200 and variable cost Rs 800 per lantern. It sells 9,000 lanterns a month. Next month its rent rises so fixed costs become Rs 2,700,000, and to meet a competitor it will cut its price to Rs 1,150. Sales are expected to stay at 9,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the break-even output before and after the changes.
parts.answer: Before 6,000; after 7,715 lanterns (7,714.3 rounded up)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the margin of safety after the changes as a percentage of sales. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one way SunGlow could restore its margin of safety.
parts.answer: Reduce variable costs, e.g. by negotiating cheaper solar panels from suppliers, which raises contribution per lantern and lowers break-even output.
parts.working: 1 mark: method (raise sales through promotion, reduce VC, reduce FC); 1 mark: application; 1 mark: effect on break-even/margin of safety.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Desert Rose Ceramics makes decorative tiles. Its capacity is 50,000 boxes a month and it currently sells 44,000 boxes a month to its regular customers at Rs 420 a box. Variable cost is Rs 260 a box. A hotel developer in Dubai offers a one-off contract for 10,000 boxes a month for 6 months at Rs 300 a box. To accept, Desert Rose would have to turn away some regular orders. The developer says further contracts are likely if this one goes well.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the change in Desert Rose Ceramics' monthly profit if it accepts the contract.
parts.answer: Profit falls by Rs 240,000 a month
parts.working: Contribution from order = 10,000 × (300 − 260) = Rs 400,000 M1; spare capacity 6,000, so 4,000 regular boxes lost M1; lost contribution = 4,000 × (420 − 260) = Rs 640,000 M1; net change = −Rs 240,000 A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate whether Desert Rose Ceramics should accept the contract.
parts.answer: On the figures, no (profit falls by Rs 240,000 a month), unless future Dubai contracts, export diversification or extra capacity (overtime) change the position; could negotiate a higher price or smaller order.
parts.working: Arguments for/against: Against: lower profit; lost regular customers may not return; price below normal may set expectations. For: entry into an export market; future contracts; diversification; could use overtime/outsourcing to avoid losing regular orders; negotiate price ≥ Rs 324 (break-even price for order including lost contribution: 260 + 640,000 ÷ 10,000). Judgement: e.g. accept only if price is renegotiated to at least about Rs 324 or capacity can be increased; strategic value of future contracts weighed against risk to regular customers. Level 3 (9–12): a supported, contextual judgement that weighs the arguments (e.g. 'it depends on…'), built on developed analysis of both sides. Level 2 (5–8): developed analysis applied to the context, with at most a simple or unsupported judgement. Level 1 (1–4): knowledge and limited application; points listed, not developed. 0: no creditable content.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the usefulness of break-even analysis for a business launching a new food-delivery app.
parts.answer: Useful to show how many orders are needed and to test 'what if' scenarios for investors, but limited because costs and prices are uncertain, demand is hard to forecast and the business may deliberately make losses to gain market share.
parts.working: Arguments for/against: Useful: shows orders needed to cover fixed costs (app development, marketing); margin of safety; supports business plan/loan; what-if analysis of commission rates. Limitations: assumes constant price and VC (discounts, promotions); sales may not equal output; estimates for a new service are uncertain; multi-product/varied order values; growth strategy may accept losses; ignores cash flow timing. Judgement: e.g. useful as a planning tool if regularly updated, but cannot be relied on alone for a fast-changing start-up. Level 3 (9–12): a supported, contextual judgement that weighs the arguments (e.g. 'it depends on…'), built on developed analysis of both sides. Level 2 (5–8): developed analysis applied to the context, with at most a simple or unsupported judgement.
