stem: Al-Madina Traders (Rs million): revenue (all on credit) 80; credit purchases 48; trade receivables at year end 12; trade payables at year end 5.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Al-Madina Traders' days' sales in receivables and its payables days. Give your answers to the nearest day.
parts.answer: Receivables 55 days; payables 38 days
parts.working: Receivables: 12 ÷ 80 × 365 M1 = 54.75 ≈ 55 days A1; payables: 5 ÷ 48 × 365 M1 = 38.02 ≈ 38 days A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the difference between these two figures could cause cash-flow problems.
parts.answer: Al-Madina pays its suppliers after about 38 days but waits about 55 days for customers to pay, so cash goes out about 17 days before it comes in; it may need an overdraft to pay its bills.
parts.working: 1 mark: cash out before cash in (using figures); 1 mark: gap must be financed; 1 mark: consequence (overdraft interest, difficulty paying suppliers/wages).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Hamza Foods plc (an invented company): profit for the year (after tax) Rs 840 million; number of ordinary shares 120 million; current share price Rs 91.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Hamza Foods plc's earnings per share and its price/earnings (P/E) ratio.
parts.answer: EPS Rs 7.00; P/E ratio 13.0

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what a high P/E ratio suggests about investors' views of a company.
parts.answer: Investors are willing to pay many times current earnings for a share, which suggests they expect profits to grow strongly in future (or see the company as low risk).
parts.working: 1 mark: investors pay a high price relative to earnings; 1 mark: expectation of future profit growth/confidence.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Pak Steel Fabricators (Rs million): share capital 150; retained earnings 180; long-term bank loans 270. Most of the loans have variable interest rates.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Pak Steel Fabricators' gearing ratio.
parts.working: Capital employed = 330 + 270 = 600 M1; gearing = 270 ÷ 600 × 100 = 45 % A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one risk to Pak Steel Fabricators of this level of gearing.
parts.answer: As a business with gearing of 45 % and variable-rate loans, a rise in interest rates would increase interest payments, reducing profit and making repayments harder; lenders may refuse further loans, and returns to shareholders become more volatile.
parts.working: 1 mark: risk (higher interest costs, repayment burden, difficulty borrowing more, more volatile shareholder returns); 1 mark: link to 45 % gearing and variable-rate loans; 1 mark: development.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Two private hospitals in the same city (Rs million):
City Care: operating profit 24; revenue 150; capital employed 200.
Medi Hub: operating profit 30; revenue 300; capital employed 160.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the operating profit margin and ROCE for each hospital.
parts.answer: City Care: OPM 16 %, ROCE 12 %; Medi Hub: OPM 10 %, ROCE 18.75 %

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain which hospital is performing better, using your answers.
parts.answer: City Care earns more profit per rupee of revenue (16 % vs 10 %), perhaps from higher-priced specialist services, but Medi Hub uses its capital far more effectively (ROCE 18.75 % vs 12 %); for investors, ROCE is usually the key measure, so Medi Hub performs better, although City Care may have recently invested in new facilities that will raise future revenue.
parts.working: 1 mark: comparison of OPM; 1 mark: comparison of ROCE; 1 mark: judgement with reason (ROCE measures return on all capital); 1 mark: caveat (one year, different services, recent investment).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Lahore Logistics plc has total equity of Rs 400 million and non-current liabilities (loans) of Rs 350 million. It plans to issue new shares worth Rs 150 million and use all the money to repay part of its loans.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the gearing ratio before and after the plan. Give your answers to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: Before 46.7 %; after 26.7 %
parts.working: Before: 350 ÷ 750 × 100 M1 = 46.7 % A1; after: loans 200, equity 550, capital employed still 750 M1; 200 ÷ 750 × 100 = 26.7 % A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one disadvantage to existing shareholders of this plan.
parts.answer: Issuing new shares dilutes ownership and earnings per share – profit is shared among more shares – and existing shareholders may lose some control unless they buy the new shares.
parts.working: 1 mark: disadvantage (dilution of control/EPS, issue costs, share price may fall); 1 mark: application; 1 mark: development.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Bright Homes sells household electrical goods. Data for the year (Rs million): cost of sales 73.0; opening inventory 8.4; closing inventory 11.6. The industry average inventory holding period is 30 days. Bright Homes started stocking a new range of air conditioners just before the year end.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Bright Homes' inventory turnover in times per year and in days. Give answers to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: 7.3 times; 50.0 days

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain whether Bright Homes' inventory management is worse than the industry average.
parts.answer: On the figure, yes: 50 days compared with 30 days means cash is tied up in inventory longer; but the closing inventory was raised by the new air-conditioner range bought just before the year end, so the ratio may overstate the problem.
parts.working: 1 mark: comparison (50 vs 30 days); 1 mark: consequence (cash tied up, storage, obsolescence); 2 marks: qualification using context (seasonal stock-building, new range, one-year data, industry average covers different businesses).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Zainab Textiles has asked its bank for a Rs 30 million, five-year loan to buy new looms. Data from its latest accounts (Rs million): current assets 42 (of which inventory 26); current liabilities 30; operating profit 9; revenue 150; capital employed 120; non-current liabilities 70. Average ratios for the textile industry: current ratio 1.6; acid test 0.9; ROCE 11 %; gearing 40 %. Zainab Textiles has won a five-year contract with a European retailer, starting next year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Zainab Textiles' current ratio, acid test ratio, ROCE and gearing.
parts.answer: Current ratio 1.40; acid test 0.53; ROCE 7.5 %; gearing 58.3 %

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate whether the bank should lend Rs 30 million to Zainab Textiles.
parts.answer: On the ratios alone the loan looks risky (weak liquidity, below-average ROCE, gearing already 58 % and rising to about 67 %), but the European contract could provide reliable future cash flows; the bank could lend with security or conditions.
parts.working: Arguments for/against: Against: acid test 0.53 vs 0.9 – heavy inventory; ROCE 7.5 % vs 11 %; gearing 58.3 % vs 40 %, would rise to (70 + 30) ÷ 150 ≈ 66.7 %; interest cover/ability to repay uncertain. For: five-year European contract gives revenue certainty; new looms may raise efficiency and ROCE; assets (looms) can be security; ratios are historical. Limitations of ratio analysis: one year only, no trend data, window dressing. Judgement: e.g. lend only with security over the looms and evidence of the contract value, or lend a smaller amount. Level 3 (9–12): a supported, contextual judgement that weighs the arguments (e.g. 'it depends on…'), built on developed analysis of both sides. Level 2 (5–8): developed analysis applied to the context, with at most a simple or unsupported judgement. author: HomiLabs

stem: The directors of Metro Malls plc want a return on capital employed of 15 %. Capital employed is Rs 480 million. The company's operating profit margin is 12 %. Last year revenue was Rs 520 million.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the operating profit needed to achieve the target ROCE.
parts.answer: Rs 72 million

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the revenue needed to achieve this operating profit if the operating profit margin stays at 12 %, and the percentage increase in revenue on last year. Give the percentage to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: Revenue Rs 600 million; increase 15.4 %

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one way Metro Malls plc could reach its target ROCE without increasing revenue.
parts.answer: Raise the operating profit margin by cutting costs (e.g. energy-efficient lighting and cooling) or reduce capital employed by selling an under-used property and repaying loans; both raise ROCE.
parts.working: 1 mark: method (raise margin/cut overheads, reduce capital employed by selling unused assets); 1 mark: application; 1 mark: explanation of effect on ROCE.

subtopic: Need for finance and sources of finance

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term 'venture capital'.
parts.answer: Finance provided to new or small, high-risk businesses with growth potential by specialist investors in return for a share of ownership (equity).
parts.working: 1 mark: finance for new/small high-risk/high-growth businesses; 1 mark: in return for shares/part ownership.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one disadvantage for a technology start-up of using venture capital.
parts.answer: The founders must give up a share of ownership and control; venture capitalists may demand a say in decisions and a fast exit, which can push the founders towards strategies they do not want.
parts.working: 1 mark: disadvantage (loss of control/ownership, pressure for high returns, share of future profits); 1 mark: application; 1 mark: development.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Need for finance and sources of finance
stem: Ayesha plans to open a cupcake shop in Hyderabad. She has savings of Rs 600,000 and needs Rs 1.5 million for equipment, shop fitting and opening inventory.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify one external source of finance Ayesha could use.
parts.answer: e.g. bank loan, microfinance loan, investment from family/friends, crowdfunding, government start-up scheme.
parts.working: 1 mark for any valid external source.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the term 'overdraft'.
parts.answer: An arrangement with a bank that lets a business withdraw more money than it has in its current account, up to an agreed limit; interest is paid only on the amount overdrawn, and it is used for short-term needs.
parts.working: 1 mark: withdraw more than in account; 1 mark: up to an agreed limit/flexible; 1 mark: short-term finance/interest on amount used/repayable on demand.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one reason why Ayesha needs finance even after the shop has opened.
parts.answer: She must pay for flour, sugar and staff wages before cupcakes are sold and customers (e.g. offices ordering on credit) pay, so working capital is needed to cover the gap.
parts.working: 1 mark: reason (working capital, unexpected costs, expansion, seasonal dips); 1 mark: application; 1 mark: development.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Need for finance and sources of finance

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term 'microfinance'.
parts.answer: Small loans (and other financial services) provided to people on low incomes, often without security, who cannot get finance from ordinary banks.
parts.working: 1 mark: small loans/financial services; 1 mark: for poor/low-income people or micro-businesses without access to banks/collateral.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one benefit of microfinance for a woman starting a tailoring business in a village.
parts.answer: She can borrow enough to buy a sewing machine without needing property as security, so she can start earning an income that she could not otherwise achieve.
parts.working: 1 mark: benefit (access without collateral, small amounts, support/training, group lending); 1 mark: application; 1 mark: development.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Need for finance and sources of finance
stem: Raza wants to open a mobile-phone repair shop. Start-up needs: tools and equipment Rs 2.4 million; shop fit-out Rs 1.1 million; opening inventory of parts Rs 0.8 million; cash for working capital Rs 0.5 million. Raza has Rs 1.8 million of savings. A bank offers a loan at 18 % interest a year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amount Raza needs to borrow and the interest he would pay in the first year.
parts.answer: Loan Rs 3,000,000; first-year interest Rs 540,000

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why the bank might refuse to lend to Raza.
parts.answer: Raza's business is new and has no trading record, so the bank cannot be sure he can repay; he may also lack assets to offer as security for a Rs 3 million loan.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Need for finance and sources of finance
stem: Speedy Couriers needs a new delivery truck. It can lease the truck for Rs 45,000 a month for 5 years, or buy it for Rs 2,200,000 using a bank loan; the truck would be sold for Rs 400,000 after 5 years. Under the lease, the leasing company pays for all maintenance.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the difference between the total cost of leasing and the net cost of buying over 5 years (ignore interest and maintenance).
parts.answer: Leasing costs Rs 900,000 more

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why Speedy Couriers might still choose to lease the truck.
parts.answer: Leasing avoids a large capital outlay and the loan interest, which the calculation ignores, and maintenance is included, so costs are predictable and cash is kept for working capital.
parts.working: 1 mark: reason (no large outlay, maintenance included, interest on loan ignored, easier upgrade, risk of lower resale value); 1 mark: application; 1 mark: development.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Need for finance and sources of finance

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse one advantage for a family-owned private limited company of using a bank loan rather than selling new shares to outside investors.
parts.answer: The family keeps full ownership and control, because lenders do not get votes; profits do not have to be shared with new shareholders, and interest is a known cost that is tax-deductible.

author: HomiLabs

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Need for finance and sources of finance
stem: FreshMart supermarket made a profit for the year of Rs 18 million. Its policy is to pay 40 % of profit as dividends. It wants to open a new branch costing Rs 15 million, financed internally if possible.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the retained earnings available from this year's profit and the shortfall for the new branch.
parts.answer: Retained Rs 10.80 million; shortfall Rs 4.20 million
parts.working: Dividends = 40 % × 18 = 7.2 M1; retained = 18 − 7.2 = Rs 10.80m A1; shortfall = 15 − 10.8 = Rs 4.20m A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one other internal source of finance FreshMart could use to cover the shortfall.
parts.answer: Reduce inventory levels (better inventory control) to release cash tied up in working capital, or sell an unused asset such as a warehouse; no interest is paid.
parts.working: 1 mark: internal source (sale of assets, sale and leaseback, reducing working capital/inventory, cutting dividends); 1 mark: application; 1 mark: development.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Need for finance and sources of finance
stem: Nadia owns Golden Crust bakery as a sole trader. She wants to buy a refrigerated delivery van costing Rs 3.5 million so she can supply cafés. Her bank offers either a 4-year loan at 17 % interest or an increased overdraft limit at 22 %. Nadia's bakery is profitable but her cash balance falls sharply before Eid each year, when she buys large amounts of ingredients.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether a bank loan or an overdraft is the better way for Nadia to finance the delivery van.
parts.answer: A bank loan is better: the van is a long-term asset, so long-term finance with fixed repayments matches it, is cheaper (17 % vs 22 %) and leaves the overdraft free for her seasonal pre-Eid cash needs.
parts.working: Arguments for/against: Loan: matches long-term asset; lower interest; fixed repayments help planning; but commits her to repayments even if café sales disappoint; may need security (sole trader – unlimited liability, personal assets at risk). Overdraft: flexible and quick, but more expensive, repayable on demand, and would use up the limit needed before Eid; risk of cash crisis. Other options: leasing, hire purchase. Judgement: e.g. bank loan (or lease) for the van; keep overdraft for working capital – depends on certainty of café orders. stem: Indus Pharma plc needs Rs 500 million to build a new factory for cancer medicines. It has total equity of Rs 1,200 million and long-term loans of Rs 800 million. parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Indus Pharma plc's gearing now, and after raising the Rs 500 million by (i) debentures and (ii) new shares. Give answers to 1 decimal place.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term 'variance' in budgeting.
parts.answer: The difference between a budgeted figure and the actual figure.
parts.working: 1 mark: difference; 1 mark: between budgeted and actual result.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one possible cause of an adverse labour cost variance for a construction company.
parts.answer: Heavy rain delayed work, so workers had to be paid overtime to finish on schedule, making labour costs higher than budgeted.
parts.working: 1 mark: cause (overtime, wage rises, inefficiency, more output than planned, unskilled workers); 1 mark: application; 1 mark: development showing why actual > budget.

stem: Kitchen King makes kitchen cabinets. Budget and actual figures for August (Rs): Revenue — budget 4,200,000, actual 4,500,000. Materials — budget 1,600,000, actual 1,750,000. Labour — budget 1,100,000, actual 1,050,000. Overheads — budget 900,000, actual 950,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the variance for each item and state whether each is favourable (F) or adverse (A).
parts.answer: Revenue 300,000 F; materials 150,000 A; labour 50,000 F; overheads 50,000 A
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct variance with F/A.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the budgeted profit, actual profit and profit variance.
parts.answer: Budgeted Rs 600,000; actual Rs 750,000; profit variance Rs 150,000 F
parts.working: Budget 4.2m − 3.6m = Rs 600,000; actual 4.5m − 3.75m = Rs 750,000 B1; variance Rs 150,000 F B1.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term 'incremental budgeting'.
parts.answer: Setting a budget by taking last period's budget (or actual figures) and adding or subtracting a small amount or percentage.
parts.working: 1 mark: based on previous year's budget/figures; 1 mark: adjusted by a small amount/percentage.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one disadvantage of incremental budgeting for a government hospital.
parts.answer: It assumes last year's spending was correct, so wasteful spending continues and money is not moved to departments where patient needs have grown, such as emergency care.
parts.working: 1 mark: disadvantage (inefficiency carried forward, 'use it or lose it', does not reflect changing needs); 1 mark: application; 1 mark: development.

stem: Galaxy Books budgeted sales revenue of Rs 1,800,000 and staff costs of Rs 750,000 for October. Actual sales revenue was Rs 1,620,000 and actual staff costs were Rs 810,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify one purpose of setting budgets.
parts.answer: e.g. planning, controlling costs, coordinating departments, motivating staff with targets, measuring performance.
parts.working: 1 mark for any valid purpose.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the variance for sales revenue and staff costs as a percentage of the budget, stating whether each is favourable or adverse.
parts.answer: Sales 10 % adverse; staff costs 8 % adverse

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one possible link between the two variances.
parts.answer: The shop may have hired extra staff or paid overtime for a book fair that attracted fewer buyers than expected, so costs rose while revenue fell.
parts.working: 1 mark: plausible link; 1 mark: application; 1 mark: development (or recognition that they may be unrelated, e.g. wage rise and new competitor).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Comfy Chairs budgeted to make and sell 8,000 office chairs in the quarter at Rs 2,500 each, with materials Rs 900 per chair, labour Rs 600 per chair and fixed costs of Rs 4,000,000. It actually made and sold 9,000 chairs. Actual results (Rs): revenue 22,050,000; materials 8,460,000; labour 5,310,000; fixed costs 4,150,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the flexed budget profit and the actual profit.
parts.answer: Flexed budget profit Rs 5,000,000; actual profit Rs 4,130,000

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the variance for each item compared with the flexed budget, stating F or A.
parts.answer: Revenue 450,000 A; materials 360,000 A; labour 90,000 F; fixed costs 150,000 A
parts.working: B1 for revenue and materials; B1 for labour and fixed costs; B1 all labelled F/A correctly.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one possible reason for the adverse revenue variance.
parts.answer: Comfy Chairs may have given discounts to win the extra 1,000 chairs of orders, so the average price was Rs 2,450 instead of Rs 2,500.
parts.working: 1 mark: reason (lower price/discounts, sales mix); 1 mark: use of data (average price Rs 2,450); 1 mark: development.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: FitLife runs 18 gyms. Head office sets every gym's budget. Analyse two benefits to FitLife of letting gym managers help set their own budgets (delegated budgeting).
parts.answer: e.g. (1) managers know local conditions – membership trends, local competition – so budgets are more realistic and useful for control; (2) involvement motivates managers (ownership of targets), making them more committed to achieving them.
parts.working: Content points (any two developed): more accurate/realistic budgets from local knowledge; motivation and commitment (Herzberg – responsibility); faster local decisions; develops managers' skills; frees head-office time; better communication. (Risk of padding/slack can be noted for balance.) Level 2 (5–8): two points, each analysed with a developed chain of reasoning and applied to the context (top of band: both points fully developed and in context). Level 1 (1–4): knowledge of relevant points, with limited application or simple statements of effect. 0: no creditable content.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse one reason why a favourable cost variance may not be good news for a textbook publisher.
parts.answer: Printing costs may be under budget because cheaper, lower-quality paper was used; books may fall apart, leading to complaints and lost school orders, so future revenue falls. Or costs were lower simply because fewer books were printed than planned.
parts.working: Knowledge/application 1–2, analysis 3–5. Content: lower quality inputs; lower output/sales than planned (fewer variable costs); delayed spending (e.g. on marketing) that harms future sales; budget may have been set too high (slack). Level 2 (3–5): developed chain of reasoning applied to the context. Level 1 (1–2): knowledge or a simple point with little context.

stem: Shine Car Wash's budget for March showed revenue Rs 4,000,000; labour Rs 2,400,000; other costs Rs 650,000. Actual results gave: revenue variance Rs 250,000 adverse; labour variance Rs 180,000 adverse; other costs variance Rs 40,000 favourable.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the actual labour cost and the actual profit for March.
parts.answer: Actual labour Rs 2,580,000; actual profit Rs 560,000

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the profit variance.
parts.answer: Rs 390,000 adverse

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why Shine Car Wash's managers should investigate the labour variance.
parts.answer: Labour cost rose even though revenue fell, which suggests inefficiency (e.g. too many staff on duty at quiet times or overtime); investigating allows rotas to be changed before next month.
parts.working: 1 mark: labour up while revenue down (data); 1 mark: possible cause; 1 mark: corrective action/control purpose of variance analysis.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Wanderlust Tours organises holiday tours to the northern areas. Bookings depend heavily on weather, road conditions and security news, and last year actual bookings were 35 % below budget in two months.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether budgeting is useful for Wanderlust Tours.
parts.answer: Yes, if budgets are flexible and regularly revised: they still help plan cash, coordinate hotels and transport, and control costs, but fixed budgets based on uncertain forecasts may be misleading and demotivating.
parts.working: Arguments for/against: Useful: planning bookings with hotels/transport; cash planning for seasonal business; cost control and variance analysis; targets for staff; required by lenders. Limitations: uncertain demand – large variances not caused by managers; time spent; inflexible budgets may lead to bad decisions; demotivation if targets unrealistic. Solutions: flexible budgets, rolling budgets, scenario planning. Judgement: e.g. useful if flexible/rolling budgets are used and variances are interpreted with care. Level 3 (9–12): a supported, contextual judgement that weighs the arguments (e.g. 'it depends on…'), built on developed analysis of both sides. Level 2 (5–8): developed analysis applied to the context, with at most a simple or unsupported judgement. Level 1 (1–4): knowledge and limited application; points listed, not developed. 0: no creditable content.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether flexible budgets are more useful than fixed budgets for a fruit juice manufacturer.
parts.answer: For a manufacturer whose output varies with fruit seasons and weather, flexible budgets give fairer comparisons and better cost control; fixed budgets remain useful for overall planning and fixed-cost control.
parts.working: Arguments for/against: Flexible: adjusts cost targets to actual output, so variances reflect efficiency not volume; fairer to managers; useful when output varies (seasonal mango/citrus). Fixed: simpler; useful for fixed costs and overall targets (e.g. marketing budget); sets clear sales targets; flexible budgets take more time and need accurate knowledge of cost behaviour. Judgement: e.g. flexible budgets more useful for production cost control; fixed budgets still needed for planning — use both. Level 3 (9–12): a supported, contextual judgement that weighs the arguments (e.g. 'it depends on…'), built on developed analysis of both sides. Level 2 (5–8): developed analysis applied to the context, with at most a simple or unsupported judgement. Level 1 (1–4): knowledge and limited application; points listed, not developed. 0: no creditable content.

stem: Aroma Candles budgeted to sell 20,000 gift boxes at Rs 1,500 each, with variable cost Rs 900 per box and fixed costs of Rs 7,500,000. The sales manager raised the price to Rs 1,620. Actual sales were 17,000 boxes, variable cost was Rs 930 per box and fixed costs were Rs 7,200,000. The managing director says, 'Profit beat the budget, so the sales manager deserves a bonus.'

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the budgeted profit, the flexed budget profit and the actual profit.
parts.answer: Budget Rs 4,500,000; flexed Rs 2,700,000; actual Rs 4,530,000

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate whether the sales manager deserves a bonus.
parts.answer: Profit beat the original budget by Rs 30,000, but volume was 15 % below budget. The gain came from the higher price (a decision the sales manager influenced) and lower fixed costs (outside his control), partly offset by higher variable costs. A bonus may be justified only if the price rise was his decision and long-term customer loyalty is not harmed; a bonus based on profit alone may reward short-term gains.
parts.working: Arguments for/against: For: actual profit Rs 4,530,000 beats budget Rs 4,500,000; price rise raised contribution per box from Rs 600 to Rs 690 – a successful pricing decision. Against: volume 3,000 boxes below budget (sales variance in units); Rs 300,000 of the gain is from lower fixed costs (not sales); higher VC; market share may be lost to rivals; bonus based on profit alone may encourage short-termism; compare with flexed budget. Judgement: Supported judgement, e.g. partial bonus tied to the pricing decision but with volume/market share targets. Level 3 (9–12): a supported, contextual judgement that weighs the arguments (e.g. 'it depends on…'), built on developed analysis of both sides. Level 2 (5–8): developed analysis applied to the context, with at most a simple or unsupported judgement. Level 1 (1–4): knowledge and limited application; points listed, not developed. 0: no creditable content.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Pure Organics sells organic food. Its budget for the quarter assumed materials would cost 35 % of sales revenue. Budgeted sales revenue was Rs 12.0 million; actual sales revenue was Rs 13.8 million. Actual materials cost was Rs 5.1 million. The purchasing manager says, 'Materials cost more than budgeted only because we sold more.'

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the original budget for materials, the flexed budget for materials, and the materials variance against each.
parts.answer: Original Rs 4,200,000; flexed Rs 4,830,000; variance vs original Rs 900,000 A; vs flexed Rs 270,000 A
parts.working: Original 35 % × 12.0m = Rs 4.2m B1; flexed 35 % × 13.8m = Rs 4.83m B1; variance vs original 5.1 − 4.2 = 0.9m A B1; vs flexed 5.1 − 4.83 = Rs 270,000 A B1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate the purchasing manager's claim.
parts.answer: Partly true: Rs 630,000 of the Rs 900,000 adverse variance is explained by higher sales, but Rs 270,000 (5.6 % above the flexed budget) is not, suggesting higher prices from suppliers, waste, or a sales mix with more costly products.
parts.working: 1 mark: identify that flexing accounts for 630,000; 1 mark: 270,000 remains unexplained; 2 marks: possible causes (supplier price rises for organic produce, wastage/spoilage, mix); 2 marks: judgement – claim only partly correct and further investigation needed.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Shahid Cycles sells bicycles and spare parts. Its figures for the year (Rs): revenue 8,400,000; cost of sales 5,880,000; distribution costs 610,000; administration expenses 540,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Shahid Cycles' gross profit for the year.

parts.label: b

author: HomiLabs

stem: Riverside Mart reports the following for the year (Rs): revenue 9,000,000; cost of sales 5,300,000; distribution costs 1,100,000; administration expenses 1,250,000; interest paid 150,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the operating profit for the year, before interest.
parts.working: Gross profit 9,000,000 − 5,300,000 = 3,700,000 (M1); less distribution costs 1,100,000 and administration expenses 1,250,000 gives 1,350,000 (A1).

parts.label: b

author: HomiLabs

stem: Hafiz Bakers made a profit of Rs 400,000 last year, but its bank balance fell during the year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two reasons why a business can make a profit for the year but still see its bank balance fall.
parts.answer: Any two, each explained, e.g.: customers have not yet paid for credit sales, so the cash is not in the bank; cash has been spent on new non-current assets, which is not an expense in the profit calculation; cash has been used to repay loan capital, which does not appear in profit; cash has been used to build up inventory that has not yet been sold.
parts.working: 1 mark for each of two reasons named (B1 B1); 1 mark for each explanation of why cash is lower than profit (B1 B1).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Kasur Dairy Products reports the following for the year (Rs): revenue 6,300,000; cost of sales 4,032,000; operating expenses 1,134,000; interest paid 90,000; tax 180,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the gross profit margin as a percentage.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the profit for the year after interest and tax, and express it as a percentage of revenue, to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: Profit after interest and tax Rs 864,000; 13.7 % of revenue

author: HomiLabs

stem: Noor Textiles (Rs million). Year 1: operating profit 6.4; equity 25; non-current liabilities (bank loans) 15. Year 2: operating profit 5.6; equity 30; non-current liabilities 22. Capital employed = equity + non-current liabilities.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the return on capital employed (ROCE) for each year, to 1 decimal place.
parts.working: Capital employed = equity + non-current liabilities: Year 1 = 40, Year 2 = 52 (B1); ROCE = operating profit ÷ capital employed × 100: 6.4 ÷ 40 = 16.0 % (B1); 5.6 ÷ 52 = 10.8 % (B1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two reasons why ROCE fell between Year 1 and Year 2.
parts.answer: Any two: the new equity and loans have not yet started earning profit; operating profit fell because of higher costs or lower sales; start-up costs of the expansion were charged in Year 2.
parts.working: 1 mark for each reason, linked to the data (B1 B1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one reason the fall in ROCE may be temporary.
parts.answer: New machinery or capacity may take time to reach full use, so profit and ROCE can rise in later years.
parts.working: 1 mark for the reason; 1 mark for explaining how it would raise profit or reduce capital employed per Rs of profit (M1 A1).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Jade Logistics (Rs). Share capital is 2,000,000 and was unchanged this year. Retained earnings at 1 January were 3,100,000. Profit after tax for the year was 1,400,000 and dividends paid during the year were 600,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the retained earnings at 31 December.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate total equity at 31 December.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one reason the directors might keep more profit in the business rather than paying a larger dividend.
parts.answer: To finance growth or new equipment without taking on more loans, or to build a reserve against future losses.
parts.working: 1 mark for the reason; 1 mark for explaining how retained profit helps the business (B1 B1).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Coral Bakeries has two branches. Last year (Rs '000): North branch revenue 2,500, operating profit 325; South branch revenue 1,900, operating profit 228.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the operating profit margin for each branch, to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: North 13.0 %; South 12.0 %

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one limitation of comparing the two branches using operating profit margin alone.
parts.answer: Any one, explained: the margin ignores how much capital each branch uses, so it does not show efficiency of investment; the branches may face different rents, wages or customers, which the margin hides; margin ignores the size of each branch (North earns more operating profit in total).
parts.working: 1 mark for the limitation; 2 marks for a development linked to the figures (B1 B1).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Ahsan Motors bought a delivery van for Rs 3,000,000 and depreciates it over five years.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how depreciation reduces profit but does not reduce the cash balance in the year it is charged.
parts.answer: Depreciation is deducted as an expense, so profit is lower; no cash leaves the business in that year because the cash was paid when the van was bought; so the cash balance is unaffected by the charge.
parts.working: 1 mark: depreciation is an expense that lowers profit; 1 mark: no cash is paid out when depreciation is charged; 1 mark: the cash outflow took place when the asset was purchased.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Coastal Fresh Seafood (Rs). Year 1: revenue 20,000,000 and gross profit margin 42 %. Year 2: revenue 23,000,000 (15 % higher) and gross profit margin 36 %, after a rise in fish supplier prices and a discount campaign.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the gross profit in Year 1 and Year 2.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the change in gross profit in Rs and state whether it rose or fell.
parts.answer: Fell by Rs 120,000

parts.label: c
parts.text: Analyse why gross profit fell even though revenue rose by 15 %.
parts.answer: Extra revenue of 3,000,000 at the Year 1 margin would add 1,260,000 of gross profit, but the fall in margin from 42 % to 36 % costs 1,380,000 on Year 2 revenue of 23,000,000. Cause: supplier price rises increased cost of sales per unit; discounts cut the selling price. Net effect: gross profit down by 120,000.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks each for two causes linked to the data (supplier price rises; discounting); up to 2 marks for the calculation that the margin fall (1,380,000) outweighs the extra gross profit from volume (1,260,000); 1 mark for a clear conclusion.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Harbour Hotels plc (an invented company) built a new wing. Operating profit rose from Rs 2.0 million to Rs 2.3 million over the same period in which capital employed rose from Rs 10 million to Rs 16 million.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate ROCE for each year, to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: Before: 20.0 %; after: 14.4 %

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate whether the investment in the new wing was successful.
parts.answer: Judgement, e.g.: profit rose by Rs 300,000 (15 %), which is a success in absolute terms; but ROCE fell from 20 % to 14.4 %, because the extra Rs 6 million of capital earned only 5 % (300,000 ÷ 6,000,000). The answer depends on whether the wing's occupancy and prices keep growing, the timing of benefits and the cost of the borrowing used; a reasoned conclusion that the investment was worthwhile only if the return improves.
parts.working: Level 3 (7–8): balanced evaluation linking the fall in ROCE to the 5 % return on the extra capital, with a supported judgement; Level 2 (4–6): identifies the profit rise and the ROCE fall and comments on both; Level 1 (1–3): basic statements without use of the data.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Oasis Furniture (Rs). Gross profit margin is 35 % of revenue. Cost of sales for the year was 7,800,000 and operating expenses were 3,000,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the revenue for the year.
parts.working: Cost of sales is 65 % of revenue (B1): 7,800,000 ÷ 0.65 = 12,000,000 (B1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the operating profit for the year.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the operating profit margin, to 1 decimal place, and comment briefly on what it shows about the control of expenses.
parts.answer: 10.0 %; operating expenses take up 25 % of revenue, leaving a margin of 10 %; a reasoned comment on expense control.
parts.working: 1,200,000 ÷ 12,000,000 × 100 = 10.0 % (B1); a reasoned comment linked to the expense ratio (B1).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Two businesses in the same sector are compared. Business A has a gross profit margin of 48 % and a ROCE of 9 %. Business B has a gross profit margin of 22 % and a ROCE of 18 %.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether profitability ratios, such as gross profit margin and ROCE, give a reliable picture of which business is the better performer.
parts.answer: Level-based essay. Content: gross profit margin shows pricing and control of production costs, while ROCE shows how well capital is used; business B has the higher ROCE (18 % v 9 %) and so uses its capital more efficiently, even with a lower margin, which suggests a high-turnover model; A may be leaning on high prices with slow sales. Limitations: different capital structures and accounting policies, one-off items, inflation, and non-financial factors such as quality and customer loyalty; ratios need trend data and sector comparison. A reasoned conclusion is required.
parts.working: Level 4 (16–20): balanced, sustained evaluation linking both ratios to strategy (e.g. margin versus asset turnover), with limitations and a justified conclusion; Level 3 (11–15): good analysis with some evaluation; Level 2 (6–10): describes both ratios with some explanation; Level 1 (1–5): basic statements.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Bloom Florist (Rs). Opening bank balance on 1 January: 80,000. Forecast: January receipts 310,000 and payments 340,000; February receipts 260,000 and payments 290,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the closing bank balance at the end of January and at the end of February.
parts.answer: January Rs 50,000; February Rs 20,000

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one action the florist could take to avoid a negative balance in February.
parts.answer: Any one, e.g. ask customers to pay a deposit on wedding orders, or arrange a larger overdraft before it is needed.
parts.working: 1 mark for a relevant action; 1 mark for explaining how it increases receipts or delays payments.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Ali runs a small hardware shop with a few regular trade customers and a large stock of paint and tools.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two causes of a cash-flow problem for a small business and suggest one solution for each.
parts.answer: Causes, e.g.: customers paying late on credit sales; too much money tied up in stock; seasonal dip in sales; a large one-off payment such as a tax bill. Solutions, e.g.: tighter credit control; reducing stock; arranging an overdraft in advance; negotiating longer supplier payment terms.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two causes (B1 B1); 1 mark each for a relevant solution matched to its cause (B1 B1).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Hafiz Grocers holds stock worth Rs 2,400,000 at the start of the month and plans to cut it to Rs 1,900,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cash released if the stock is reduced to this level, and state its effect on the cash balance.
parts.answer: Rs 500,000; the cash balance increases by Rs 500,000 as the stock is sold and not replaced.
parts.working: 2,400,000 − 1,900,000 = 500,000 (M1); the cash is released as stock is sold without replacement, so the balance rises (A1).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the terms working capital and trade payables.
parts.answer: Working capital: current assets minus current liabilities, the funds used in day-to-day operations. Trade payables: amounts a business owes to its suppliers for goods or services bought on credit.
parts.working: Working capital: current assets less current liabilities (B1), with its day-to-day purpose (B1); trade payables: amounts owed to suppliers (B1) for goods bought on credit (B1).

stem: Sharma Fashions (Rs) starts April with a bank balance of 150,000. Monthly forecast (receipts; payments): April 420,000; 480,000. May 380,000; 550,000. June 510,000; 460,000. July 470,000; 500,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the closing balance at the end of each month, April to July.
parts.answer: April Rs 90,000; May −Rs 80,000; June −Rs 30,000; July −Rs 60,000

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the first month in which the business needs an overdraft, and suggest one way to avoid or reduce it.
parts.answer: May; any sensible action such as delaying a supplier payment, offering an early-payment discount to customers, or asking for a larger overdraft in advance.
parts.working: 1 mark for May; 1 mark for a relevant action; 1 mark for explaining how it improves the balance.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Mehran Pharma Distributors keeps stock for an average of 45 days before it is sold. Customers take an average of 60 days to pay. The business takes an average of 30 days to pay its suppliers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the length of time, in days, between paying suppliers and receiving cash from customers.
parts.answer: 75 days
parts.working: Inventory days 45 + receivable days 60 − payable days 30 = 75 days (M1 A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the new figure if customers are asked to pay in 45 days instead of 60 days, with the other figures unchanged.
parts.answer: 60 days

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one drawback of asking customers to pay faster.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Zafar Hardware makes all its sales on credit. Annual credit sales are Rs 36,000,000 (use a 365-day year). At present customers pay after 30 days; the owner plans to offer 60 days to attract large builders.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the extra trade receivables the business will carry if the plan goes ahead, to the nearest Rs 1,000.
parts.answer: Rs 2,959,000 (approximately)

parts.label: b
parts.text: State and explain the effect of this plan on working capital and on cash flow.
parts.answer: Working capital rises because receivables are a current asset; cash flow worsens in the short term because cash from sales arrives later; the business may need an overdraft or loan to cover the gap.
parts.working: 1 mark: working capital increases; 1 mark: cash flow is worse as cash arrives later; 1 mark: a need for borrowing to fund the gap.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Gulzar Printers is a small company. Many of its customers pay late, and it holds a large stock of printing paper.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse two ways a business can improve its cash flow without taking on new borrowing.
parts.answer: Any two analysed, e.g.: invoicing quickly and chasing late payers, which brings cash in sooner; negotiating longer supplier payment terms, which delays cash out; reducing stock levels, which frees cash tied up in goods; selling surplus non-current assets, which brings in cash directly.
parts.working: 1 mark for each method named (B1 B1); 1 mark each for analysing how it changes the timing or amount of cash, linked to the context (B1 B1).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Kiran Foods (Rs). Opening bank balance on 1 January: 220,000. January: receipts 690,000; payments 610,000. February: receipts 480,000; payments 720,000. March: receipts 760,000; payments 690,000, plus a loan capital repayment of 50,000 (interest is excluded).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the closing bank balance at the end of January, February and March.
parts.answer: January Rs 300,000; February Rs 60,000; March Rs 80,000

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the lowest closing balance and explain what it shows about the business's liquidity.
parts.answer: Lowest is Rs 60,000 at the end of February; this is a thin buffer, so a small fall in receipts would push the business into overdraft.
parts.working: 1 mark for February and Rs 60,000; 2 marks for an explanation of the thin safety margin and sensitivity to a fall in receipts (B1 B1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Evaluate whether Kiran Foods should arrange an overdraft to protect against this risk, or cut costs, or reschedule the loan repayment.
parts.answer: Judgement, e.g.: an overdraft gives flexible cover but costs interest and can be withdrawn at short notice; cutting costs may harm operations or sales; rescheduling the loan may save cash but can reduce lender confidence. A combination, such as a standby overdraft plus a review of payment timing, is likely to be sensible, with the decision based on the size of the forecast gap and the cost of each option.
parts.working: Level 3 (6–8): evaluates at least two options with the figures (for example the 60,000 February buffer against the 50,000 repayment) and reaches a supported judgement; Level 2 (3–5): describes options with limited use of data; Level 1 (1–2): basic statements.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Crescent Electronics buys components from a supplier. The supplier offers 2 % off the invoice if paid within 10 days; otherwise the full amount is due in 30 days. The business could borrow by overdraft at 14 % a year instead. Use a 365-day year and simple interest.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the implied annual cost of not taking the discount, as a percentage to 1 decimal place.
parts.working: Paying 20 days later costs 2 % of the early amount: 2 ÷ 98 = 2.04 % for 20 days (M1); annualised: 2.04 % × 365 ÷ 20 = 37.2 % (M1 A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate whether the business should take the discount if its only alternative is a bank overdraft at 14 % a year.
parts.answer: Yes, provided the cash is available: paying the invoice early (98 on day 10) instead of 100 on day 30 means borrowing 98 by overdraft for the 20 days, which costs 98 × 14 % × 20 ÷ 365 ≈ Rs 0.75, far less than the Rs 2 discount. Equivalently, the annual cost of not taking the discount (37.2 %) exceeds the overdraft rate (14 %). Judgement should also consider the size of the overdraft limit and whether the bank would allow it.
parts.working: Level 3 (5–6): compares the annualised cost of 37.2 % with the 14 % overdraft, or the Rs 0.75 interest on the 20-day borrowing against the Rs 2 discount, and reaches a supported judgement; Level 2 (3–4): comparison with limited figures; Level 1 (1–2): basic statement.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A retailer's current assets are Rs 4.0 million and its current liabilities are Rs 5.2 million.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by negative working capital, and calculate its amount.
parts.answer: Current liabilities exceed current assets; −Rs 1,200,000
parts.working: Negative working capital means current liabilities are greater than current assets (B1); 4,000,000 − 5,200,000 = −1,200,000 (B1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate whether negative working capital always means that the business faces a liquidity risk.
parts.answer: Balanced judgement, e.g.: it is common in businesses that take cash quickly from customers but pay suppliers later (such as supermarkets or restaurants), so it may pose little risk; but if the cash flow forecast shows shortfalls, the business may be unable to pay debts when due, suppliers may withdraw credit, and banks may refuse to renew facilities. The assessment should consider inventory turnover, the speed of cash receipts, the forecast and the ability to renew borrowing.
parts.working: Level 3 (9–12): balanced evaluation linking negative working capital to the business model (fast cash sales against slower payments) and the forecast, with a reasoned conclusion; Level 2 (5–8): explains the liquidity risk with some evaluation; Level 1 (1–4): descriptive points only.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Bilal Wholesale buys goods on credit worth Rs 14,600,000 a year (use a 365-day year). Its suppliers currently require payment within 30 days.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cash gained if the business negotiates payment in 45 days instead of 30 days.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one benefit and one risk of this change for Bilal Wholesale.
parts.answer: Benefit: cash is kept in the business for longer, which can reduce overdraft use; risk: suppliers may refuse future credit, raise prices or withdraw discounts, which could disrupt supply.
parts.working: 1 mark for the benefit (B1) and 1 mark for its explanation (B1); 1 mark for the risk (B1) and 1 mark for its explanation (B1).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Frozen Delight is buying a cold room for Rs 1,800,000. Expected net cash inflows: Year 1 600,000; Year 2 600,000; Year 3 900,000; Year 4 900,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the payback period, in years and months.
parts.answer: 2 years 8 months (2.67 years)
parts.working: Cumulative inflow after 2 years = 1,200,000 (B1); remaining 600,000 ÷ 900,000 = 0.67 years (M1); 0.67 × 12 = 8 months (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one limitation of using payback to decide on this project.
parts.answer: Payback ignores the cash flows after the payback point, so the Year 4 inflow of 900,000 has no effect on the decision; it also ignores the time value of money.
parts.working: 1 mark for the limitation; 1 mark for linking it to the project data (B1 B1).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the terms payback period and net cash flow.
parts.answer: Payback period: the time taken for a project's cumulative cash inflows to equal its initial investment. Net cash flow: total cash inflows less total cash outflows in a period.
parts.working: Payback: time to recover the initial investment (B1), using cumulative cash flows (B1); net cash flow: inflows minus outflows (B1), for a stated period (B1).

stem: A bakery is buying an oven costing Rs 500,000. Profit after depreciation is 60,000 in Year 1, 70,000 in Year 2, 50,000 in Year 3 and 60,000 in Year 4.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the average annual rate of return (ARR), using the initial cost of the oven as the investment.
parts.working: Total profit 240,000 ÷ 4 years = 60,000 average annual profit (M1); 60,000 ÷ 500,000 × 100 = 12.0 % (M1 A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why ARR can give a misleading picture of an investment.
parts.answer: ARR ignores when the profits arrive, so a profit earned in Year 1 counts the same as one earned in Year 4 and the timing of cash is lost.
parts.working: 1 mark for the point; 1 mark for explaining why it matters.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A business expects to receive Rs 1,000 in three years' time. It uses a discount rate of 5 % a year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the present value of the Rs 1,000, to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what the present value tells the business.
parts.answer: Rs 863.84 is what Rs 1,000 received in three years is worth today at 5 %; the business would be indifferent between Rs 863.84 now and Rs 1,000 in three years.
parts.working: 1 mark for the meaning of present value; 1 mark for linking it to a choice between money now and later.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Harmony Dairy is considering a new processing line costing Rs 5,800,000. Expected net cash inflows: Year 1 2,500,000; Year 2 2,500,000; Year 3 2,000,000. The business uses a discount rate of 8 %. Ignore any residual value.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the net present value (NPV) of the project, to the nearest Rs 1,000.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the NPV decision rule and what this result means for the business.
parts.answer: Accept a project with a positive NPV; the project is expected to add Rs 246,000 in today's value to the business, so on this measure it should go ahead.
parts.working: 1 mark for the rule (accept when NPV is positive); 1 mark for interpreting the result in today's terms.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Sunrise Textiles buys a machine for Rs 800,000 that will last 4 years with no residual value. Depreciation is Rs 200,000 a year. The machine is expected to bring in Rs 350,000 of extra cash each year before depreciation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the extra profit after depreciation each year, and the ARR using the initial cost.
parts.answer: Profit Rs 150,000 a year; ARR 18.75 %

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why depreciation is deducted when calculating ARR but not when calculating payback.
parts.answer: Depreciation is a non-cash allocation of the asset's cost. ARR uses accounting profit, so depreciation is deducted. Payback uses cash flows, and the cash cost was paid when the machine was bought, so depreciation is not counted again.
parts.working: 1 mark: depreciation is non-cash; 1 mark: ARR is based on profit, so it is deducted; 1 mark: payback uses cash flows and the purchase cost, not depreciation.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Two machines each cost Rs 1,200,000. Expected net cash inflows (Rs): Machine X: 500,000; 400,000; 600,000; 500,000. Machine Y: 300,000; 400,000; 500,000; 900,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the payback period for each machine.
parts.answer: Machine X 2.5 years; Machine Y 3.0 years
parts.working: X: cumulative 500,000 then 900,000 after two years; 300,000 of the 600,000 in Year 3 is needed: 2 + 300 ÷ 600 = 2.5 years (M1 A1); Y: cumulative 300,000, 700,000 and 1,200,000 at the end of Year 3, so 3.0 years (M1 A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Recommend one machine using payback only, and explain one weakness of this rule using the data.
parts.answer: Recommend Machine X (shorter payback). Weakness: payback ignores Machine Y's Year 4 inflow of 900,000, which is larger than any of X's later inflows, so it may understate Y's total return.
parts.working: 1 mark for the recommendation; 1 mark for the weakness (cash after payback is ignored); 1 mark for quoting the data (Y earns 900,000 in Year 4).

author: HomiLabs

stem: A transport company is choosing between two long-life projects, a fleet renewal and a depot extension.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two reasons why NPV is usually considered a better appraisal method than payback for long-life projects.
parts.answer: Any two explained: NPV uses all the cash flows over the project's whole life, not just those up to payback; NPV discounts future cash flows to reflect the time value of money; NPV gives a monetary measure of the increase in value to the business; so it reflects returns after the payback point.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two reasons (B1 B1); 1 mark each for a clear explanation (B1 B1).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Summit Engineering must choose one of two projects, each costing Rs 4,000,000. The discount rate is 10 %. Project P: net cash inflows of 1,800,000 in each of Years 1, 2 and 3, plus a residual (scrap) value of 500,000 at the end of Year 3. Project Q: net cash inflows of 1,000,000 in Year 1, 1,600,000 in Year 2 and 2,400,000 in Year 3.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the NPV of Project P and of Project Q, to the nearest Rs 1,000.
parts.answer: Project P: Rs 852,000; Project Q: Rs 35,000

parts.label: b
parts.text: Recommend one project using NPV, and state one assumption on which the decision depends.
parts.answer: Recommend Project P. The decision depends on the Rs 500,000 residual value at the end of Year 3; without it, P's NPV falls by about Rs 376,000 to about Rs 476,000, which is still well above Q's Rs 35,000.
parts.working: 1 mark for the recommendation with the NPVs; 1 mark for naming the residual value assumption; 2 marks for the sensitivity check (500,000 ÷ 1.1³ = 375,657 removed from NPV).

author: HomiLabs

stem: A business is investing Rs 3,000,000 in equipment with a five-year life and no residual value. It uses a discount rate of 10 %.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the annual cash inflow that would give an NPV of exactly zero, using the 5-year discount factor of 3.7908 at 10 %, to the nearest Rs 1,000.
parts.answer: Rs 791,000 (approximately)
parts.working: Required annual inflow × 3.7908 = 3,000,000 (M1); 3,000,000 ÷ 3.7908 = 791,390 (M1); to the nearest Rs 1,000 = Rs 791,000 (A1). Give 1 mark for a correct discount factor method (B1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why this break-even inflow is a useful figure for the business's managers.
parts.answer: It sets a minimum level of yearly cash inflow the project must achieve; managers can compare it with their realistic forecasts to judge the margin of safety and the risk of loss.
parts.working: 1 mark for the meaning of break-even inflow; 2 marks for an explanation of how it is used in decision-making (margin of safety, risk of a negative NPV).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Bright Pack plans a packaging line costing Rs 5,000,000 with a life of 3 years and no residual value. Expected net cash inflows are Rs 2,200,000 a year. The discount rate is 9 %.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the NPV of the project, to the nearest Rs 1,000.
parts.answer: Rs 569,000 (NPV = Rs 568,848 before rounding)
parts.working: Annuity factor for 3 years at 9 % = 2.5313 (or discount factors 0.9174, 0.8417, 0.7722); present value of inflows = 2,200,000 × 2.5313 = Rs 5,568,848 (M1 for the discounting and summing); NPV = 5,568,848 − 5,000,000 = Rs 568,848, to the nearest Rs 1,000 = Rs 569,000 (M1 A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the NPV if annual cash inflows are 10 % lower than forecast.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Evaluate whether the business should go ahead, referring to the sensitivity of the decision.
parts.answer: Judgement, e.g.: the NPV is positive in both cases, but a fall of only about 10.2 % in inflows would make it zero, so the margin of safety is very small; the base NPV rests on a forecast that could easily be wrong; the business should test other scenarios, check costs and the reliability of the forecast, and consider qualitative risks before committing.
parts.working: Level 3 (5–6): uses the sensitivity result (break-even fall of about 10 %) to reach a supported judgement; Level 2 (3–4): comments on the sensitivity with limited use of data; Level 1 (1–2): basic statements.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A family-owned business is considering building a second factory costing Rs 25 million, which would expand its capital employed from Rs 40 million.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether the business should rely on investment appraisal techniques (payback, ARR and NPV) or on qualitative factors when deciding to build the second factory.
parts.answer: Balanced judgement, e.g.: payback, ARR and NPV give measurable comparisons, but each has limitations (payback ignores later cash flows, ARR ignores timing, NPV depends on the discount rate and forecasts); qualitative factors such as family control, staff, market and risk matter for a family firm; a sound decision combines both, with sensitivity testing.
parts.working: Level 3 (9–12): balanced evaluation of the techniques against qualitative factors with a reasoned conclusion; Level 2 (5–8): explains the techniques and some qualitative factors with limited judgement; Level 1 (1–4): descriptive points only.
